metadata.title: Inhomogeneous Kaufman Measures and Diophantine Approximation

extraction_notes.note: Theorem 1.1(ii) is proved by Section 5 with no proof environment (subsections 5.1-5.5, with Lemmas 5.1, 5.3, 5.6, Corollary 5.4 and Remarks 5.2, 5.5 inside). It is one proof node (PP21) with the subsections as steps; since part (i) is proved separately (one sentence citing Lemma 4.2), the two parts of Theorem 1.1 are nested claims ClP1/ClP2.
PP21 ends at 'as required.' after (5.44); the closing Remark 5.7, which restates that (5.44) proves Theorem 1.1(ii), is left outside it.
The sentence stating Jarnik's theorem continues with 'so (3.3)', the paper's own consequence combining Good and Jarnik; equation (3.3) is therefore nested in the external Jarnik node.

The law-of-large-numbers sentence fixing j_0 and the set E (with (4.6)-(4.7)) is typed definition (it introduces E, used throughout) rather than claim; similarly parameter choices (4.1), (4.2), (4.4), (4.5) are typed assumption.

Standard notation (O, o, Vinogradov notation, bold tuples) in the Notation subsection, the narrative subsections 'The new idea' and 'Organisation' (whose figure is omitted in this source), and funding/rights are not nodes.
Theorem 1.4 has no proof of its own; it follows from Theorem 1.9 (divergence) and Theorem 6.5 with Remark 6.6 (convergence), recorded as inferred uses edges.

nodes.name: Badly approximable numbers
nodes.statement: The set of \emph{badly approximable} numbers comprises reals for which the right-hand side cannot be replaced by $o(1)$, i.e. \[ {\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}} = \{ {\alpha} \in \mathbb R: \inf_{n \in \mathbb N} n \| n {\alpha} \| > 0 \}. \]
differentia: the right-hand side cannot be replaced by $o(1)$

nodes.name: Kaufman's measures
nodes.statement: For any $s \in (0,1)$, Kaufman \cite{Kau1980} constructed a probability measure $\mu$ supported on ${\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}$ with the following two properties that are important for applications: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item (Large Frostman dimension) For any interval $I \subseteq [0,1]$, we have \[ \mu(I) \ll_s {\lambda}(I)^s, \] where ${\lambda}$ denotes Lebesgue measure. \item (Polynomial Fourier decay) We have \[ \widehat \mu(\xi) \ll (1 + |\xi|)^{-7/10^4} \qquad (\xi \in \mathbb R). \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For each $s<1$ there is a probability measure on Bad with Frostman exponent $s$ and polynomial Fourier decay.
conclusions: Kaufman \cite{Kau1980} constructed a probability measure $\mu$ supported on ${\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}$

nodes.name: Kaufman measures on Bad_gamma conjecture
nodes.statement: In \cite{PVZZ2022}, it is conjectured that if ${\gamma} \in \mathbb R$ then the set \[ {\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}_{\gamma} = \{ {\alpha} \in \mathbb R: \inf_{n \in \mathbb N} n \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| > 0 \} \] supports a probability measure $\mu$ with the same two essential properties.
nodes.statement_short: For every $\gamma$, the inhomogeneous badly approximable set $\mathbf{Bad}_\gamma$ supports a measure with large Frostman dimension and polynomial Fourier decay.
conclusions: supports a probability measure $\mu$ with the same two essential properties

nodes.name: The set B of doubly badly approximable pairs
nodes.statement: Define \[ \mathcal B = \{ ({\alpha},{\gamma}) \in \mathbb R^2: {\alpha} \in {\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}} \cap {\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}_{\gamma} \}. \]

nodes.name: Inhomogeneous Kaufman measure on B (main theorem)
nodes.statement_short: Some $\eta>0$ works for all $s\in(0,2)$: a probability measure on $\mathcal B$ with Frostman dimension $s$ and Fourier decay exponent $\eta$.
conclusions: there exists a probability measure $\nu$ supported on $\mathcal B$ with the following two properties
nodes.label: MainThm

nodes.name: Large Frostman dimension of nu
nodes.statement: (Large Frostman dimension) For any ball $I$ of radius $r(I)$, we have \begin{equation} \nu(I) \ll_s r(I)^s. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Frostman bound for nu (1.1)
nodes.statement: \nu(I) \ll_s r(I)^s.
nodes.label: Frostman

nodes.name: Polynomial Fourier decay of nu
nodes.statement: (Polynomial Fourier decay) For any ${\boldsymbol{\xi}} \in \mathbb Z^2$, we have \[ \widehat \nu({\boldsymbol{\xi}}) \ll_\eta (1 + \| {\boldsymbol{\xi}} \|_\infty)^{-\eta}. \]

nodes.name: Admissible value of eta
nodes.statement: It will be seen in the proof of Theorem~\ref{MainThm} that we can take $\eta$ to be any positive constant smaller than $1/30$. See Remark~\ref{rem_justification_concrete_eta} following the proof of Theorem~\ref{MainThm}.
nodes.label: rem_concrete_eta

nodes.name: Pollington-Velani-Zafeiropoulos-Zorin lacunary theorem
nodes.statement: Fix a real number $A > 2$, and let $\mu$ be a probability measure supported on $[0,1]$ such that \[ \widehat \mu(\xi) \ll_A (\log |\xi|)^{-A} \qquad (|\xi| \to \infty). \] Let $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers, let ${\delta} \in \mathbb R$, let $\psi: \mathbb N \to [0,1]$, and write $\mathcal W_{\delta}(\psi)$ for the set of ${\beta} \in [0,1]$ such that \[ \| n_t {\beta} - {\delta} \| < \psi(t) \] has infinitely many solutions $t \in \mathbb N$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Then \[ \mu(\mathcal W_{\delta}(\psi)) = \begin{cases} 0, &\text{if } \displaystyle \sum_{t=1}^\infty \psi(t) < \infty \\ \\ 1, &\text{if } \displaystyle \sum_{t=1}^\infty \psi(t) = \infty. \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: Zero-one law for inhomogeneous lacunary approximation, $\mu$-almost surely, for measures with logarithmic Fourier decay.
assumptions: $\mu$ be a probability measure supported on $[0,1]$ such that \[ \widehat \mu(\xi) \ll_A (\log |\xi|)^{-A} \qquad (|\xi| \to \infty). \]
$n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers

nodes.name: Two-dimensional lacunary zero-one law
nodes.statement:
Let $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers, let $A > 2$ be sufficiently large, and let $

Then \[

nodes.statement_short: For $\nu$ on $[0,1]^2$ with logarithmic Fourier decay, $\nu(\mathcal W(\psi))$ is 0 or 1 according as $\sum\psi(t)$ converges or diverges.
assumptions: $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers

$\nu$ be a probability measure supported on $[0,1]^2$ such that \begin{equation} \label{LogDecay} \widehat \nu({\boldsymbol{\xi}}) \ll_A (\log \| {\boldsymbol{\xi}} \|_\infty)^{-A} \qquad (\|{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \|_\infty \to \infty). \end{equation}
nodes.label: LacApprox

nodes.name: Logarithmic Fourier decay condition (1.2)
nodes.statement: \widehat \nu({\boldsymbol{\xi}}) \ll_A (\log \| {\boldsymbol{\xi}} \|_\infty)^{-A} \qquad (\|{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \|_\infty \to \infty).
nodes.label: LogDecay

nodes.name: Lacunary inhomogeneous inequality (1.3)
nodes.statement: \| n_t {\beta} - {\delta} \| \leqslant \psi(t)
nodes.label: LacIneq

nodes.name: Hausdorff dimension
nodes.statement: We write $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal A)$ for the Hausdorff dimension of a Borel set $\mathcal A$, see \cite{Fal2014}.

nodes.name: Mass distribution principle
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a Borel subset of $\mathbb R^n$, for some $n \in \mathbb N$, and suppose $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure supported on $F$. Assume that, for some $\varepsilon >0 $ and some $s > 0$, we have \[ \mu(U) \ll {\mathrm{diam}}(U)^s \] for all Borel sets $U$ such that ${\mathrm{diam}}(U) \leqslant \varepsilon$. Then \[ \mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(F) \geqslant s. \]
assumptions: $F$ be a Borel subset of $\mathbb R^n$
$\mu$ is a Borel probability measure supported on $F$
for some $\varepsilon >0 $ and some $s > 0$, we have \[ \mu(U) \ll {\mathrm{diam}}(U)^s \] for all Borel sets $U$ such that ${\mathrm{diam}}(U) \leqslant \varepsilon$
nodes.label: MDP

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.6
nodes.statement: Combining Theorems \ref{MainThm} and \ref{LacApprox}, and applying the mass distribution principle, delivers the following assertion.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 with the mass distribution principle.

nodes.name: Full-dimensional lacunary inhomogeneous approximation in B
nodes.statement: Let $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers, and let $\psi: \mathbb N \to [0,1]$ with \[ \sum_{t=1}^\infty \psi(t) = \infty. \] Then there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal B$ with $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 2$ such that if $({\beta}, {\delta}) \in \mathcal G$ then the inequality \eqref{LacIneq} has infinitely many solutions $t \in \mathbb N$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\sum\psi(t)$ diverges, a 2-dimensional subset of $\mathcal B$ has infinitely many solutions to $\|n_t\beta-\delta\|\le\psi(t)$.
assumptions: $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers
conclusions: there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal B$ with $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 2$ such that if $({\beta}, {\delta}) \in \mathcal G$ then the inequality \eqref{LacIneq} has infinitely many solutions $t \in \mathbb N$.
nodes.label: LacThm

nodes.name: Chow-Technau lacunary theorem
nodes.statement: Let $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers. Then there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal B$ for which $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 2$ such that if $({\beta}, {\delta}) \in \mathcal G$ then there exist infinitely many $t \in \mathbb N$ such that \[ \| n_t {\beta} - {\delta} \| < \frac{(\log t)^{3 + \varepsilon}}{t}. \]
nodes.statement_short: A 2-dimensional subset of $\mathcal B$ has infinitely many $t$ with $\|n_t\beta-\delta\|<(\log t)^{3+\varepsilon}/t$.
assumptions: $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers
conclusions: there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal B$ for which $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 2$ such that if $({\beta}, {\delta}) \in \mathcal G$ then there exist infinitely many $t \in \mathbb N$ such that \[ \| n_t {\beta} - {\delta} \| < \frac{(\log t)^{3 + \varepsilon}}{t}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.6 via the counting theorem
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{LacThm} follows directly from a more precise counting result, namely Theorem~\ref{CountingThm} below.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce from the counting result Theorem 1.8.

nodes.name: Counting function N(alpha,gamma,psi,N)
nodes.statement: For any $({\alpha},{\gamma}) \in \mathcal B$ and any $N\in\mathbb N$, define \begin{equation} \mathcal N({\alpha},{\gamma},\psi,N) = \# \left\{ t \leqslant N : \| n_t {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| \leqslant \psi(n_t) \right\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Counting function N (1.4)
nodes.statement: \mathcal N({\alpha},{\gamma},\psi,N) = \# \left\{ t \leqslant N : \| n_t {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| \leqslant \psi(n_t) \right\}.
nodes.label: def_cN

nodes.name: Partial sums Psi(N)
nodes.statement: Given $\psi: \mathbb N \to [0,1]$, we write \begin{equation} \Psi(N) = \sum_{t \leqslant N} \psi(n_t). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of Psi(N) (1.5)
nodes.statement: \Psi(N) = \sum_{t \leqslant N} \psi(n_t).
nodes.label: PsiDef

nodes.name: Set R(psi) of pairs with the expected count
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal R(\psi)$ the set of $({\alpha},{\gamma}) \in \mathbb R^2$ for which \begin{equation} \mathcal N({\alpha},{\gamma},\psi,N) = 2\Psi(N) + O(\Psi(N)^{2/3} \left(\log (2+\Psi(N))\right)^3). \end{equation} The implied constant may depend on $({\alpha},{\gamma})$, but not on $N$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic count of lacunary approximations (1.6)
nodes.statement: \mathcal N({\alpha},{\gamma},\psi,N) = 2\Psi(N) + O(\Psi(N)^{2/3} \left(\log (2+\Psi(N))\right)^3).
nodes.label: countlacresult

nodes.name: Counting theorem for lacunary approximation in B
nodes.statement: Let $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers, and let $\psi: \mathbb N \to [0,1]$. Then, $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}} (\mathcal R(\psi) \cap \mathcal B) = 2$.
nodes.statement_short: The set of pairs in $\mathcal B$ obeying the asymptotic count of lacunary approximations has full Hausdorff dimension 2.
assumptions: $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers
nodes.label: CountingThm

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.8
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{CountingThm}, in turn, follows from Theorem \ref{MainThm}, the mass distribution principle, and the following result.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Theorem 1.1, the mass distribution principle and Theorem 1.9.

nodes.name: Asymptotic counting for measures with logarithmic Fourier decay
nodes.statement: Fix $A > 2$, and let $\nu$ be a probability measure supported on $[0,1]^2$ satisfying \eqref{LogDecay}. Let $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers, and let $\psi: \mathbb N \to [0,1]$. Then, \[ \nu(\mathcal R(\psi)) = 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: For $\nu$ with logarithmic Fourier decay, $\nu$-almost every pair satisfies the asymptotic count of lacunary approximations.
assumptions: $\nu$ be a probability measure supported on $[0,1]^2$ satisfying \eqref{LogDecay}
$n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers
nodes.label: GeneralCountingThm

nodes.name: Littlewood's conjecture
nodes.statement: A famous conjecture of Littlewood, from around 1930, asserts that if ${\alpha}, {\beta} \in \mathbb R$ then \[ \inf_{n \in \mathbb N} n \| n {\alpha} \| \cdot \| n {\beta} \| = 0. \]

nodes.name: Pollington-Velani theorem
nodes.statement: Let ${\alpha} \in {\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}$. Then there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq {\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}$ with $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 1$ such that if ${\beta} \in \mathcal G$ then \[ \liminf_{n \to \infty} n(\log n) \| n {\alpha} \| \cdot \| n {\beta} \| \leqslant 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: For badly approximable $\alpha$, a full-dimensional set of badly approximable $\beta$ satisfies Littlewood with a $\log n$ factor.
conclusions: there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq {\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}$ with $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 1$ such that if ${\beta} \in \mathcal G$ then \[ \liminf_{n \to \infty} n(\log n) \| n {\alpha} \| \cdot \| n {\beta} \| \leqslant 1.

nodes.name: The set K
nodes.statement: The assumption that ${\alpha} \in {\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}$ was relaxed to ${\alpha} \in \mathcal K$ in \cite{CZ2021}, where \begin{equation} \mathcal K = \{ {\alpha} \in \mathbb R: \sup \{ k^{-1} \log q_k({\alpha}) \} < \infty \}. \end{equation} Here $q_1({\alpha}), q_2({\alpha}), \ldots$ is the sequence of continued fraction denominators for ${\alpha} \in \mathbb R \setminus \mathbb Q$.

nodes.name: Definition of K (1.7)
nodes.statement: \mathcal K = \{ {\alpha} \in \mathbb R: \sup \{ k^{-1} \log q_k({\alpha}) \} < \infty \}.
nodes.label: Kdef

nodes.name: Chow-Zafeiropoulos theorem
nodes.statement: Let ${\alpha} \in \mathcal K$ and ${\gamma}, {\delta} \in \mathbb R$. Then there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq {\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}$ with $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 1$ such that if ${\beta} \in \mathcal G$ then \begin{equation} \liminf_{n \to \infty} n (\log n) \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| \cdot \| n {\beta} - {\delta} \| \leqslant 1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Fully inhomogeneous Pollington-Velani for $\alpha\in\mathcal K$.
conclusions: there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq {\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}$ with $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 1$ such that if ${\beta} \in \mathcal G$ then \begin{equation} \label{LogThreshold} \liminf_{n \to \infty} n (\log n) \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| \cdot \| n {\beta} - {\delta} \| \leqslant 1. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Inhomogeneous log-threshold Littlewood inequality (1.8)
nodes.statement: \liminf_{n \to \infty} n (\log n) \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| \cdot \| n {\beta} - {\delta} \| \leqslant 1.
nodes.label: LogThreshold

nodes.name: Chow-Technau multiplicative theorem
nodes.statement: Let ${\alpha} \in \mathcal K$ and ${\gamma} \in \mathbb R$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal B$ with $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 2$ such that if ${\beta}, {\delta} \in \mathcal G$ then \[ n \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| \cdot \| n {\beta} - {\delta} \| < \frac{(\log \log n)^{3+\varepsilon}} {\log n} \] has infinitely many solutions $t \in \mathbb N$.
nodes.statement_short: Full-dimensional set in $\mathcal B$ with a fully inhomogeneous multiplicative bound up to $(\log\log n)^{3+\varepsilon}$.
conclusions: there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal B$ with $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 2$ such that if ${\beta}, {\delta} \in \mathcal G$ then \[ n \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| \cdot \| n {\beta} - {\delta} \| < \frac{(\log \log n)^{3+\varepsilon}} {\log n} \] has infinitely many solutions $t \in \mathbb N$.
nodes.label: CTlift

nodes.name: Fully inhomogeneous multiplicative approximation on B
nodes.statement: Let ${\alpha} \in \mathcal K$ and ${\gamma} \in \mathbb R$. Then there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal B$ with $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 2$ such that if $({\beta}, {\delta}) \in \mathcal G$ then \eqref{LogThreshold} holds.
nodes.statement_short: For $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, a 2-dimensional subset of $\mathcal B$ satisfies the fully inhomogeneous $n\log n$ Littlewood bound.
conclusions: there exists $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal B$ with $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal G) = 2$ such that if $({\beta}, {\delta}) \in \mathcal G$ then \eqref{LogThreshold} holds.
nodes.label: MultThm

nodes.name: Multiplicative counting function
nodes.statement: For any ${\beta}, {\delta} \in \mathbb R$ and any $N \in \mathbb N$, write $\widetilde{\mathcal N}(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta,N)$ for the number of positive integers $n \leqslant N$ such that \begin{equation} \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| \cdot \| n {\beta} - {\delta} \| \leqslant \frac{1} {n\log n}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Multiplicative inequality n log n (1.9)
nodes.statement: \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| \cdot \| n {\beta} - {\delta} \| \leqslant \frac{1} {n\log n}.
nodes.label: strong_Littlewood_ie

nodes.name: Set R(alpha,gamma)
nodes.statement: Further, write $\mathcal R({\alpha}, {\gamma})$ for the set of $({\beta}, {\delta}) \in \mathcal G$ such that \[ \widetilde{\mathcal N}(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta,N) \gg \log\log N \] holds for any sufficiently large $N$.

nodes.name: Counting refinement for multiplicative approximation
nodes.statement: Let ${\alpha} \in \mathcal K$ and ${\gamma} \in \mathbb R$. Then \[ \mathrm{dim}_H\mathcal R(\alpha,\gamma) =2. \]
nodes.statement_short: The set $\mathcal R(\alpha,\gamma)$ of pairs with $\gg\log\log N$ good multiplicative approximations has Hausdorff dimension 2.
nodes.label: MultThmQ

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.14
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{MultThmQ} follows from Theorem \ref{MainThm}, the mass distribution principle, and the following result.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Theorem 1.1, the mass distribution principle and Theorem 1.15.

nodes.name: Multiplicative counting for measures with logarithmic Fourier decay
nodes.statement: Fix $A > 2$, and let $\nu$ be a probability measure supported on $[0,1]^2$ satisfying \eqref{LogDecay}. Let ${\alpha} \in \mathcal K$ and ${\gamma} \in \mathbb R$. Then \[ \nu(\mathcal R(\alpha,\gamma)) = 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: For $\nu$ with logarithmic Fourier decay, $\nu(\mathcal R(\alpha,\gamma))=1$.
assumptions: $\nu$ be a probability measure supported on $[0,1]^2$ satisfying \eqref{LogDecay}
nodes.label: GeneralMultThmQ

nodes.name: Lebesgue measure case
nodes.statement: Theorems \ref{GeneralCountingThm} and \ref{GeneralMultThmQ} can be applied with $\nu$ as two-dimensional Lebesgue measure. However, the results obtained in this way were already established in \cite{PVZZ2022}.

nodes.name: Consequences of the Bad_gamma conjecture
nodes.statement: The aforementioned conjecture about ${\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}_{\gamma}$ remains open. Resolving it would have several desirable consequences. Most of these are similar in flavour to the results presented here. In addition, we would find that ${\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}_{\gamma}$ contains a one-dimensional set of normal numbers.

nodes.name: Fourier dimension
nodes.statement: For any Borel set $\mathcal A \subseteq \mathbb R^2$, we write $\mathcal M(\mathcal A)$ for the set of Borel probability measures $\mu$ supported on a compact subset of $\mathcal A$. The \emph{Fourier dimension} of $\mathcal A$ is \[ \mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{F}}(\mathcal A) = \sup \{ s \leqslant 2: \exists \mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal A) \quad \widehat \mu(\xi) \ll_s (1+|{\boldsymbol{\xi}}|)^{-s/2} \: ({\boldsymbol{\xi}} \in \mathbb R^2) \}. \]

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.16
nodes.statement: We have the following direct consequence of Theorem \ref{GeneralCountingThm}.
nodes.statement_short: Direct consequence of Theorem 1.9.

nodes.name: Fourier dimension of the lacunary exceptional set
nodes.statement: Let $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers. Then \[ \mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{F}} ([0,1]^2 \setminus \mathcal R(\psi)) = 0. \]
assumptions: $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ be a lacunary sequence of positive integers

nodes.name: Hausdorff dimension of the lacunary exceptional set
nodes.statement: However, we do not know whether $ \mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}} ([0,1]^2 \setminus \mathcal R(\psi)) < 1.$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.17
nodes.statement: We also have the following direct consequence of Theorem \ref{MainThm}.
nodes.statement_short: Direct consequence of Theorem 1.1.

nodes.name: Fourier dimension of B
nodes.statement: Let $\eta > 0$ be as in Theorem \ref{MainThm}. Then \[ \mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{F}}(\mathcal B) \geqslant 2\eta. \]

nodes.name: Fourier dimension of B at least 1/15
nodes.statement: In view of Remark \ref{rem_concrete_eta}, we have $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{F}}(\mathcal B) \geqslant 1/15$.

nodes.name: B has Hausdorff dimension 2
nodes.statement: We know from Theorem \ref{MainThm} and the mass distribution principle that $\mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal B) = 2$.

nodes.name: Is B a Salem set?
nodes.statement: However, we do not know whether $\mathcal B$ is a Salem set, i.e. whether \[ \mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{F}}(\mathcal B) = \mathrm{dim}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathcal B). \]

nodes.name: Is Bad a Salem set?
nodes.statement: This is likely to be a difficult question to answer, since we do not know the answer to the seemingly simpler question of whether ${\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}}$ is a Salem set.

nodes.name: Integer intervals [M] and [M]_0
nodes.statement: For $M \in \mathbb N$, we write $[M] = \{1,2,\ldots,M\}$ for the set of the positive integers up to $M$ and $[M]_0 = \{0,1,\ldots, M\}$ for the set of non-negative integers up to $M.$

nodes.name: log^+
nodes.statement: We write $\log^+(x) = \log \max \{x, e \}$.

nodes.name: Continued fraction expansion and partial quotients
nodes.statement: Given $\alpha\in [0,1) \setminus \mathbb Q,$ we denote its continued fraction expansion by \[ \alpha = [a_1, a_2, \ldots] = \cfrac{1}{a_1 + \cfrac{1}{a_2 + \dots }}, \] where the {\it partial quotients} $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ are positive integers.

nodes.name: Convergents
nodes.statement: Given any $k \in \mathbb N$, the $k^{\mathrm{th}}$ \emph{convergent} of $\alpha$ is the rational number \[ \frac{p_k}{q_k} = [a_1,\ldots, a_k] = \cfrac{1}{a_1 + \cfrac{1}{ \dots + \cfrac{1}{a_k}}} \, . \] Here the integers $p_k$ and $q_k$ are relatively prime.

nodes.name: Recursive relations for convergents (2.1)
nodes.statement: p_{k+1} = a_{k+1}p_k + p_{k-1}, \quad q_{k+1} = a_{k+1}q_k + q_{k-1} \qquad (k \geqslant 0),
nodes.label: recursive

nodes.name: Approximation by convergents (2.2)
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{2q_k q_{k+1}} < \left| {\alpha} - \frac{p_k}{q_k}\right| < \frac{1}{q_k q_{k+1}} \qquad (k\geqslant 1),
nodes.label: rate

nodes.name: Lower bound for ||q alpha|| with bounded partial quotients
nodes.statement: In particular, if $a_k \leqslant M$ for all $k\geqslant 1,$ then \begin{equation} \| q{\alpha}\| \geqslant \frac{1}{2(M+1)q} \qquad (q\geqslant 1). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Lower bound for badly approximable (2.3)
nodes.statement: \| q{\alpha}\| \geqslant \frac{1}{2(M+1)q} \qquad (q\geqslant 1).
nodes.label: bad_lower_bound

nodes.name: Proof of (2.3)
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose $q, k \in \mathbb N$ with $q_k \leqslant q < q_{k+1}.$ Then $\|q{\alpha}\| \geqslant \|q_k{\alpha}\|$, see \cite[Chapter II.2]{RS1992}. By \eqref{rate}, we have \[ \|q{\alpha}\| \geqslant \|q_k {\alpha}\| \geqslant \frac{1}{2q_{k+1}}. \] Now $q_{k+1} = a_{k+1}q_{k}+q_{k-1} \leqslant (M+1)q,$ whence \eqref{bad_lower_bound} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Best-approximation property of convergents plus (2.2) and the recursion for $q_{k+1}$.

nodes.name: Determinant identity for convergents (2.4)
nodes.statement: p_{k-1}q_k - p_k q_{k-1} = (-1)^{k} \qquad (k\geqslant 1),
nodes.label: pkqk

nodes.name: Mirror continued fraction for q_{k-1}/q_k (2.5)
nodes.statement: \frac{q_{k-1}}{q_k}=[a_k,\dots,a_1] \qquad (k\geqslant 1).
nodes.label: cf_inverse

nodes.name: Size of q_k (2.6)
nodes.statement: 2^{(k-2)/2} \leqslant q_k \leqslant (a_1 + 1)\cdots (a_k +1) \qquad (k\geqslant 1).
nodes.label: q_k_size

nodes.name: Remainders r_k
nodes.statement: The continued fraction expansion of $\alpha$ further gives rise to the sequence of {\it remainders} \begin{equation} r_k = [a_{k+1}, a_{k+2}, \dots] \qquad (k\geqslant 0). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of remainders (2.7)
nodes.statement: r_k = [a_{k+1}, a_{k+2}, \dots] \qquad (k\geqslant 0).
nodes.label: rk_def

nodes.name: alpha in terms of remainders (2.8)
nodes.statement: {\alpha} = \frac{p_k + r_{k}p_{k-1}}{q_k + r_{k}q_{k-1}} \qquad (k\geqslant 1).
nodes.label: relation_remainders

nodes.name: Denominators as functions of partial quotients
nodes.statement: As seen from \eqref{recursive}, the denominator $q_k$ of the $k^{\mathrm{th}}$ convergent of ${\alpha}$ is a function of the first $k$ partial quotients of $\alpha,$ and we shall often stress this dependence by writing \[ q_k = q_k(a_1,\ldots,a_k). \]

nodes.name: Mirror symmetry of q_k (2.9)
nodes.statement: q_k(a_1,\ldots,a_k)=q_k(a_k,\ldots,a_1),
nodes.label: q_k_inverse

nodes.name: Concatenation inequality for q_k (2.10)
nodes.statement: 1 \leqslant \frac{q_{k+\ell}(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{k+\ell})}{q_{k}(a_1,\ldots,a_k) q_{\ell}(a_{k+1},\ldots,a_{k+\ell})} \leqslant 2.
nodes.label: concatenation

nodes.name: Approximation errors D_k
nodes.statement: Moreover, we define the approximation errors \[ D_k = D_k({\alpha}) = q_k {\alpha} - p_k \qquad (k \geqslant 0). \]

nodes.name: Size of D_k (2.11)
nodes.statement: |D_k| \leqslant \frac{1}{q_{k+1}} \qquad (k\geqslant 1).
nodes.label: Dk_size

nodes.name: Endpoint identity (2.12)
nodes.statement: \sum_{i=0}^\infty a_{k+2i} |D_{k+2i-1}| = |D_k| \qquad (k \geqslant 0),
nodes.label: EndpointIdentity

nodes.name: Ostrowski expansion of a real number
nodes.statement: Given an irrational ${\alpha}\in [0,1),$ any ${\gamma} \in [-{\alpha},1-{\alpha})$ can be uniquely written in the form \begin{equation} {\gamma} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty b_{k+1} D_k, \end{equation} where the integers $b_{k+1} = b_{k+1}({\alpha},\gamma), \, k=0,1,\ldots$ satisfy \begin{align*} & 0 \leqslant b_1 \leqslant a_1 - 1, \\ & 0 \leqslant b_{k+1} \leqslant a_{k+1} \quad (k \in \mathbb N), \qquad \text{ and} \\ & b_{k+1} = a_{k+1} \Longrightarrow b_k = 0 \quad (k \in \mathbb N). \end{align*} The expression in \eqref{ostrowski} is called the \emph{Ostrowski expansion} of $\gamma$ with respect to ${\alpha}$, see \cite{BHV, RS1992}.

nodes.name: Ostrowski expansion of gamma (2.13)
nodes.statement: {\gamma} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty b_{k+1} D_k,
nodes.label: ostrowski

nodes.name: Ostrowski expansion of an integer
nodes.statement: For a fixed irrational ${\alpha}\in [0,1),$ any $n\in \mathbb N$ can be uniquely written in the form \begin{equation} n= \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_{k+1} q_k, \end{equation} where $(c_{k+1})_{k\geqslant 0}$ is a sequence of integers such that \begin{align*} & 0 \leqslant c_1 < a_1, \\ & 0 \leqslant c_{k+1} \leqslant a_{k+1} \qquad (k \in \mathbb N), \qquad \text{ and} \\ & c_{k+1} = a_{k+1} \Longrightarrow c_k = 0 \qquad (k \in \mathbb N). \end{align*} The right-hand side of \eqref{Ostrowski_expansion_integers} is called \emph{Ostrowski expansion} of the positive integer $n \in \mathbb N$ with respect to the ${\alpha}\in [0,1) \setminus \mathbb Q.$

nodes.name: Ostrowski expansion of n (2.14)
nodes.statement: n= \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_{k+1} q_k,
nodes.label: Ostrowski_expansion_integers

nodes.name: Ostrowski formula for the inhomogeneous approximation error
nodes.statement: Let ${\alpha} \in [0,1)\setminus \mathbb Q,$ let ${\gamma}\in[-{\alpha},1-{\alpha})$, and suppose ${\gamma}\notin {\alpha}\mathbb Z + \mathbb Z.$ If $n\in\mathbb N$ then, with reference to the expansions \eqref{ostrowski} and \eqref{Ostrowski_expansion_integers}, put \begin{equation} {\delta}_{k+1} = c_{k+1} - b_{k+1} \qquad (k \geqslant 0). \end{equation} Let $m\geqslant 0$ be the smallest integer such that $\delta_{m+1}\neq 0$ and set \[ S = S(n,{\alpha},{\gamma}) = \sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\delta_{k+1}D_k. \] Then \[ \|n{\alpha} -{\gamma}\| = \|S\| = \min\{|S|, 1-|S|\}, \qquad |S| = \mathrm{sgn}(\delta_{m+1}D_m)S. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\|n\alpha-\gamma\|$ is computed from the differences of the Ostrowski digits of $n$ and $\gamma$.
nodes.label: nag

nodes.name: Digit differences delta_k (2.15)
nodes.statement: {\delta}_{k+1} = c_{k+1} - b_{k+1} \qquad (k \geqslant 0).
nodes.label: delta_k_def

nodes.name: Upper bound for the inhomogeneous error with bounded digit differences
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Lemma~\ref{nag}, let us assume in addition that there exists a constant $B>0$ such that $|\delta_k|\leqslant B$ for all $k\in\mathbb N$. Then \[ \|n{\alpha}-{\gamma}\|\leqslant \frac{4 B}{q_m}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bounded Ostrowski digit differences give $\|n\alpha-\gamma\|\le 4B/q_m$.
assumptions: there exists a constant $B>0$ such that $|\delta_k|\leqslant B$ for all $k\in\mathbb N$
nodes.label: cor_nag

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.2
nodes.statement: We will use the inequalities \begin{equation} q_{m+k} \geqslant F_k q_m \quad (m, k \geqslant 0), \qquad \sum_{k=1}^\infty F_k^{-1} < 4, \end{equation} where $F_k$ denotes the $k^{\mathrm{th}}$ Fibonacci number. The latter is a standard fact. For the former, observe from~\eqref{Dk_size} that $|D_k|\leqslant q_{k+1}^{-1}$ for all $k\in\mathbb N$. Furthermore, it follows from~\eqref{recursive} that $q_{k+2}\geqslant q_{k+1}+q_k$ for all $k \geqslant 0$, so we have $q_{m+k} \geqslant F_k q_m$. Together with Lemma~\ref{nag}, the inequalities \eqref{useful} lead to the upper bound \[ \begin{aligned} \|n{\alpha}-{\gamma}\| & = \left\|\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\delta_{k+1}D_k\right\|\leqslant B\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}|D_k|\\ &\leqslant B\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}q_{k+1}^{-1}\leqslant Bq_m^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{F_k} < 4Bq_m^{-1}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Fibonacci growth of $q_k$ bounds $\sum|D_k|$; combine with Lemma 2.1.

nodes.name: Fibonacci inequalities
nodes.statement: We will use the inequalities \begin{equation} q_{m+k} \geqslant F_k q_m \quad (m, k \geqslant 0), \qquad \sum_{k=1}^\infty F_k^{-1} < 4, \end{equation} where $F_k$ denotes the $k^{\mathrm{th}}$ Fibonacci number. The latter is a standard fact.
nodes.statement_short: State the Fibonacci lower bound for $q_{m+k}$ and $\sum 1/F_k<4$.

nodes.name: Fibonacci inequalities (2.16)
nodes.statement: q_{m+k} \geqslant F_k q_m \quad (m, k \geqslant 0), \qquad \sum_{k=1}^\infty F_k^{-1} < 4,
nodes.label: useful

nodes.name: Prove the Fibonacci bound
nodes.statement: For the former, observe from~\eqref{Dk_size} that $|D_k|\leqslant q_{k+1}^{-1}$ for all $k\in\mathbb N$. Furthermore, it follows from~\eqref{recursive} that $q_{k+2}\geqslant q_{k+1}+q_k$ for all $k \geqslant 0$, so we have $q_{m+k} \geqslant F_k q_m$.

nodes.name: Sum the error series
nodes.statement: Together with Lemma~\ref{nag}, the inequalities \eqref{useful} lead to the upper bound \[ \begin{aligned} \|n{\alpha}-{\gamma}\| & = \left\|\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\delta_{k+1}D_k\right\|\leqslant B\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}|D_k|\\ &\leqslant B\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}q_{k+1}^{-1}\leqslant Bq_m^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{F_k} < 4Bq_m^{-1}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 2.1 and sum $B|D_k|$ against Fibonacci numbers.

nodes.name: J-th tail t
nodes.statement: There, given ${\alpha} \in [0,1)\setminus \mathbb Q $ with continued fraction expansion ${\alpha} = [a_1, a_2, \ldots],$ a positive integer $J$ will be fixed and we will need to relate the continued fraction data of ${\alpha}$ with to that of the $J^{\mathrm{th}}$ tail \[ t = [a_{J+1}, a_{J+2}, \ldots]. \]

nodes.name: alpha in terms of the tail t (2.17)
nodes.statement: {\alpha} = \frac{p_J + t p_{J-1}} {q_J + tq_{J-1}} .
nodes.label: alphaoft

nodes.name: Approximation errors of the tail
nodes.statement: With $\alpha, t$ as above, for any $k\geqslant 0$ we have \begin{equation} D_k(t) = - \: \frac{D_{J+k}(\alpha)}{D_{J-1}(\alpha)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The approximation errors of the $J$th tail $t$ are ratios of those of $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Tail approximation errors (2.18)
nodes.statement: D_k(t) = - \: \frac{D_{J+k}(\alpha)}{D_{J-1}(\alpha)}.
nodes.label: DkRelation

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement: We first observe that \begin{equation} D_k({\alpha}) = (-1)^k r_0({\alpha}) r_1({\alpha}) \cdots r_k({\alpha}) \qquad (k\geqslant 0) \end{equation} where $r_k$ are the remainders defined in \eqref{rk_def}. This can be shown via induction. For $k \geqslant 0$, we abbreviate $D_k = D_k({\alpha})$. For $k=0$, we have $D_0 = {\alpha} = r_0.$ Assume that for some $k\geqslant 1$ we have \[ D_i = (-1)^i r_0 r_1 \cdots r_i \qquad (i\leqslant k). \] Then \begin{align*} D_{k+1} &= q_{k+1}{\alpha} - p_{k+1} = a_{k+1}D_{k} + D_{k-1} \\&= (-1)^ka_{k+1}r_0r_1\cdots r_k + (-1)^{k-1}r_0\cdots r_{k-1} \\&= (-1)^{k+1} r_0\ldots r_{k-1} (1- a_{k+1}r_k) \\ &= (-1)^{k+1} r_0\cdots r_{k-1}r_k(r_k^{-1} - a_{k+1}) \\ &= (-1)^{k+1} r_0\cdots r_k r_{k+1}. \end{align*} The definition of $t$ implies that $r_k(t) = r_{J+k}({\alpha})$ for all $k\geqslant 0.$ Together with \eqref{Dk_product}, this gives the desired relation \eqref{DkRelation}.
nodes.statement_short: Induction gives $D_k=(-1)^k r_0\cdots r_k$; the tail's remainders are shifted remainders of $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Product formula for D_k
nodes.statement: We first observe that \begin{equation} D_k({\alpha}) = (-1)^k r_0({\alpha}) r_1({\alpha}) \cdots r_k({\alpha}) \qquad (k\geqslant 0) \end{equation} where $r_k$ are the remainders defined in \eqref{rk_def}. This can be shown via induction.
nodes.statement_short: Claim $D_k=(-1)^k r_0\cdots r_k$, to be shown by induction.

nodes.name: Product formula for D_k (2.19)
nodes.statement: D_k({\alpha}) = (-1)^k r_0({\alpha}) r_1({\alpha}) \cdots r_k({\alpha}) \qquad (k\geqslant 0)
nodes.label: Dk_product

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: For $k \geqslant 0$, we abbreviate $D_k = D_k({\alpha})$. For $k=0$, we have $D_0 = {\alpha} = r_0.$
nodes.statement_short: Check $k=0$: $D_0=\alpha=r_0$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Assume that for some $k\geqslant 1$ we have \[ D_i = (-1)^i r_0 r_1 \cdots r_i \qquad (i\leqslant k). \] Then \begin{align*} D_{k+1} &= q_{k+1}{\alpha} - p_{k+1} = a_{k+1}D_{k} + D_{k-1} \\&= (-1)^ka_{k+1}r_0r_1\cdots r_k + (-1)^{k-1}r_0\cdots r_{k-1} \\&= (-1)^{k+1} r_0\ldots r_{k-1} (1- a_{k+1}r_k) \\ &= (-1)^{k+1} r_0\cdots r_{k-1}r_k(r_k^{-1} - a_{k+1}) \\ &= (-1)^{k+1} r_0\cdots r_k r_{k+1}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Use the recursion $D_{k+1}=a_{k+1}D_k+D_{k-1}$.

nodes.name: Shift the remainders
nodes.statement: The definition of $t$ implies that $r_k(t) = r_{J+k}({\alpha})$ for all $k\geqslant 0.$ Together with \eqref{Dk_product}, this gives the desired relation \eqref{DkRelation}.
nodes.statement_short: Remainders of $t$ are shifted remainders of $\alpha$, giving (2.18).

nodes.name: First derivative test on subintervals
nodes.statement: Let $a,b > 0$, and suppose $F \in C^2([-1,1])$ satisfies \[ |F'(t)| \geqslant a, \quad |F''(t)| \leqslant b \qquad (-1 \leqslant t \leqslant 1). \] Then, for any subinterval $\mathcal I$ of $[-1,1]$, we have \[ \int_{\mathcal I} e(F(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t \ll \frac1a + \frac{b}{a^2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Oscillatory integral over any subinterval bounded by $1/a+b/a^2$ when $|F'|\ge a$, $|F''|\le b$.
nodes.label: lem_ub_nozero_fv

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4
nodes.statement: We denote by $\alpha$ and $\beta$ the endpoints of $\mathcal I$, so that $\mathcal I=[\alpha,\beta]$. Integration by parts yields \[ \begin{aligned} \int_{\mathcal I} e(F(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t &=\int_{\mathcal I} e(F(t))F'(t)\frac{1}{F'(t)} {\,{\rm d}} t=\int_{\mathcal I} \left(\frac{{\,{\rm d}}}{{\,{\rm d}} t} e(F(t)) \right) \frac{1}{2\pi i F'(t)} {\,{\rm d}} t\\ &=\left.\frac{e(F(t))}{2\pi i F'(t)}\right|_{\alpha}^{\beta} + \int_{\mathcal I} e(F(t))\frac{F''(t)}{2\pi i \left(F'(t)\right)^2} {\,{\rm d}} t. \end{aligned} \] Thus, using the triangle inequality, we find that \[ \int_{\mathcal I} e(F(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t \ll \frac{1}{\min_{t\in\mathcal I}\left|F'(t)\right|} + \frac{\max_{t\in\mathcal I}\left|F''(t)\right|}{ \min_{t\in\mathcal I}\left|F'(t)\right|^2}\leqslant \frac1a + \frac{b}{a^2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Integration by parts, then the triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Integration by parts
nodes.statement: We denote by $\alpha$ and $\beta$ the endpoints of $\mathcal I$, so that $\mathcal I=[\alpha,\beta]$. Integration by parts yields \[ \begin{aligned} \int_{\mathcal I} e(F(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t &=\int_{\mathcal I} e(F(t))F'(t)\frac{1}{F'(t)} {\,{\rm d}} t=\int_{\mathcal I} \left(\frac{{\,{\rm d}}}{{\,{\rm d}} t} e(F(t)) \right) \frac{1}{2\pi i F'(t)} {\,{\rm d}} t\\ &=\left.\frac{e(F(t))}{2\pi i F'(t)}\right|_{\alpha}^{\beta} + \int_{\mathcal I} e(F(t))\frac{F''(t)}{2\pi i \left(F'(t)\right)^2} {\,{\rm d}} t. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Name the endpoints and integrate by parts.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement: Thus, using the triangle inequality, we find that \[ \int_{\mathcal I} e(F(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t \ll \frac{1}{\min_{t\in\mathcal I}\left|F'(t)\right|} + \frac{\max_{t\in\mathcal I}\left|F''(t)\right|}{ \min_{t\in\mathcal I}\left|F'(t)\right|^2}\leqslant \frac1a + \frac{b}{a^2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound boundary and integral terms by $1/a$ and $b/a^2$.

nodes.name: Van der Corput-type oscillatory integral estimate
nodes.statement: Let $k \in \mathbb N$ and ${\lambda} > 0$. Let $\mathcal I \subseteq \mathbb R$ be an open interval and suppose $F \in C^k(\mathcal I)$ satisfies $|F^{(k)}(t)| \geqslant {\lambda}$ for all $t\in \mathcal I$. In the case $k = 1$, assume further that $F'$ is monotonic. Then \[ \int_{\mathcal I} e(F(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t \ll_k {\lambda}^{-1/k}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\int e(F)\ll_k\lambda^{-1/k}$ when $|F^{(k)}|\ge\lambda$ (monotone $F'$ if $k=1$).
assumptions: $\mathcal I \subseteq \mathbb R$ be an open interval and suppose $F \in C^k(\mathcal I)$ satisfies $|F^{(k)}(t)| \geqslant {\lambda}$ for all $t\in \mathcal I$
In the case $k = 1$, assume further that $F'$ is monotonic
nodes.label: lem_ub_nozero

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.5
nodes.statement: This follows from \cite[Chapter VIII, \S 1, Proposition 2]{Ste1993}.
nodes.statement_short: Cited from Stein's Harmonic Analysis.

nodes.name: Oscillatory integral with a linear factor in the phase derivative
nodes.statement: Let $m\in\mathbb{N}$, $f\in C^2([0,1])$ and assume that $f''$ has at most $m$ zeros in $[0,1]$. Let $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ be real numbers such that \begin{equation} 0\leqslant a\leqslant mb. \end{equation} Suppose \[ f'(t) = (A t + B) G(t), \] where $A, B \in \mathbb R$ with $A \ne 0$ and \[ |G(t)| \geqslant a, \quad |G'(t)| \leqslant b \qquad (0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1). \] Then, for $0 \leqslant X \leqslant Y \leqslant 1$, we have \begin{equation} \int_X^Y e(f(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t \ll \frac{m b}{a^{3/2} |A|^{1/2}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: If $f'=(At+B)G$ with $|G|\ge a$, $|G'|\le b$, then $\int_X^Y e(f)\ll mb/(a^{3/2}|A|^{1/2})$.
assumptions: $m\in\mathbb{N}$, $f\in C^2([0,1])$ and assume that $f''$ has at most $m$ zeros in $[0,1]$
$a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ be real numbers such that \begin{equation} \label{a_less_than_b} 0\leqslant a\leqslant mb. \end{equation}
f'(t) = (A t + B) G(t), \] where $A, B \in \mathbb R$ with $A \ne 0$ and \[ |G(t)| \geqslant a, \quad |G'(t)| \leqslant b \qquad (0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1).
nodes.label: ExpInt

nodes.name: Equation (2.20)
nodes.statement: 0\leqslant a\leqslant mb.
nodes.label: a_less_than_b

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.6
nodes.statement: First of all, note that the left-hand side of \eqref{lem_ub_zero_result} is trivially bounded above by $1$. Because of this, in the rest of the proof it is enough to consider parameters such that the right-hand side of~\eqref{lem_ub_zero_result} is strictly less than 1, that is \begin{equation} \frac{b}{|A|^{1/2} a^{3/2}} < \frac{1}{m} \cdot \end{equation} Further, note that the right-hand side of~\eqref{lem_ub_zero_result} is decreasing with respect to the parameter $a$. So, without loss of generality, we can assume that \begin{equation} a = \min \{ G(t): 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1 \} = G(x_0) \end{equation} for some $x_0 \in [0,1].$ Define \[ F(x) = f(x-B/A) \qquad (B/A \leqslant x \leqslant 1+B/A). \] Then \[ \int_X^Y e(f(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t = \int_{X+B/A}^{Y+B/A} e(F(x)) {\,{\rm d}} x. \] We compute that \[ F'(x) = A x G(x - B/A), \qquad F''(x) = A G(x - B/A) + A x G'(x - B/A). \] Put $\mathcal I = [X+B/A, Y+B/A]$ and $c = a/(2b)$. For $|x| \leqslant c$, we have \[ |F''(x)| \geqslant |A| (a - cb) = |A|a/2, \] and Lemma~\ref{lem_ub_nozero} yields \[ \int_{\mathcal I \cap [-c,c]} e(F(x)) {\,{\rm d}} x \ll (|A| a)^{-1/2}. \] Next, decompose $\mathcal I \setminus [-c,c]$ into a disjoint union \[ \mathcal I \setminus [-c,c] = \mathcal I_1 \cup \cdots \cup \mathcal I_{m+2} \] of intervals on which $F'$ is monotonic, and consider some $j \in [m+2]$. For all $x\in \mathcal I \setminus [-c, c]$, we have \[ |F'(x)| > |A|ca \gg |A|a^2/b. \] Now Lemma~\ref{lem_ub_nozero} yields \[ \int_{\mathcal I_j} e(F(x)) \mathrm{d}x \ll \frac{b}{|A|a^2}. \] Combining the estimates above and applying~\eqref{rhs_is_small} and \eqref{a_less_than_b}, we conclude that \begin{align*} \int_X^Y e(f(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t &\ll (|A|a)^{-1/2} + (m+2)\frac{b}{|A|a^{2}} \\ &\leqslant \Big(1 + \frac{m+2}{m}\Big) \frac{1}{|A|^{1/2} a^{1/2}} \ll \frac{mb}{|A|^{1/2} a^{3/2}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Shift the zero of $f'$ to the origin; use the second-derivative bound near it and first-derivative bounds on monotone pieces away from it.

nodes.name: Reduce to small right-hand side
nodes.statement: First of all, note that the left-hand side of \eqref{lem_ub_zero_result} is trivially bounded above by $1$. Because of this, in the rest of the proof it is enough to consider parameters such that the right-hand side of~\eqref{lem_ub_zero_result} is strictly less than 1, that is \begin{equation} \frac{b}{|A|^{1/2} a^{3/2}} < \frac{1}{m} \cdot \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Trivial bound by 1 lets us assume (2.22).

nodes.name: Normalise a
nodes.statement: Further, note that the right-hand side of~\eqref{lem_ub_zero_result} is decreasing with respect to the parameter $a$. So, without loss of generality, we can assume that \begin{equation} a = \min \{ G(t): 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1 \} = G(x_0) \end{equation} for some $x_0 \in [0,1].$
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $a$ is the minimum of $G$.

nodes.name: Equation (2.23)
nodes.statement: a = \min \{ G(t): 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1 \} = G(x_0)
nodes.label: a_is_min_g

nodes.name: Translate the phase
nodes.statement: Define \[ F(x) = f(x-B/A) \qquad (B/A \leqslant x \leqslant 1+B/A). \] Then \[ \int_X^Y e(f(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t = \int_{X+B/A}^{Y+B/A} e(F(x)) {\,{\rm d}} x. \] We compute that \[ F'(x) = A x G(x - B/A), \qquad F''(x) = A G(x - B/A) + A x G'(x - B/A). \]
nodes.statement_short: Shift so that $F'(x)=AxG(x-B/A)$.

nodes.name: Near the zero
nodes.statement: Put $\mathcal I = [X+B/A, Y+B/A]$ and $c = a/(2b)$. For $|x| \leqslant c$, we have \[ |F''(x)| \geqslant |A| (a - cb) = |A|a/2, \] and Lemma~\ref{lem_ub_nozero} yields \[ \int_{\mathcal I \cap [-c,c]} e(F(x)) {\,{\rm d}} x \ll (|A| a)^{-1/2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Second-derivative bound and Lemma 2.5 on $[-c,c]$.

nodes.name: Away from the zero
nodes.statement: Next, decompose $\mathcal I \setminus [-c,c]$ into a disjoint union \[ \mathcal I \setminus [-c,c] = \mathcal I_1 \cup \cdots \cup \mathcal I_{m+2} \] of intervals on which $F'$ is monotonic, and consider some $j \in [m+2]$. For all $x\in \mathcal I \setminus [-c, c]$, we have \[ |F'(x)| > |A|ca \gg |A|a^2/b. \] Now Lemma~\ref{lem_ub_nozero} yields \[ \int_{\mathcal I_j} e(F(x)) \mathrm{d}x \ll \frac{b}{|A|a^2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: First-derivative bound and Lemma 2.5 on monotone pieces.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Combining the estimates above and applying~\eqref{rhs_is_small} and \eqref{a_less_than_b}, we conclude that \begin{align*} \int_X^Y e(f(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t &\ll (|A|a)^{-1/2} + (m+2)\frac{b}{|A|a^{2}} \\ &\leqslant \Big(1 + \frac{m+2}{m}\Big) \frac{1}{|A|^{1/2} a^{1/2}} \ll \frac{mb}{|A|^{1/2} a^{3/2}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Sum the estimates using (2.22) and (2.21).

nodes.name: Parameters M and R
nodes.statement: Let $M \geqslant 2$ and $R \geqslant 3$ be integers.

nodes.name: Set F_M of bounded-type numbers
nodes.statement: We write \[ \mathcal F_M = \left\{{\alpha} \in [0,1)\setminus \mathbb Q : 1\leqslant a_k \leqslant M \text{ for all } k \in \mathbb N \right\} \] for the set of irrational numbers ${\alpha}$ in $[0,1)$ whose partial quotients are all bounded above by $M$.

nodes.name: Bad as a union of the sets F_M
nodes.statement: By a standard characterisation of badly approximable numbers, we have \[ {\mathrm{\mathbf{Bad}}} \cap [0,1) = \bigcup_{M=2}^\infty \mathcal F_M. \]

nodes.name: Set O_R(alpha) of periodically constrained inhomogeneous parts
nodes.statement: For ${\alpha} \in \mathbb R \setminus \mathbb Q$, denote by $\mathcal O_{R}({\alpha})$ the set of ${\gamma} \in [-{\alpha},1-{\alpha})$ such that the sequence of digits associated with the Ostrowski expansion of ${\gamma}$ with respect to ${\alpha}$ as in \eqref{ostrowski} satisfies \begin{equation} 1 \leqslant b_k \leqslant a_k-1 \qquad (k \mmod R \in \{0,1\}). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Periodic digit constraint (3.1)
nodes.statement: 1 \leqslant b_k \leqslant a_k-1 \qquad (k \mmod R \in \{0,1\}).
nodes.label: PeriodicConstraint

nodes.name: Set B_{M,R}
nodes.statement: Finally, define \[ \mathcal B_{M,R} = \{ ({\alpha}, {\gamma}) \in \mathbb R^2: {\alpha} \in \mathcal F_M \text{ and } {\gamma} \in \mathcal O_{R}({\alpha}) \}. \]

nodes.name: B_{M,R} is contained in B
nodes.statement: We have $\mathcal B_{M,R} \subseteq \mathcal B$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: Let $({\alpha},{\gamma}) \in \mathcal B_{M,R}$. Let $n\in \mathbb N$, and write \[ n = \sum_{k=0}^K c_{k+1} q_k \asymp q_K \] for the Ostrowski expansion of $n$ with respect to ${\alpha}$. As in Lemma~\ref{nag}, we let $m \geqslant 0$ be minimal such that ${\delta}_{m+1} \ne 0,$ where ${\delta}_k$ is as in \eqref{delta_k_def}. Note from Lemma \ref{nag} that \[ \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| = \min \{ |S|, 1-|S| \}, \] where \[ S = \sum_{k=m}^\infty {\delta}_{k+1} D_m. \] It therefore suffices to find lower bounds for $|S|$ and $1-|S|$. It follows from \cite[Lemma 4.4]{BHV} that there exists some $\ell \leqslant \max\{2, K-m + 1\}$ such that $|S| \geqslant |D_{m+\ell +1}|.$ Since $({\alpha},{\gamma}) \in \mathcal B_{M,R}$ implies that $m \leqslant K + R$, this gives \[ |S| \geqslant |D_{m+1+\ell}| \gg \min \{ q_m^{-1}, q_K^{-1} \} \gg q_K^{-1} \gg n^{-1}. \] Regarding $1-|S|,$ it is shown in \cite[Lemma 4.5]{BHV} that for some positive integer $L \leqslant K+2$, \[ 1 - |S| \geqslant |D_L| \gg q_L^{-1} \gg n^{-1}. \] Combining, we deduce that \[ \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| \gg n^{-1}, \] where the implied constant depends at most on $M$ and $R$, whence $\mathcal B_{M,R} \subseteq \mathcal B$.
nodes.statement_short: Lower-bound $|S|$ and $1-|S|$ via Ostrowski-expansion lemmas of Beresnevich-Haynes-Velani, using the periodic digit constraint.

nodes.name: Ostrowski expansion of n
nodes.statement: Let $({\alpha},{\gamma}) \in \mathcal B_{M,R}$. Let $n\in \mathbb N$, and write \[ n = \sum_{k=0}^K c_{k+1} q_k \asymp q_K \] for the Ostrowski expansion of $n$ with respect to ${\alpha}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $(\alpha,\gamma)\in\mathcal B_{M,R}$ and expand $n$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: As in Lemma~\ref{nag}, we let $m \geqslant 0$ be minimal such that ${\delta}_{m+1} \ne 0,$ where ${\delta}_k$ is as in \eqref{delta_k_def}. Note from Lemma \ref{nag} that \[ \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| = \min \{ |S|, 1-|S| \}, \] where \[ S = \sum_{k=m}^\infty {\delta}_{k+1} D_m. \]
nodes.statement_short: Express $\|n\alpha-\gamma\|$ via $S$.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It therefore suffices to find lower bounds for $|S|$ and $1-|S|$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to lower bounds for $|S|$ and $1-|S|$.

nodes.name: Lower bound for |S|
nodes.statement: It follows from \cite[Lemma 4.4]{BHV} that there exists some $\ell \leqslant \max\{2, K-m + 1\}$ such that $|S| \geqslant |D_{m+\ell +1}|.$ Since $({\alpha},{\gamma}) \in \mathcal B_{M,R}$ implies that $m \leqslant K + R$, this gives \[ |S| \geqslant |D_{m+1+\ell}| \gg \min \{ q_m^{-1}, q_K^{-1} \} \gg q_K^{-1} \gg n^{-1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: BHV Lemma 4.4 and $m\le K+R$ give $|S|\gg n^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Lower bound for 1-|S|
nodes.statement: Regarding $1-|S|,$ it is shown in \cite[Lemma 4.5]{BHV} that for some positive integer $L \leqslant K+2$, \[ 1 - |S| \geqslant |D_L| \gg q_L^{-1} \gg n^{-1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: BHV Lemma 4.5 gives $1-|S|\gg n^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Combining, we deduce that \[ \| n {\alpha} - {\gamma} \| \gg n^{-1}, \] where the implied constant depends at most on $M$ and $R$, whence $\mathcal B_{M,R} \subseteq \mathcal B$.
nodes.statement_short: So $\|n\alpha-\gamma\|\gg n^{-1}$ and $\mathcal B_{M,R}\subseteq\mathcal B$.

nodes.name: R-fold left shift operator
nodes.statement: The \emph{$R$-fold left shift operator} acts on $\mathcal B_{M,R}$ by \[ {\sigma}^R({\alpha}, {\gamma}) = ({\alpha}', {\gamma}') \] where, if $ {\alpha} = [a_1,a_2,\ldots] $ and ${\gamma}$ has Ostrowski expansion $\displaystyle \sum_{k \geqslant 0} b_{k+1} D_k$ then \[ {\alpha}' = [a_{R+1},\ldots], \qquad {\gamma}' = \sum_{k \geqslant 0} b_{R+k+1} D_k. \] Symbolically, we have \[ ((a_k)_{k=1}^\infty, (b_k)_{k=1}^\infty) \mapsto ((a_{R+k})_{k=1}^\infty, (b_{R+k})_{k=1}^\infty). \]
nodes.statement_short: Shifts both the partial quotients of $\alpha$ and the Ostrowski digits of $\gamma$ by $R$ places.

nodes.name: Parameters m and a
nodes.statement: Let $m$ be a positive multiple of $R$, and let $\mathbf a \in \mathbb N^m$.

nodes.name: Digit sets V_k(a) and exponents kappa_{M,R,m}, omega_{M,m}
nodes.statement:
For $k \in [m]$, denote by $\mathcal V_k(\mathbf a)$ the set of \[ \mathbf b = (b_1,\ldots,b_k) \in \mathbb Z^k \] such that  egin{align} &1 \leqslant b_k \leqslant a_k - 1 \qquad (k \mmod R \in \{0,1\}), 
otag \ &0 \leqslant b_k \leqslant a_k \qquad (k \in [t]), 
otag \ &b_{k+1} = a_{k+1} \Rightarrow b_k = 0 \qquad (k \in [t-1]).
otag \end{align} Let ${\kappa}_{M,R,m} > 1/2$ be the value of ${\kappa}$ for which  egin{equation} \sum_{\mathbf a \in [M]^m} q_m(\mathbf a)^{1-2 {\kappa}} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a)| = 1, \end{equation} and let ${\omega}_{M,m} > 0$ be the value of ${\omega}$ for which \[ \sum_{\mathbf a \in [M]^m} q_m(\mathbf a)^{-2 {\omega}} = 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: Defines the admissible Ostrowski digit words $\mathcal V_k(\mathbf a)$ and the dimension exponents $\kappa_{M,R,m}$, $\omega_{M,m}$ via pressure-type equations.
nodes.label: Vdef

nodes.name: Defining equation of kappa_{M,R,m} (3.2)
nodes.statement: \sum_{\mathbf a \in [M]^m} q_m(\mathbf a)^{1-2 {\kappa}} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a)| = 1,
nodes.label: def_kappa_MRm

nodes.name: Good's theorem
nodes.statement: Good \cite{Good} showed that \[ {\omega}_{M,m} \to \mathrm{dim}_H \mathcal F_M \qquad (m \to \infty), \] see \cite[Theorem 3.1]{QR2003}.

nodes.name: Jarnik's theorem
nodes.statement: Jarn\'ik \cite{Jar1928} showed that \[ \mathrm{dim}_H \mathcal F_M \to 1 \qquad (M \to \infty), \] so \begin{equation} {\omega}_{M,m} = 1 + o(1) \qquad (\min \{ M, m \} \to \infty). \end{equation}

nodes.name: omega_{M,m} tends to 1 (3.3)
nodes.statement: {\omega}_{M,m} = 1 + o(1) \qquad (\min \{ M, m \} \to \infty).
nodes.label: GoodJarnik

nodes.name: Counts v_k
nodes.statement: For $k \in [m]$, write $v_k = |\mathcal V_k(\mathbf a)|$, and note that if $v_m > 0$ and $k \mmod R \in \{0,1\}$ then $a_k \geqslant 2$.

nodes.name: Initial values and recursion of v_k
nodes.statement: Moreover, we have \[ v_1 = a_1 - 1, \qquad v_2 = a_2(a_1 - 1), \] Further, if $k \geqslant 3$ and $k \mmod R \in \{0,1\}$ then \[ v_k = (a_k - 1)v_{k-1}. \]

nodes.name: Recursion for v_k
nodes.statement: Let $k \in [3,m]$ be an integer such that $k \mmod R \notin \{0,1\}$. Then \[ v_k = \begin{cases} a_k v_{k-1}, &\text{if } k \equiv 2 \mmod R \\ a_k v_{k-1} + v_{k-2}, &\text{if } k \not \equiv 2 \mmod R. \end{cases} \]
assumptions: $k \in [3,m]$ be an integer such that $k \mmod R \notin \{0,1\}$
conclusions: v_k = \begin{cases} a_k v_{k-1}, &\text{if } k \equiv 2 \mmod R \\ a_k v_{k-1} + v_{k-2}, &\text{if } k \not \equiv 2 \mmod R. \end{cases}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement: Write \[ v_{k-1} = y_{k-1} + z_{k-1}, \] where $y_{k-1}$ counts $\mathbf b \in \mathcal V_{k-1}(\mathbf a)$ such that $b_{k-1} \ne 0$, and $z_{k-1}$ counts $\mathbf b \in \mathcal V_{k-1}(\mathbf a)$ such that $b_{k-1} = 0$. Then \[ v_k = a_k y_{k-1} + (a_k + 1) z_{k-1} = a_k v_{k-1} + z_{k-1}, \] and \[ z_{k-1} = \begin{cases} 0, &\text{if } k \equiv 2 \mmod R \\ v_{k-2}, &\text{if } k \not \equiv 2 \mmod R. \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: Split $v_{k-1}$ by whether the last digit is zero.

nodes.name: Growth of v_k
nodes.statement: We now see that if $k \in \mathbb N$ then \[ v_{k+2} \geqslant v_k, \] and hence \[ v_{2k} \geqslant 2^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor}. \]

nodes.name: Comparison of v_k with q_k
nodes.statement: Assume that for $r \mmod R \in \{0,1\}$ we have $a_r \geqslant 2$. Then \[ v_k \leqslant q_k(\mathbf a) \leqslant 3^{n_k} v_k \qquad (k \in [m]), \] where $n_k$ denotes the number of $j \in [k]$ such that $j \mmod R \in \{0,1,2\}$. Consequently \[ v_k \leqslant q_k(\mathbf a) \leqslant 27^{\lceil k/R \rceil} v_k \qquad (1 \leqslant k \leqslant m). \] In particular, there exists an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that \[ v_m \leqslant q_m(\mathbf a) \leqslant v_m^{1+c/R}. \]
nodes.statement_short: The digit count $v_k$ and the denominator $q_k$ agree up to a factor $27^{\lceil k/R\rceil}$.
nodes.label: vq

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement: We induct on $k$. We have \[ q_1 = a_1, \qquad q_2 = a_2 a_1 + 1 \] and \[ v_1 = a_1 - 1 \in [q_1/2,q_1], \qquad v_2 = a_2 (a_1 - 1) \in [q_2/3,q_2]. \] Next, let $k \in [3,m] \cap \mathbb Z$, and assume that the result holds with $k$ replaced by $k-1$ or $k-2$. Then \[ v_k \leqslant a_k v_{k-1} + v_{k-2} \leqslant a_k q_{k-1} + q_{k-2} = q_k. \] If $k \mmod R \notin \{0,1,2\}$ then \[ q_k = a_k q_{k-1} + q_{k-2} \leqslant 3^{n_k} (a_k v_{k-1} + v_{k-2}) = 3^{n_k} v_k. \] If $k \mmod R \in \{0,1,2\}$ then \[ q_k = a_k q_{k-1} + q_{k-2} \leqslant (a_k + 1) q_{k-1} \leqslant 3^{n_k - 1} (a_k + 1) v_{k-1} \leqslant 3^{n_k} v_k. \]
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$ with the recursions for $q_k$ and $v_k$.

nodes.name: Base cases
nodes.statement: We induct on $k$. We have \[ q_1 = a_1, \qquad q_2 = a_2 a_1 + 1 \] and \[ v_1 = a_1 - 1 \in [q_1/2,q_1], \qquad v_2 = a_2 (a_1 - 1) \in [q_2/3,q_2]. \]
nodes.statement_short: Check $k=1,2$ directly.

nodes.name: Inductive lower bound
nodes.statement: Next, let $k \in [3,m] \cap \mathbb Z$, and assume that the result holds with $k$ replaced by $k-1$ or $k-2$. Then \[ v_k \leqslant a_k v_{k-1} + v_{k-2} \leqslant a_k q_{k-1} + q_{k-2} = q_k. \]
nodes.statement_short: Show $v_k\le q_k$ from the recursions.

nodes.name: Unconstrained index
nodes.statement: If $k \mmod R \notin \{0,1,2\}$ then \[ q_k = a_k q_{k-1} + q_{k-2} \leqslant 3^{n_k} (a_k v_{k-1} + v_{k-2}) = 3^{n_k} v_k. \]
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound when $k\bmod R\notin\{0,1,2\}$.

nodes.name: Constrained index
nodes.statement: If $k \mmod R \in \{0,1,2\}$ then \[ q_k = a_k q_{k-1} + q_{k-2} \leqslant (a_k + 1) q_{k-1} \leqslant 3^{n_k - 1} (a_k + 1) v_{k-1} \leqslant 3^{n_k} v_k. \]
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound when $k\bmod R\in\{0,1,2\}$.

nodes.name: kappa_{M,R,m} tends to 2
nodes.statement: We have \[ {\kappa}_{M,R,m} = 2 + o(1) \qquad (\min\{M, R, m\} \to \infty). \]
nodes.label: lem_kappa_tends_to_two

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.5
nodes.statement: It is convenient to abbreviate ${\kappa} = {\kappa}_{M,R,m}$ and ${\omega} = {\omega}_{M,m}$ in the following calculation. By Lemma \ref{vq}, we have \begin{align*} \sum_{\mathbf a \in [M]^m} q_m(\mathbf a)^{-2{\omega}} &= 1 = \sum_{\mathbf a \in [M]^m} q_m(\mathbf a)^{1-2{\kappa}} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a)| \\&= \sum_{\mathbf a \in [M]^m} q_m(\mathbf a)^{2-2{\kappa}+O(1/R)}, \end{align*} and so \[ {\kappa} = 1 + {\omega} + o(1) \qquad (R \to \infty). \] Combining this with \eqref{GoodJarnik} completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Compare the defining sums of $\kappa$ and $\omega$ via Lemma 3.4, then apply Good-Jarnik.

nodes.name: Parameters epsilon and kappa
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon \in (0,1/4)$ and ${\kappa} \in (1,2)$ be fixed.

nodes.name: Partition function T_m(kappa)
nodes.statement: For any such integer $m$, we define \[ T_m({\kappa}) = \sum_{\mathbf a \in [M]^m} q_m(\mathbf a)^{1-2{\kappa}}|\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a)|. \] Here we write $|\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a)|$ for the cardinality of the set $\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a)$ introduced in Definition \ref{Vdef}.

nodes.name: Parameters chosen so that kappa_{M,R,m} > kappa
nodes.statement: In view of Lemma~\ref{lem_kappa_tends_to_two}, if $M,R,m$ are large enough, then we can ensure that $\kappa_{M,R,m}$ is arbitrarily close to 2, and we choose these parameters large enough so that \begin{equation} \kappa_{M,R,m}>\kappa. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Equation (4.1)
nodes.statement: \kappa_{M,R,m}>\kappa.
nodes.label: kappa_MRm_bigger_than_kappa

nodes.name: T_m(kappa) tends to infinity
nodes.statement: The definition of $\kappa_{M,R,m}$ and the inequality \eqref{kappa_MRm_bigger_than_kappa} imply that \[ T_m({\kappa}) \to \infty \qquad (m \to \infty). \]

nodes.name: T_m(kappa) > 4
nodes.statement: We take $m \geqslant 100$ large enough to ensure that \begin{equation} T_m({\kappa}) > 4. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Equation (4.2)
nodes.statement: T_m({\kappa}) > 4.
nodes.label: T_m_is_large

nodes.name: Digit alphabet J
nodes.statement: Consider the set \[ \mathcal J = \left\{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \in [M]^m \times [M]_0^m : \mathbf b \in \mathcal V_m(\mathbf a) \right\}. \]

nodes.name: Measure lambda_m
nodes.statement: Define a probability measure $\lambda_m$ on $\mathcal J$ by setting \begin{equation} {\lambda}_m(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) = \frac{1}{T_m({\kappa})}q_m(\mathbf a)^{1-2{\kappa}} \qquad ((\mathbf a, \mathbf b) \in \mathcal J). \end{equation} Note that we write ${\lambda}_m(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$ for notational convenience, instead of the more formal ${\lambda}_m(\{ (\mathbf a, \mathbf b)\}).$

nodes.name: Definition of lambda_m (4.3)
nodes.statement: {\lambda}_m(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) = \frac{1}{T_m({\kappa})}q_m(\mathbf a)^{1-2{\kappa}} \qquad ((\mathbf a, \mathbf b) \in \mathcal J).
nodes.label: def_lambda_m

nodes.name: Mean sigma_m(kappa)
nodes.statement: Next, we define ${\sigma}_m({\kappa})$ so that $m {\sigma}_m({\kappa})$ is the mean of the random variable $\log q_m(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$ with respect to the measure ${\lambda}_m$. In other words, \[ m {\sigma}_m({\kappa}) = \sum_{(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \in \mathcal J} \log q_m(\mathbf a) \lambda_m(\mathbf a,\mathbf b). \]

nodes.name: sigma_m(kappa) at least 1/3
nodes.statement: The assumption that $m \geqslant 100$, along with \eqref{q_k_size}, imply that if $\mathbf{a}\in [M]^m$ then \[ \log q_m(\mathbf{a})\geqslant m/3, \] whence $\sigma_m({\kappa}) \geqslant 1/3$.

nodes.name: m large in terms of epsilon
nodes.statement: Henceforth, we assume that $m$ is large enough so that \begin{equation} \max \left(\frac{\log 2}{m\sigma_m({\kappa}) }, \frac{3}{m} \right) < \varepsilon. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Equation (4.4)
nodes.statement: \max \left(\frac{\log 2}{m\sigma_m({\kappa}) }, \frac{3}{m} \right) < \varepsilon.
nodes.label: m_conditions

nodes.name: R large in terms of epsilon
nodes.statement: In preparation for Section~\ref{section_FD}, we also assume that $R$ is sufficiently large to ensure that \[ \frac{3 \log 27}{R} (1+c) < \varepsilon, \] where $c$ is as in Lemma \ref{vq}, whence \begin{equation} \frac{c}{R} < \varepsilon, \qquad \frac{\log 27}{ R\sigma_m(\kappa)} <\varepsilon. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Equation (4.5)
nodes.statement: \frac{c}{R} < \varepsilon, \qquad \frac{\log 27}{ R\sigma_m(\kappa)} <\varepsilon.
nodes.label: R_is_large

nodes.name: Product measure and random variables Y_n
nodes.statement: On the space $\mathcal J \times \mathcal J \times \ldots$, we define the probability measure \[ \lambda_m \times \lambda_m \times \ldots, \] and let $(Y_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be the sequence of random variables on this probability space defined by \[ Y_1 = q_m(a_1,\ldots,a_m), \quad Y_2 = q_m(a_{m+1},\ldots,a_{2m}),\ldots. \]

nodes.name: Typical set E
nodes.statement: By the law of large numbers, there exists $j_0 \geqslant 1$ such that the set \[ \mathcal E = \mathcal E(j_0) \subseteq \mathcal J^{j_0} \] on which \begin{equation} \left| \frac{\log Y_1 + \cdots + \log Y_{j_0}}{j_0} - \mathbb E(\log Y_1) \right| \leqslant \varepsilon \mathbb E(\log Y_1) \end{equation} has measure \begin{equation} {\lambda}^{j_0}(\mathcal E) > 1/2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: By the law of large numbers, fix $j_0$ so that the set $\mathcal E$ of words with near-average $\log q$ has measure $>1/2$.

nodes.name: Law of large numbers condition (4.6)
nodes.statement: \left| \frac{\log Y_1 + \cdots + \log Y_{j_0}}{j_0} - \mathbb E(\log Y_1) \right| \leqslant \varepsilon \mathbb E(\log Y_1)
nodes.label: Edef

nodes.name: E has measure > 1/2 (4.7)
nodes.statement: {\lambda}^{j_0}(\mathcal E) > 1/2.
nodes.label: cEisLarge

nodes.name: Block length J_0 and measure P
nodes.statement: We fix such a value of $j_0$, and write $\mathbb P = {\lambda}^{j_0}$ as well as \[ J_0 = j_0m. \]

nodes.name: Concentration of log q on E^N
nodes.statement: Using \eqref{concatenation} and \eqref{Edef}, we deduce that if $N \geqslant 1$ and $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \in \mathcal E^N$ then \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & |\log q_{J_0 N}(a_1,\ldots,a_{J_0 N}) - J_0 N {\sigma}_m({\kappa})| \\ & \qquad \leqslant \varepsilon J_0 N {\sigma}_m({\kappa}) + (j_0N-1) \log 2 \\ & \qquad \leqslant \left(\varepsilon + \log 2\frac{j_0 N -1}{J_0 N \sigma_m(\kappa) } \right) J_0 N {\sigma}_m({\kappa})\\ & \qquad < 2\varepsilon J_0 N {\sigma}_m({\kappa}), \end{aligned} \end{equation} and consequently \begin{equation} Q^{1-2\varepsilon} \leqslant q_{J_0N}(a_1,\ldots,a_{J_0N}) \leqslant Q^{1+2\varepsilon}, \end{equation} where $Q = \exp\left(J_0 N {\sigma}_m({\kappa})\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: On $\mathcal E^N$, $q_{J_0N}$ lies between $Q^{1-2\varepsilon}$ and $Q^{1+2\varepsilon}$.

nodes.name: Concentration of log q_{J_0N} (4.8)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & |\log q_{J_0 N}(a_1,\ldots,a_{J_0 N}) - J_0 N {\sigma}_m({\kappa})| \\ & \qquad \leqslant \varepsilon J_0 N {\sigma}_m({\kappa}) + (j_0N-1) \log 2 \\ & \qquad \leqslant \left(\varepsilon + \log 2\frac{j_0 N -1}{J_0 N \sigma_m(\kappa) } \right) J_0 N {\sigma}_m({\kappa})\\ & \qquad < 2\varepsilon J_0 N {\sigma}_m({\kappa}), \end{aligned}
nodes.label: ie_logQJ

nodes.name: Two-sided bound for q_{J_0N} (4.9)
nodes.statement: Q^{1-2\varepsilon} \leqslant q_{J_0N}(a_1,\ldots,a_{J_0N}) \leqslant Q^{1+2\varepsilon},
nodes.label: Qest

nodes.name: Conditioned measure lambda
nodes.statement: Let ${\lambda}$ be the probability measure induced by $\mathbb P$ on $\mathcal E$, i.e. \[ \lambda(A) = \frac{1}{\mathbb P(\mathcal E)}\mathbb P(A\cap \mathcal E) \qquad (A \subseteq \mathcal J^{j_0}). \]

nodes.name: Normalising constant c_lambda
nodes.statement: The normalising factor above is the constant \begin{equation} c_{\lambda}:=\frac{1}{\mathbb P(\mathcal E)}, \end{equation} which will appear frequently in subsequent calculations.

nodes.name: Definition of c_lambda (4.10)
nodes.statement: c_{\lambda}:=\frac{1}{\mathbb P(\mathcal E)},
nodes.label: def_c_lambda

nodes.name: Bounds on c_lambda
nodes.statement: By~\eqref{cEisLarge}, we have \[ 1\leqslant c_\lambda < 2. \]

nodes.name: The measure nu
nodes.statement: Finally we define the probability measure $\nu$ by setting \begin{equation} \nu = {\lambda}\times{\lambda}\times\ldots. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of nu (4.11)
nodes.statement: \nu = {\lambda}\times{\lambda}\times\ldots.
nodes.label: def_nu

nodes.name: Frostman dimension
nodes.statement: Recall that this dimension is defined as the supremum of $s \in \mathbb R$ such that \[ \nu(B_r(\mathbf x)) \ll r^s \qquad (0 < r < 1, \: \mathbf x \in \mathbb R^2), \] where $B_r(\mathbf x)$ denotes the ball of radius $r$ centred at $\mathbf x$.
nodes.origin_citation: Falconer, Fraser & Kaenmaki 2023; Kleptsyn, Pollicott & Vytnova 2022

nodes.name: Frostman dimension bounded by Hausdorff dimension
nodes.statement: By the mass distribution principle (Lemma \ref{MDP}), the Frostman dimension of a Borel probability measure is bounded above by the Hausdorff dimension of its support.

nodes.name: Cylinder set C(a)
nodes.statement: In the sequel, it will be convenient to refer to certain subsets of $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R^2$ as \emph{cylinder sets}. Given $N\geqslant 1$ and $\mathbf a = (a_1,\ldots, a_N) \in \mathbb N^N,$ we define the cylinder set $C(\mathbf a)$ as \[ C(\mathbf a) = \{ \alpha \in [0,1) : a_i({\alpha}) = a_i \quad (1\leqslant i \leqslant N) \}. \]

nodes.name: Cylinder set C(a,b)
nodes.statement: Further, given $N\geqslant 1,$ $\mathbf a\in \mathbb N^N$ and $\mathbf b\in\mathcal V_N(\mathbf a)$, we define the cylinder set $C(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$ as \[ \{ (\alpha,\gamma) \in \mathbb R^2 : {\alpha} \in C(\mathbf a), \: -\alpha \leqslant \gamma < 1-\alpha, \: b_i({\alpha},{\gamma}) = b_i \quad (1\leqslant i \leqslant N) \}. \]

nodes.name: Measure of cylinder sets
nodes.statement: We use the notation and assumptions of this section, and assume that $\kappa>1/2$, so that $1-2\kappa<0$. Put $ Q_0 = \exp(J_0 \sigma_m(\kappa)), $ and let $N \geqslant 1$. Then, for any cylinder set $C=C(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$ with $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\in\mathcal E^N$, we have \[ \frac{1}{2^{j_0-1}} \frac{Q_0^{(1-2\kappa) (1-2\varepsilon)N}} {T_m(\kappa)^{j_0 N}} \leqslant \nu(C)\leqslant 2^{N} \frac{Q_0^{(1-2\kappa)(1+2\varepsilon)N}} {T_m(\kappa)^{j_0 N}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Two-sided bounds for $\nu$ of a level-$N$ cylinder in terms of $Q_0$ and $T_m(\kappa)$.
nodes.label: lem_size_of_cylinder_set

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement:
Writing $\mathbf a = (\mathbf a_1, \ldots, \mathbf a_N)$ and $\mathbf b = (\mathbf b_1, \ldots, \mathbf b_N)$ where \[ (\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i) \in \mathcal E \qquad (i\leqslant N), \] the definition of $
u$ in \eqref{def_nu} gives \[ 
u(C) = \lambda(\mathbf a_1,\mathbf b_1) \cdots \lambda(\mathbf a_N, \mathbf b_N). \] The definition of $\lambda$ and~\eqref{cEisLarge} imply that  egin{equation*} \lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i) \leqslant \lambda(\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i)\leqslant 2\lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i) \qquad ( i\leqslant N). \end{equation*} Combining these facts, we infer  egin{equation} \lambda_m^{j_0 }(\mathbf a_1, \mathbf b_1)\cdots \lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_N,\mathbf b_N) \leqslant 
u(C)\leqslant 2^N \lambda_m^{j_0 }(\mathbf a_1, \mathbf b_1)\cdots \lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_N,\mathbf b_N). \end{equation} Further, from the definition~\eqref{def_lambda_m}, we have  egin{equation*} \lambda_m^{j_0 }(\mathbf a_i, \mathbf b_i) = \prod_{k=0}^{j_0-1}  rac{q_m(a_{(i-1)J_0+km+1},\dots,a_{(i-1)J_0+(k+1)m})^{1-2{\kappa}}}{T_m({\kappa})} \quad (i\leqslant N). \end{equation*} Using the inequality \eqref{concatenation}, we deduce that for $i=1, \dots, N$,  egin{equation}  egin{aligned}  rac{1}{2^{j_0-1}}  rac{ q_{J_0}(a_{(i-1)J_0+1},\dots,a_{iJ_0})^{1-2{\kappa}}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0}} &\leqslant {\lambda}_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_i, \mathbf b_i) \& \leqslant  rac{q_{J_0}(a_{(i-1)J_0+1},\dots,a_{iJ_0})^{1-2{\kappa}}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0}} \cdot \end{aligned} \end{equation} We further estimate, by using~\eqref{ie_logQJ}, that for $i=1, \dots, N$ we have  egin{equation} Q_0^{(1-2\varepsilon)(1-2{\kappa})} \leqslant q_{J_0}(a_{(i-1)J_0+1},\dots,a_{iJ_0})^{1-2{\kappa}}\leqslant Q_0^{(1+2\varepsilon)(1-2{\kappa})}. \end{equation} The assertion of the lemma follows by putting together~\eqref{lem_size_of_cylinder_set_db_nu}, \eqref{lem_size_of_cylinder_set_db_denominator} and~\eqref{lem_size_of_cylinder_set_db_q_m}.
nodes.statement_short: Product structure of $\nu$ plus the concatenation inequality and the law-of-large-numbers bounds on $q_{J_0}$.

nodes.name: Product structure
nodes.statement: Writing $\mathbf a = (\mathbf a_1, \ldots, \mathbf a_N)$ and $\mathbf b = (\mathbf b_1, \ldots, \mathbf b_N)$ where \[ (\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i) \in \mathcal E \qquad (i\leqslant N), \] the definition of $\nu$ in \eqref{def_nu} gives \[ \nu(C) = \lambda(\mathbf a_1,\mathbf b_1) \cdots \lambda(\mathbf a_N, \mathbf b_N). \]
nodes.statement_short: Split the words into blocks; $\nu(C)$ is a product of $\lambda$-masses.

nodes.name: Compare lambda with lambda_m
nodes.statement: The definition of $\lambda$ and~\eqref{cEisLarge} imply that \begin{equation*} \lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i) \leqslant \lambda(\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i)\leqslant 2\lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i) \qquad ( i\leqslant N). \end{equation*} Combining these facts, we infer \begin{equation} \lambda_m^{j_0 }(\mathbf a_1, \mathbf b_1)\cdots \lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_N,\mathbf b_N) \leqslant \nu(C)\leqslant 2^N \lambda_m^{j_0 }(\mathbf a_1, \mathbf b_1)\cdots \lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_N,\mathbf b_N). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda$ and $\lambda_m^{j_0}$ agree up to a factor 2, giving (4.12).

nodes.name: Equation lambda_and_lambda_m0_are_comparable
nodes.statement: \lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i) \leqslant \lambda(\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i)\leqslant 2\lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i) \qquad ( i\leqslant N).
nodes.label: lambda_and_lambda_m0_are_comparable

nodes.name: Equation (4.12)
nodes.statement: \lambda_m^{j_0 }(\mathbf a_1, \mathbf b_1)\cdots \lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_N,\mathbf b_N) \leqslant \nu(C)\leqslant 2^N \lambda_m^{j_0 }(\mathbf a_1, \mathbf b_1)\cdots \lambda_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_N,\mathbf b_N).
nodes.label: lem_size_of_cylinder_set_db_nu

nodes.name: Expand lambda_m
nodes.statement: Further, from the definition~\eqref{def_lambda_m}, we have \begin{equation*} \lambda_m^{j_0 }(\mathbf a_i, \mathbf b_i) = \prod_{k=0}^{j_0-1} \frac{q_m(a_{(i-1)J_0+km+1},\dots,a_{(i-1)J_0+(k+1)m})^{1-2{\kappa}}}{T_m({\kappa})} \quad (i\leqslant N). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $\lambda_m^{j_0}$ as a product of $q_m$ powers.

nodes.name: Concatenation
nodes.statement: Using the inequality \eqref{concatenation}, we deduce that for $i=1, \dots, N$, \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2^{j_0-1}} \frac{ q_{J_0}(a_{(i-1)J_0+1},\dots,a_{iJ_0})^{1-2{\kappa}}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0}} &\leqslant {\lambda}_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_i, \mathbf b_i) \\& \leqslant \frac{q_{J_0}(a_{(i-1)J_0+1},\dots,a_{iJ_0})^{1-2{\kappa}}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0}} \cdot \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Concatenation inequality gives (4.13).

nodes.name: Equation (4.13)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2^{j_0-1}} \frac{ q_{J_0}(a_{(i-1)J_0+1},\dots,a_{iJ_0})^{1-2{\kappa}}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0}} &\leqslant {\lambda}_m^{j_0}(\mathbf a_i, \mathbf b_i) \\& \leqslant \frac{q_{J_0}(a_{(i-1)J_0+1},\dots,a_{iJ_0})^{1-2{\kappa}}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0}} \cdot \end{aligned}
nodes.label: lem_size_of_cylinder_set_db_denominator

nodes.name: Size of q_{J_0}
nodes.statement: We further estimate, by using~\eqref{ie_logQJ}, that for $i=1, \dots, N$ we have \begin{equation} Q_0^{(1-2\varepsilon)(1-2{\kappa})} \leqslant q_{J_0}(a_{(i-1)J_0+1},\dots,a_{iJ_0})^{1-2{\kappa}}\leqslant Q_0^{(1+2\varepsilon)(1-2{\kappa})}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: (4.8) bounds the $q_{J_0}$ powers, giving (4.14).

nodes.name: Equation (4.14)
nodes.statement: Q_0^{(1-2\varepsilon)(1-2{\kappa})} \leqslant q_{J_0}(a_{(i-1)J_0+1},\dots,a_{iJ_0})^{1-2{\kappa}}\leqslant Q_0^{(1+2\varepsilon)(1-2{\kappa})}.
nodes.label: lem_size_of_cylinder_set_db_q_m

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: The assertion of the lemma follows by putting together~\eqref{lem_size_of_cylinder_set_db_nu}, \eqref{lem_size_of_cylinder_set_db_denominator} and~\eqref{lem_size_of_cylinder_set_db_q_m}.

nodes.name: Denominator bounds and Frostman dimension of nu
nodes.statement:
Let $
u$ be the measure constructed in Subsection~ef{subsection_ConstructionOfMeasures}, and assume in addition that the parameter ${\kappa}$ from that section lies in the range $(3/2,2)$. Then we have the following.  egin{enumerate}[(a)] \item For all positive integer multiples $J$ of $J_0$, the inequalities  egin{equation} Q^{1-2\varepsilon} \leqslant q_J({\alpha}) \leqslant Q^{1+2\varepsilon}, \qquad  rac{Q^{1-2\varepsilon}}{2M} \leqslant q_{J-1}({\alpha}) \leqslant Q^{1+2\varepsilon} \end{equation} hold for $
u$-almost all $({\alpha},{\gamma}),$ where $Q = \exp(J {\sigma}_m({\kappa}))$. \item There exists a constant $c_1>0$ depending only on $M, J_0 \geqslant 1$ and ${\sigma}_m({\kappa})$ such that if $\mathbf x \in \mathbb R^2$ and $r \in (0,1]$ then \[ 
u(B_r(\mathbf x)) \leqslant c_1 r^{2\kappa-2-4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon}. \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For $\nu$-almost all points $q_J\approx Q$, and balls of radius $r$ have $\nu$-measure $\ll r^{2\kappa-2-4(2-\kappa)\varepsilon}$.
assumptions: the parameter ${\kappa}$ from that section lies in the range $(3/2,2)$
conclusions: For all positive integer multiples $J$ of $J_0$, the inequalities \begin{equation} \label{denominator_bounds} Q^{1-2\varepsilon} \leqslant q_J({\alpha}) \leqslant Q^{1+2\varepsilon}, \qquad \frac{Q^{1-2\varepsilon}}{2M} \leqslant q_{J-1}({\alpha}) \leqslant Q^{1+2\varepsilon} \end{equation} hold for $\nu$-almost all $({\alpha},{\gamma}),$ where $Q = \exp(J {\sigma}_m({\kappa}))$.

There exists a constant $c_1>0$ depending only on $M, J_0 \geqslant 1$ and ${\sigma}_m({\kappa})$ such that if $\mathbf x \in \mathbb R^2$ and $r \in (0,1]$ then \[ \nu(B_r(\mathbf x)) \leqslant c_1 r^{2\kappa-2-4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon}.
nodes.label: lem_FD

nodes.name: Equation (4.15)
nodes.statement: Q^{1-2\varepsilon} \leqslant q_J({\alpha}) \leqslant Q^{1+2\varepsilon}, \qquad \frac{Q^{1-2\varepsilon}}{2M} \leqslant q_{J-1}({\alpha}) \leqslant Q^{1+2\varepsilon}
nodes.label: denominator_bounds

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement_short: Part (a) from (4.9); part (b) counts cylinders meeting a ball, first the $\mathbf a$-words then the $\mathbf b$-words, and multiplies by the cylinder measure bound.

nodes.name: Part (a)
nodes.statement: \eqref{point_sizeQJ} The first inequality was already shown in \eqref{Qest}. The second inequality then follows from the bounds \[ 1 \leqslant \frac{q_J({\alpha})}{q_{J-1}({\alpha})} \leqslant 2M. \]
nodes.statement_short: Denominator bounds from (4.9) and $q_J/q_{J-1}\le 2M$.

nodes.name: Part (b)
nodes.statement_short: Count cylinders meeting the ball and multiply by the cylinder bound.

nodes.name: Choose the level N
nodes.statement: \eqref{point_dimFrostman} Fix $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^2$ and $r>0.$ If $\nu(B_r(\mathbf x))=0$ then the claim is straightforward, so in the rest of the proof we assume that $\nu(B_r(\mathbf x))>0$. Define \begin{equation} Q_0:=\exp(J_0 \sigma_m(\kappa)) \qquad \text{ and } \qquad N:=\left\lfloor\frac{\log r}{-\log Q_0}\right\rfloor+1. \end{equation} These definitions imply \begin{equation} Q_0^{-N} < r \leqslant Q_0^{1-N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Fix the ball and pick $N$ with $Q_0^{-N}<r\le Q_0^{1-N}$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.16)
nodes.statement: Q_0:=\exp(J_0 \sigma_m(\kappa)) \qquad \text{ and } \qquad N:=\left\lfloor\frac{\log r}{-\log Q_0}\right\rfloor+1.
nodes.label: def_Q0_N

nodes.name: Equation (4.17)
nodes.statement: Q_0^{-N} < r \leqslant Q_0^{1-N}.
nodes.label: r_level

nodes.name: Denominator size
nodes.statement: Let $C=C(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$ be a cylinder set with $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\in\mathcal E^N$ such that \begin{equation} \nu\left(B_r(\mathbf x)\cap C\right)>0. \end{equation} Setting $J=J_0 N$ and $Q=\exp(J{\sigma}_m({\kappa}))=Q_0^N$ as above, point~\eqref{point_sizeQJ} of the lemma gives \begin{equation} Q^{1-2\varepsilon} \leqslant q_{J}(\mathbf a)\leqslant Q^{1+2\varepsilon}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Part (a) gives the size of $q_J$ for relevant cylinders.

nodes.name: Equation (4.18)
nodes.statement: \nu\left(B_r(\mathbf x)\cap C\right)>0.
nodes.label: lem_FD_nontrivial_intersection

nodes.name: Equation (4.19)
nodes.statement: Q^{1-2\varepsilon} \leqslant q_{J}(\mathbf a)\leqslant Q^{1+2\varepsilon}.
nodes.label: lem_FD_size_q

nodes.name: Count the a-words
nodes.statement: We aim to provide an upper bound for the number of cylinder sets $C(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$, where $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \in \mathcal E^N$, satisfying \eqref{lem_FD_nontrivial_intersection}. We do so by first bounding the number of possible tuples $\mathbf a$ and then the number of possible tuples $\mathbf b$. For each $\mathbf a\in [M]^{J}$, the cylinder set $C(\mathbf a)$ has length \[ |C(\mathbf a)| \geqslant \frac1{2Q^{2(1+2\varepsilon)}}, \] for the elements of $C(\mathbf a)$ are given by \eqref{alphaoft} for $t \in [0,1)$. Hence, there exist at most \begin{equation} 2r\cdot 2Q^{2(1+2\varepsilon)}+1 \leqslant 4Q^{1+4\varepsilon} +1 \leqslant 5Q^{1+4\varepsilon} \end{equation} tuples $\mathbf a$ such that the cylinder set $C(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$ satisfies \eqref{lem_FD_nontrivial_intersection} for some $\mathbf b$.
nodes.statement_short: Cylinders $C(\mathbf a)$ are long, so few $\mathbf a$ meet the ball.

nodes.name: Equation (4.20)
nodes.statement: 2r\cdot 2Q^{2(1+2\varepsilon)}+1 \leqslant 4Q^{1+4\varepsilon} +1 \leqslant 5Q^{1+4\varepsilon}
nodes.label: lem_FD_ub_cylinders_a

nodes.name: Count the b-words
nodes.statement: Now for a fixed $\mathbf a= (a_1, \ldots, a_{J}) \in [M]^{J}$, we find an upper bound for the number of different $J$--tuples $\mathbf b\in \mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)$ such that $C(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$ satisfies \eqref{lem_FD_nontrivial_intersection}. Set $$\alpha=\alpha(\mathbf a) = [a_1,\ldots, a_{J}, M, M, \ldots].$$ For $\mathbf b = (b_1, \ldots, b_{J}) \in \mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)$, let \[ n = n(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) = b_{1}q_0(\alpha) + b_2q_1(\alpha) + \ldots + b_{J}q_{J-1}(\alpha) \] be the integer whose digits in the Ostrowski expansion~\eqref{Ostrowski_expansion_integers} with respect to $\alpha$ are the entries of $\mathbf b$.
