By Corollary~\ref{cor_nag}, if $(\alpha,\gamma) \in C(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$ then \[ \|\gamma-n(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\alpha\| < 4M/ q_{J}(\mathbf a). \] This means that $\gamma$ belongs to an interval in $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ centred at $n(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\alpha$ and of length at most $8 M/q_{J}(\mathbf a)$. Note from \eqref{useful} that if $\mathbf b_1, \mathbf b_2 \in \mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)$ then \[ |n(\mathbf a,\mathbf b_1)-n(\mathbf a,\mathbf b_2)| \leqslant 4M q_{J}(\mathbf a), \] so by \eqref{bad_lower_bound} the centres of the aforementioned intervals are separated by a distance of at least \begin{align*} \|n(\mathbf a,\mathbf b_1)\alpha-n(\mathbf a,\mathbf b_2)\alpha\| &\geqslant (2(M+1)|n(\mathbf a,\mathbf b_1)-n(\mathbf a,\mathbf b_2)|)^{-1}\\ & \geqslant \left(8M(M+1) q_{J}(\mathbf a)\right)^{-1}. \end{align*} Thus, any interval of length $2r$ can intersect at most \[ 8M(M+1) Q^{1+2\varepsilon}\cdot 2r+2 \leqslant 16 (M+1)^2Q^{2\varepsilon} \] intervals centred at points $n(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\alpha$ of length at most $8 M q_{J}(\mathbf a)^{-1}$. We conclude that for a fixed $\mathbf a$, there are at most $16 (M+1)^2 Q^{2\varepsilon}$ values of $\mathbf b$ such that the set $C(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$ satisfies~\eqref{lem_FD_nontrivial_intersection}.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 2.2 and (2.3) separate the $\gamma$-intervals, bounding the $\mathbf b$ count.

nodes.name: Total mass bound
nodes.statement: Combining the two bounds, we deduce that the number of sets $C(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$ that satisfy \eqref{lem_FD_nontrivial_intersection} is at most \[ 5Q^{1+4\varepsilon}\cdot 16 (M+1)^2 Q^{2\varepsilon} = 80 (M+1)^2 Q^{1+6\varepsilon}. \] For any such set the upper bound of Lemma~\ref{lem_size_of_cylinder_set}, together with~\eqref{T_m_is_large}, gives \begin{equation} \nu(C(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)) < Q^{(1+2\varepsilon) (1-2\kappa)}. \end{equation} Using~\eqref{ub_nu_C} together with the upper bound for the number of cylinder sets satisfying~\eqref{lem_FD_nontrivial_intersection}, we infer the upper bound \[ \begin{aligned} \nu\left(B_r(\mathbf x)\right) &< 80 (M+1)^2 Q^{1+6\varepsilon} \cdot Q^{(1+2\varepsilon)(1-2\kappa)} \\ &= 80 (M+1)^2 \cdot Q^{2-2\kappa+4(2-\kappa)\varepsilon}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the count by the cylinder bound from Lemma 4.1.

nodes.name: Equation (4.21)
nodes.statement: \nu(C(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)) < Q^{(1+2\varepsilon) (1-2\kappa)}.
nodes.label: ub_nu_C

nodes.name: Express in r
nodes.statement: Using \eqref{r_level}, this results in the upper bound \[ \nu\left(B_r(\mathbf x)\right) \leqslant 80 (M+1)^2 Q_0 r^{2\kappa-2-4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Convert $Q$ to $r$ via (4.18).

nodes.name: Projection E_1
nodes.statement: We additionally define the set \[ \mathcal E_1 =\left\{\mathbf a\in [M]^{J_0} : (\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\in \mathcal E \text{ for some }\mathbf b\in [M]_{0}^{J_0} \right\}. \]

nodes.name: J and Q_N
nodes.statement: As before, for $N\geqslant 1$ we write $J=J_0 N$ and \[ Q = Q_N = \exp(J{\sigma}_m({\kappa})). \]

nodes.name: Mirror image of a word
nodes.statement: Given $\mathbf a = (a_1, \ldots, a_{J}),$ we write $\bar{\mathbf a} = (a_{J}, \ldots, a_1)$ for the mirror image of the word $\mathbf a$.

nodes.name: Digit-saturated sets
nodes.statement: We are interested in sets $A\subseteq \mathcal E^N$ such that \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &(\mathbf a, \mathbf b_0) \in A \text{ for some } \mathbf b_0\in \mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a) \\ &\Rightarrow \quad (\mathbf a, \mathbf b) \in A \text{ for all } \mathbf b \in \mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a). \end{aligned} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Digit-saturation property (4.22)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &(\mathbf a, \mathbf b_0) \in A \text{ for some } \mathbf b_0\in \mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a) \\ &\Rightarrow \quad (\mathbf a, \mathbf b) \in A \text{ for all } \mathbf b \in \mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a). \end{aligned}
nodes.label: full

nodes.name: Mirror set of A
nodes.statement: For any such set $A\subseteq \mathcal E^N,$ we define \begin{equation} \bar{A} = \left\{ (\bar{\mathbf a},\mathbf b): \begin{aligned} &\mathbf b\in \mathcal V_{J}(\bar{\mathbf a}), \\ &(\mathbf a,\mathbf b')\in A \text{ for some } \mathbf b' \in \mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a) \end{aligned} \right\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of mirror set (4.23)
nodes.statement: \bar{A} = \left\{ (\bar{\mathbf a},\mathbf b): \begin{aligned} &\mathbf b\in \mathcal V_{J}(\bar{\mathbf a}), \\ &(\mathbf a,\mathbf b')\in A \text{ for some } \mathbf b' \in \mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a) \end{aligned} \right\}.
nodes.label: mirror_set

nodes.name: Almost invariance of lambda^N under mirroring
nodes.statement: Let $N\geqslant 1$ and $A\subset\mathcal E^N$ be a set satisfying \eqref{full}. Then \[ {\lambda}^N(\bar{A}) Q^{-(1+2\varepsilon)c/(R+c)}\leqslant {\lambda}^N(A) \leqslant {\lambda}^N(\bar{A}) Q^{(1+2\varepsilon) c/(R+c)}, \] where the constant $c$ is as in Lemma~\ref{vq}.
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda^N(A)$ and $\lambda^N$ of its mirror image agree up to a factor $Q^{\pm(1+2\varepsilon)c/(R+c)}$.
nodes.label: prop_almost_invariance

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement:
It is enough to prove the proposition for sets of the form \[ A=\{(\mathbf a,\mathbf b): \mathbf b \in \mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)\} \] for some $\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_{J})$; the result will then follow by taking unions over words $\mathbf a \in [M]^{J}$. Note from the definition of $\mathcal E_1$ that we have $\mathbf a \in \mathcal E_1^N$ if and only if $ ar{\mathbf a}\in \mathcal E_1^N.$ The result is trivially true when $\mathbf a
otin \mathcal E_1^N,$ as then $
u(A) = 
u( ar{A})=0.$ If $\mathbf a\in \mathcal E_1^N$ then, for $A$ as above, by the definition of ${\lambda}$ we have \[ {\lambda}^N(A) =  rac{c_{\lambda}^N |\mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)|}{T_m(\kappa)^{j_0 N}}\prod_{i=0}^{j_0 N-1}q_m\left(a_{im+1},\dots, a_{(i+1)m}ight)^{1-2\kappa}. \] In light of the symmetry \eqref{q_k_inverse}, we similarly have \[ {\lambda}^N( ar{A}) =  rac{c_{\lambda}^N |\mathcal V_{J}( ar{\mathbf a})|}{T_m(\kappa)^{j_0 N}}\prod_{i=0}^{j_0 N-1}q_m\left(a_{im+1},\dots, a_{(i+1)m}ight)^{1-2\kappa}. \] By Lemma~ef{vq}, we find that for every $\mathbf a\in\mathcal E_1^N$, \[ |\mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)|\leqslant q_{J}(\mathbf a) \leqslant |\mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)|^{1+ rac{c}{R}} \quad 	ext{ and } \quad |\mathcal V_{J}( ar{\mathbf a})| \leqslant q_{J}( ar{\mathbf a}) \leqslant |\mathcal V_{J}( ar{\mathbf a})|^{1+ rac{c}{R}}. \] By \eqref{q_k_inverse} we have $q_{J}(\mathbf a) = q_{J}( ar{\mathbf a})$ and therefore, employing~\eqref{Qest}, we get \[  egin{aligned} |\mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)| &\geqslant |\mathcal V_{J}( ar{\mathbf a})|^{1/(1+ rac{c}{R})} = |\mathcal V_J( ar{\mathbf a})| \cdot |\mathcal V_{J}( ar{\mathbf a})|^{-c/(c+R)}\ &\geqslant |\mathcal V_{J}( ar{\mathbf a})| Q^{-(1+2\varepsilon)c/(R+c)}.\end{aligned} \] This gives \[ {\lambda}^N(A) \geqslant {\lambda}^N( ar{A}) Q^{-(1+2\varepsilon) c/(R+c)}, \] and the other inequality follows by interchanging the roles of the sets $A$ and $ ar{A}.$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to single words; mirror symmetry of $q_J$ and Lemma 3.4 compare $|\mathcal V_J(\mathbf a)|$ with $|\mathcal V_J(\bar{\mathbf a})|$.

nodes.name: Reduce to single words
nodes.statement: It is enough to prove the proposition for sets of the form \[ A=\{(\mathbf a,\mathbf b): \mathbf b \in \mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)\} \] for some $\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_{J})$; the result will then follow by taking unions over words $\mathbf a \in [M]^{J}$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to treat sets with a fixed $\mathbf a$.

nodes.name: Trivial case
nodes.statement:
Note from the definition of $\mathcal E_1$ that we have $\mathbf a \in \mathcal E_1^N$ if and only if $ ar{\mathbf a}\in \mathcal E_1^N.$ The result is trivially true when $\mathbf a
otin \mathcal E_1^N,$ as then $
u(A) = 
u( ar{A})=0.$
nodes.statement_short: If $\mathbf a\notin\mathcal E_1^N$ both sides vanish.

nodes.name: Compute both masses
nodes.statement: If $\mathbf a\in \mathcal E_1^N$ then, for $A$ as above, by the definition of ${\lambda}$ we have \[ {\lambda}^N(A) = \frac{c_{\lambda}^N |\mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)|}{T_m(\kappa)^{j_0 N}}\prod_{i=0}^{j_0 N-1}q_m\left(a_{im+1},\dots, a_{(i+1)m}\right)^{1-2\kappa}. \] In light of the symmetry \eqref{q_k_inverse}, we similarly have \[ {\lambda}^N(\bar{A}) = \frac{c_{\lambda}^N |\mathcal V_{J}(\bar{\mathbf a})|}{T_m(\kappa)^{j_0 N}}\prod_{i=0}^{j_0 N-1}q_m\left(a_{im+1},\dots, a_{(i+1)m}\right)^{1-2\kappa}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Write $\lambda^N(A)$ and $\lambda^N(\bar A)$ explicitly using the symmetry (2.9).

nodes.name: Compare digit counts
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{vq}, we find that for every $\mathbf a\in\mathcal E_1^N$, \[ |\mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)|\leqslant q_{J}(\mathbf a) \leqslant |\mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)|^{1+\frac{c}{R}} \quad \text{ and } \quad |\mathcal V_{J}(\bar{\mathbf a})| \leqslant q_{J}(\bar{\mathbf a}) \leqslant |\mathcal V_{J}(\bar{\mathbf a})|^{1+\frac{c}{R}}. \] By \eqref{q_k_inverse} we have $q_{J}(\mathbf a) = q_{J}(\bar{\mathbf a})$ and therefore, employing~\eqref{Qest}, we get \[ \begin{aligned} |\mathcal V_{J}(\mathbf a)| &\geqslant |\mathcal V_{J}(\bar{\mathbf a})|^{1/(1+\frac{c}{R})} = |\mathcal V_J(\bar{\mathbf a})| \cdot |\mathcal V_{J}(\bar{\mathbf a})|^{-c/(c+R)}\\ &\geqslant |\mathcal V_{J}(\bar{\mathbf a})| Q^{-(1+2\varepsilon)c/(R+c)}.\end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.4, (2.9) and (4.9) compare $|\mathcal V_J(\mathbf a)|$ and $|\mathcal V_J(\bar{\mathbf a})|$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This gives \[ {\lambda}^N(A) \geqslant {\lambda}^N(\bar{A}) Q^{-(1+2\varepsilon) c/(R+c)}, \] and the other inequality follows by interchanging the roles of the sets $A$ and $\bar{A}.$
nodes.statement_short: Deduce one inequality; swap roles for the other.

nodes.name: Measure of pairs with close denominator ratios
nodes.statement: Let $N\geqslant 1$ and $0<T<1$. Define \[ S = \left\{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal E^N \times \mathcal E^N : \left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right|<T \right\}. \] Then \[ {\lambda}^{2N}(S) \ll T^{2\kappa-3-4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon} Q^{(1+2\varepsilon)2c/(R+c)}, \] where the constant $c$ is as in Lemma~\ref{vq}.
nodes.statement_short: Pairs of words with $q_{J-1}/q_J$ within $T$ have $\lambda^{2N}$-measure $\ll T^{2\kappa-3-\dots}Q^{o(1)}$.
nodes.label: prop_close_ratios

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.4
nodes.statement: By~\eqref{cf_inverse}, we have \[ \left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right| = \left|\frac{p_J(\bar{\mathbf a})}{q_J(\bar{\mathbf a})}-\frac{p_J(\bar{\mathbf a^*})}{q_J(\bar{\mathbf a^*})}\right|. \] Observe that, upon mapping each $(\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*) \in S$ to $(\mathbf a \mathbf a^*, \mathbf b \mathbf b^*)$, the set $S$ satisfies the property described in \eqref{full}. The set $\bar{S}$ as in \eqref{mirror_set} is therefore well defined, and \[ \bar{S} \subseteq \left\{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal E^N\times \mathcal E^N : \left|\frac{p_J}{q_J}-\frac{p_J^*}{q_J^*}\right| < T \right\}, \] where $p_J^* = p_J(\mathbf a^*)$ and $q_J^* = q_J(\mathbf a^*)$. For any $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\in \mathcal E^N,$ the set \[ \bar{S}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) := \left\{ (\mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal E^{N} : \left| \frac{p_J}{q_J} - \frac{p_J^*}{q_J^*} \right| < T \right\} \] lifts to a vertical strip with base length $2T$ given by \[ \tilde S(\mathbf a, \mathbf b) = \bigcup_{(\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \bar{S}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)} C(\mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*). \] If we cover it by $1/(2T)$ squares of side $2T$, then each such square is contained in a ball of radius $O(T)$. Therefore \[ {\lambda}^N (\bar{S}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)) = \nu(\tilde{S}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)) \ll \frac{1}{2T}\cdot T^{2\kappa - 2 -4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon} \ll T^{2\kappa - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon } \] and \[ {\lambda}^{2N}(\bar{S}) \ll \int {\lambda}^N(\bar{S}(\mathbf a, \mathbf b)){\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^N \ll T^{2\kappa - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon}. \] The conclusion now follows from Proposition \ref{prop_almost_invariance}.
nodes.statement_short: Mirror the ratio condition into closeness of convergents, cover the resulting strip by balls and apply Lemma 4.2 and Proposition 4.3.

nodes.name: Mirror the ratio
nodes.statement: By~\eqref{cf_inverse}, we have \[ \left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right| = \left|\frac{p_J(\bar{\mathbf a})}{q_J(\bar{\mathbf a})}-\frac{p_J(\bar{\mathbf a^*})}{q_J(\bar{\mathbf a^*})}\right|. \]
nodes.statement_short: By (2.5) the ratio difference equals a difference of convergents of mirrored words.

nodes.name: Mirror set
nodes.statement: Observe that, upon mapping each $(\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*) \in S$ to $(\mathbf a \mathbf a^*, \mathbf b \mathbf b^*)$, the set $S$ satisfies the property described in \eqref{full}. The set $\bar{S}$ as in \eqref{mirror_set} is therefore well defined, and \[ \bar{S} \subseteq \left\{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal E^N\times \mathcal E^N : \left|\frac{p_J}{q_J}-\frac{p_J^*}{q_J^*}\right| < T \right\}, \] where $p_J^* = p_J(\mathbf a^*)$ and $q_J^* = q_J(\mathbf a^*)$.
nodes.statement_short: $S$ satisfies (4.15), so $\bar S$ is defined and lies in a set of close convergents.

nodes.name: Vertical strip
nodes.statement: For any $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\in \mathcal E^N,$ the set \[ \bar{S}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) := \left\{ (\mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal E^{N} : \left| \frac{p_J}{q_J} - \frac{p_J^*}{q_J^*} \right| < T \right\} \] lifts to a vertical strip with base length $2T$ given by \[ \tilde S(\mathbf a, \mathbf b) = \bigcup_{(\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \bar{S}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)} C(\mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*). \]
nodes.statement_short: Fibres of $\bar S$ lift to vertical strips of width $2T$.

nodes.name: Cover by balls
nodes.statement: If we cover it by $1/(2T)$ squares of side $2T$, then each such square is contained in a ball of radius $O(T)$. Therefore \[ {\lambda}^N (\bar{S}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)) = \nu(\tilde{S}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)) \ll \frac{1}{2T}\cdot T^{2\kappa - 2 -4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon} \ll T^{2\kappa - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon } \] and \[ {\lambda}^{2N}(\bar{S}) \ll \int {\lambda}^N(\bar{S}(\mathbf a, \mathbf b)){\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^N \ll T^{2\kappa - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Cover the strip by balls and apply Lemma 4.2(b), then integrate.

nodes.name: Return via mirroring
nodes.statement: The conclusion now follows from Proposition \ref{prop_almost_invariance}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 4.3.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1(ii): polynomial Fourier decay
nodes.statement_short: Use the self-similarity to write the Fourier transform as an average of $F(t,u)$ and apply the comparison lemma. The key step bounds the second moment of $F$ by off-diagonal oscillatory-integral estimates with the mirror symmetry of Proposition 4.4.

nodes.name: Plan of Section 5
nodes.statement: In this section, we will upper bound the decay of the Fourier transform of the measure constructed in Section~\ref{subsection_ConstructionOfMeasures}, thereby establishing Theorem~\ref{MainThm}~\eqref{MainThm_point_decay}. As Theorem~\ref{MainThm}~\eqref{MainThm_point_Frostman_dimension} follows from Lemma~\ref{lem_FD} point~\eqref{point_dimFrostman}, this will complete the proof of Theorem \ref{MainThm}.
nodes.statement_short: This section proves the Fourier decay; Frostman dimension came from Lemma 4.2.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1(i)
nodes.statement: As Theorem~\ref{MainThm}~\eqref{MainThm_point_Frostman_dimension} follows from Lemma~\ref{lem_FD} point~\eqref{point_dimFrostman}, this will complete the proof of Theorem \ref{MainThm}.
nodes.statement_short: Part (i) is Lemma 4.2(b).

nodes.name: Comparison lemma
nodes.statement_short: State and prove the comparison Lemma 5.1.

nodes.name: Comparison lemma
nodes.statement:
Let $M_1, M_2 \in (0,\infty)$, let $F(t,u)$ be a $C^1$ function on $B = [0,1] 	imes [-1,1]$ such that \[ \| F \|_\infty \leqslant 1, \qquad \| \partial_t F\|_\infty \leqslant M_1, \qquad \| \partial_u F \|_\infty \leqslant M_2, \] and put \[ m_2 = \int_B |F(t,u)|^2 {\,{m d}} t {\,{m d}} u. \] Let $
u$ be a probability measure on $B$, let $r > 0$, and denote by ${\Lambda}(r)$ the maximum of $
u(\mathcal R)$ as $\mathcal R$ ranges over axis-parallel filled rectangles of respective side lengths $r/M_1$ and $r/M_2$ in $B$. Then \[ \int_B |F(t,u)| {\,{m d}} 
u(t,u) \leqslant 3r + {\Lambda}(r) \left(2 +  rac{M_1}r +  rac{2M_2}r +  rac{m_2 M_1 M_2}{r^4} ight). \]
nodes.statement_short: Bounds $\int|F|d\nu$ via sup-norms of partial derivatives, the $L^2$ mass $m_2$ and the $\nu$-measure of small rectangles.
nodes.label: ComparisonLemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: Consider $\lfloor M_1/r \rfloor \cdot \lfloor 2 M_2/r \rfloor$ axis-parallel filled rectangles of respective side lengths $r/M_1$ and $r/M_2$, with non-overlapping interiors, whose union covers \[ \left[0, 1 - \: \frac{r}{M_1} \right] \times \left[-1, 1 - \: \frac{r}{M_2} \right]. \] Let $N$ be the number of these filled rectangles $\mathcal R$ on which \[ \max \{ |F(t,u)|: (t,u) \in \mathcal R \} \geqslant 3r. \] Within any such filled rectangle $\mathcal R$, there exists a pair $(t_0,u_0)$ such that $|F(t_0,u_0)| \geqslant 3r$. Thus, for any $(t,u) \in \mathcal R$, we have \begin{align*} |F(t,u)| &\geqslant |F(t_0,u_0)| - |F(t,u)-F(t,u_0)| - |F(t,u_0) - F(t_0,u_0)| \\ &\geqslant 3r - r - r = r, \end{align*} by the mean value theorem. Therefore \[ m_2 \geqslant N \frac{r^2}{M_1 M_2} r^2 = N \frac{r^4}{M_1M_2}. \] At most $\lceil M_1/r \rceil + \lceil 2M_2 / r \rceil$ filled rectangles, further to our original ones, are needed to cover $B$, so \begin{align*} \int_B |F(t,u)| {\,{\rm d}} \nu (t,u) &\leqslant 3r + (N + \lceil M_1/r \rceil + \lceil 2M_2 / r \rceil) {\Lambda}(r) \\ &\leqslant 3r + {\Lambda}(r) \left(2 + \frac{M_1}r + \frac{2M_2}r + \frac{m_2 M_1 M_2}{r^4} \right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Cover by rectangles; on rectangles where $|F|$ is large, $|F|\ge r$ throughout, bounding their number by $m_2$.

nodes.name: Rectangle cover
nodes.statement: Consider $\lfloor M_1/r \rfloor \cdot \lfloor 2 M_2/r \rfloor$ axis-parallel filled rectangles of respective side lengths $r/M_1$ and $r/M_2$, with non-overlapping interiors, whose union covers \[ \left[0, 1 - \: \frac{r}{M_1} \right] \times \left[-1, 1 - \: \frac{r}{M_2} \right]. \] Let $N$ be the number of these filled rectangles $\mathcal R$ on which \[ \max \{ |F(t,u)|: (t,u) \in \mathcal R \} \geqslant 3r. \]
nodes.statement_short: Tile $B$ by rectangles and let $N$ count those where $|F|\ge 3r$ somewhere.

nodes.name: Mean value theorem
nodes.statement: Within any such filled rectangle $\mathcal R$, there exists a pair $(t_0,u_0)$ such that $|F(t_0,u_0)| \geqslant 3r$. Thus, for any $(t,u) \in \mathcal R$, we have \begin{align*} |F(t,u)| &\geqslant |F(t_0,u_0)| - |F(t,u)-F(t,u_0)| - |F(t,u_0) - F(t_0,u_0)| \\ &\geqslant 3r - r - r = r, \end{align*} by the mean value theorem.
nodes.statement_short: On such rectangles $|F|\ge r$ throughout.

nodes.name: Bound N by m_2
nodes.statement: Therefore \[ m_2 \geqslant N \frac{r^2}{M_1 M_2} r^2 = N \frac{r^4}{M_1M_2}. \]

nodes.name: Integrate
nodes.statement: At most $\lceil M_1/r \rceil + \lceil 2M_2 / r \rceil$ filled rectangles, further to our original ones, are needed to cover $B$, so \begin{align*} \int_B |F(t,u)| {\,{\rm d}} \nu (t,u) &\leqslant 3r + (N + \lceil M_1/r \rceil + \lceil 2M_2 / r \rceil) {\Lambda}(r) \\ &\leqslant 3r + {\Lambda}(r) \left(2 + \frac{M_1}r + \frac{2M_2}r + \frac{m_2 M_1 M_2}{r^4} \right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Sum the contributions of small and large rectangles.

nodes.name: Rewrite the Fourier transform
nodes.statement_short: Using self-similarity, write $\widehat\nu(k_1,k_2)=\int_B F\,d\nu$ with $F$ an average over the first $J$ digits.

nodes.name: Simplification for large delta
nodes.statement: For the proof, we may assume that $\delta$ is large, see Remark~\ref{rem_justification_concrete_eta}. For $\delta$ large enough, some of the cases considered below become simpler, for instance the cases described by~\eqref{third_scenario_description} or~\eqref{Case_2i_subcase_one}. For the sake of robustness, we also allow ${\delta}$ to be small. However, the busy reader may wish to assume that ${\delta}$ and hence $\phi$ is sufficiently large. For $\phi\geqslant 2$ (and $Q$ large enough, which we can assume without loss of generality), the inequality ~\eqref{third_scenario_description} implies that $q_J=q_J^*$ and $q_{J-1}=q_{J-1}^*$, and~\eqref{Case_2i_subcase_one} becomes $q_{J-1}=q_{J-1}^*$. The two simplified cases then reduce to the diagonal setting considered at the start of Subsection~\ref{ss_diagonal_contribution}.

nodes.name: Range of u
nodes.statement: We have \[ -t \leqslant u \leqslant 1-t. \]
nodes.section: 5.2 The Fourier transform of our measure

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: Observe that $u$ is given by an Ostrowski expansion in $t$. We use the fact that $D_0, D_1, D_2, \ldots$ alternate in sign, together with the identity \eqref{EndpointIdentity}. Further, as $R \mid J$, we have $b_{J+1} \leqslant a_{J+1} - 1 = a_1(t) - 1$. Using this information, we compute that \[ u \geqslant a_2(t) D_1(t) + a_4(t) D_3(t) + \dots = a_2(t) D_1(t) - D_2(t) = - t \] and \begin{align*} u &\leqslant (a_1(t) - 1) D_0(t) + a_3(t) D_2(t) + a_5(t) D_3(t) + \dots \\ &= (a_1(t) - 1) D_0(t) - D_1(t) = 1 - t. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Extremal Ostrowski expansions and the endpoint identity give $-t\le u\le1-t$.
nodes.section: 5.2 The Fourier transform of our measure

nodes.name: Ostrowski expansion of u
nodes.statement: Observe that $u$ is given by an Ostrowski expansion in $t$. We use the fact that $D_0, D_1, D_2, \ldots$ alternate in sign, together with the identity \eqref{EndpointIdentity}. Further, as $R \mid J$, we have $b_{J+1} \leqslant a_{J+1} - 1 = a_1(t) - 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Use alternating signs, the endpoint identity and $b_{J+1}\le a_1(t)-1$.
nodes.section: 5.2 The Fourier transform of our measure

nodes.name: Extremal expansions
nodes.statement: Using this information, we compute that \[ u \geqslant a_2(t) D_1(t) + a_4(t) D_3(t) + \dots = a_2(t) D_1(t) - D_2(t) = - t \] and \begin{align*} u &\leqslant (a_1(t) - 1) D_0(t) + a_3(t) D_2(t) + a_5(t) D_3(t) + \dots \\ &= (a_1(t) - 1) D_0(t) - D_1(t) = 1 - t. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Compute the extreme values of $u$.

nodes.name: Periodic extension of nu
nodes.statement: Clearly, translations by $\mathbb Z^2$ of $P$, defined by~\eqref{def_B} above, tile the plane $\mathbb R^2$, hence we can extend the measure $\nu$ to $\mathbb R^2$ by periodicity. We could also consider this measure as being defined on $[0,1]^2$. Indeed, the parallelogram $P$ consists of two triangles: \[ \begin{aligned} P&=T_1\cup T_2,\\ T_1&:=\left\{(t,u)\in [0,1]\times [0,1] : 0 \leqslant u\leqslant 1-t \right\},\\ T_2&:=\left\{(t,u)\in [0,1]\times [-1,0] : -t \leqslant u\leqslant 0 \right\}, \end{aligned} \] and $[0,1]^2$ is the union of $T_1$ and the translation of $T_2$ by the vector $(0,1)$.
