nodes.name: Equation (5.8)
nodes.statement: \notag F(t,u) &= \int_{\mathcal E^K} e \left( -k_1 \frac{p_J + t p_{J-1}}{q_J + tq_{J-1}} \: - k_2 \left(g(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,t) + \frac{u}{q_J + tq_{J-1}}\right) \right) \\ & \qquad {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^K(\mathbf a,\mathbf b).
nodes.section: 5.2 The Fourier transform of our measure
nodes.label: F_definition

nodes.name: Partial derivatives of F
nodes.statement: For $k \geqslant 0$, we have \[ \partial_t\alpha = \partial_t \left( \frac{p_J + t p_{J-1}}{q_J + tq_{J-1}} \right) = \frac{1}{(q_J+tq_{J-1})^2} \] and \[ \partial_t D_k({\alpha}) = q_k\cdot \partial_t {\alpha} = \frac{q_k}{(q_J+tq_{J-1})^2}. \] Hence \begin{equation} \partial_t g = \sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}\partial_t D_k({\alpha}) = (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k \end{equation} and \[ \partial_t \left( \frac{u}{q_J + tq_{J-1}}\right) = \frac{-u q_{J-1}}{(q_J+tq_{J-1})^2 }. \] The partial derivative of $F$ with respect to $t$ is therefore \begin{align*} &\partial_t F(t,u) \\ &= \int_{\mathcal E^K} \frac{-2 \pi i}{(q_J+tq_{J-1})^2}\left(k_1 + k_2 \left(-uq_{J-1} + \sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k \right) \right) \\ & \qquad \cdot e \left( -k_1 \frac{p_J + t p_{J-1}}{q_J + tq_{J-1}} - k_2 \left(g(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,t) + \frac{u}{q_J + tq_{J-1}}\right) \right) {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^K(\mathbf a,\mathbf b). \end{align*} By uniqueness of the Ostrowski expansion, if $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \in \mathcal E^K$ then \[ \sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k < q_J, \] see \cite[Chapter II, \S 4]{RS1992}, and so \[ \left| -uq_{J-1} + \sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k \right| < q_J + q_{J-1} \qquad (-1 \leqslant u \leqslant 1). \] Therefore \[ |\partial_t F(t,u)| \leqslant 2 \pi \left( \frac{|k_1|}{Q^{2(1-2\varepsilon)}} + \frac{2|k_2|}{Q^{1-2\varepsilon}} \right). \] The partial derivative of $F(t,u)$ with respect to $u$ is \begin{align*} &\partial_u F(t,u) \\ &= \int_{\mathcal E^K}\frac{-(2 \pi i) k_2}{q_J+tq_{J-1}} e\left( -k_1 \frac{p_J + t p_{J-1}}{q_J + tq_{J-1}} - k_2 \left(g(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,t) + \frac{u}{q_J + tq_{J-1}}\right) \right) \\ &\qquad {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^K(\mathbf a,\mathbf b), \end{align*} whence \[ |\partial_u F(t,u)| \leqslant \frac{2\pi |k_2|}{ Q^{1-2\varepsilon}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\partial_tF$ and $\partial_uF$.

nodes.name: Equation (5.9)
nodes.statement: \partial_t g = \sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}\partial_t D_k({\alpha}) = (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k
nodes.label: gt

nodes.name: Second moment of F
nodes.statement: With $B = [0,1] \times [-1, 1]$, the second moment of the function $F(t,u)$ defined in \eqref{F_definition} is \begin{align*} m_2 &= \int_B |F(t,u)|^2 \mathrm{d}t \mathrm{d}u \\ &= \int_{\mathcal E^{2K}} \int_0^1 \int_{-1}^1 e\Big(k_1\Big( \frac{p_J+tp_{J-1}}{q_J+tq_{J-1}} \: - \: \frac{p_J^* +tp_{J-1}^*}{q_J^* +tq_{J-1}^*}\Big)\Big) \\ & \quad e\big(k_2(g(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,t) - g(\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*,t))\big) \\ & \quad e\Big(k_2u\Big( \frac{1}{q_J+tq_{J-1}} \: - \: \frac{1}{q_J^*+tq_{J-1}^*}\Big)\Big) {\,{\rm d}} u {\,{\rm d}} t {\,{\rm d}}\lambda^K(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) {\,{\rm d}}\lambda^K(\mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*). \end{align*} Here and in what follows, for $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b), (\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal E^K$, we write for convenience $q_J=q_J(\mathbf a)$ and $q_J^*=q_J(\mathbf a^*),$ and similarly for $q_{J-1}, q_{J-1}^*.$ Continuing with the estimation of $m_2,$ let us set \begin{equation} f_1(t) = \frac{p_J + t p_{J-1}}{q_J + tq_{J-1}} \: - \: \frac{p_J^* + tp_{J-1}^*}{q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*}, \qquad f_2(t) = g(\mathbf a,\mathbf b, t) - g(\mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*, t) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} z(t) = z(t;k_2) = k_2 \left( \frac1{q_J + tq_{J-1}} \: - \: \frac1{q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*} \right), \end{equation} and write \begin{equation} f(t) = f(t; k_1, k_2) = k_1 f_1(t) + k_2 f_2(t). \end{equation} Now \begin{align} m_2 &= \int_{\mathcal E^{2K}} \mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K}, \end{align} where \[ \mathfrak J = \mathfrak J(\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*) = \int_0^1 e(f(t)) \int_{-1}^1 e(u z(t)) {\,{\rm d}} u {\,{\rm d}} t. \] Observe that if $z \in \mathbb R$ then \[ \int_{-1}^1 e(zu) {\,{\rm d}} u = 2 \mathrm{sinc}(2 \pi z). \] This is immediate if $z = 0$, and otherwise \[ \int_{-1}^1 e(zu) {\,{\rm d}} u = \frac{e(z) - e(-z)}{2 \pi i z} = \frac{\sin (2 \pi z)}{\pi z} = 2 \mathrm{sinc}(2\pi z). \] Therefore \begin{equation} \mathfrak J = \mathfrak J(\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*) = 2 \int_0^1 e(f(t)) \mathrm{sinc}(2 \pi z(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t. \end{equation} We now estimate $m_2$ by partitioning $\mathcal E^K\times \mathcal E^K$ into suitably chosen subsets and bounding the corresponding contribution of $\mathfrak J$. \subsubsection{The diagonal contribution} Write \[ \mathcal D = \{ (\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal E^{2K}: \mathbf a = \mathbf a^* \} \] for the set of quadruples $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal E^{2K}$ such that $\mathbf a = \mathbf a^*$. Since $|\mathfrak J| \leqslant 2,$ the contribution of $\mathcal D$ to the integral in \eqref{m2} is \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal D}\mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ll (\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\mathcal D). \end{equation} The right-hand side of \eqref{diagonal} is equal to \begin{align*} (\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\mathcal D) & = \sum_{\mathbf a \in \mathcal E_1^{K}}\mathop{\sum\sum}_{\mathbf b, \mathbf b^* \in \mathcal V_{KJ_0}(\mathbf a)}(\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a,\mathbf b^*)\\ & = \sum_{\mathbf a \in \mathcal E_1^{K}} \Bigg(\sum_{\mathbf b\in \mathcal V_{KJ_0}(\mathbf a)}\!\!\lambda^K(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\Bigg)^2 . \end{align*} By Lemmas \ref{lem_size_of_cylinder_set} and \ref{vq}, the innermost sum satisfies \begin{align*} \sum_{\mathbf b\in \mathcal V_{KJ_0}(\mathbf a)}\!\!\lambda^K(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) &\leqslant | \mathcal V_{KJ_0}(\mathbf a)| \frac{2^K}{T_m(\kappa)^{j_0K}}Q_0^{(1+2\varepsilon)(1-2\kappa)K}\\ &\leqslant \frac{2^{K}Q_0^{(1-2{\kappa})(1+2\varepsilon)K+(1+2\varepsilon)K}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0K}}. \end{align*} This gives \begin{align*} (\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\mathcal D) &\leqslant \frac{2^{K}Q_0^{(1-2{\kappa})(1+2\varepsilon)K+(1+2\varepsilon)K}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0K}} \sum_{\mathbf a \in \mathcal E_1^{K}} \sum_{\mathbf b\in \mathcal V_{KJ_0}(\mathbf a)}\!\!\lambda^K(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \\ & = \frac{2^{K}Q_0^{(1-2{\kappa})(1+2\varepsilon)K+(1+2\varepsilon)K}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0K}}, \end{align*} where in the last step we have used the fact that $\lambda^K$ is a probability measure. The assumption \eqref{T_m_is_large} now yields \[ (\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\mathcal D) \leqslant Q_0^{(1-2{\kappa})(1+2\varepsilon)K+(1+2\varepsilon)K} \] and, recalling that $Q = Q_0^K$, we finally have \[ \int_{\mathcal D}\mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ll Q^{2-2\kappa + 4(1-\kappa)\varepsilon}. \] \subsubsection{The off-diagonal contribution} We now turn to the contribution of the complement of $\mathcal D$ to the integral in \eqref{m2}. Bounding the ${\lambda}^{2K}$ measure of the domain of integration alone will not be enough, so we aim to establish alternative upper bounds for the integrand $\mathfrak J.$ \par Write \begin{equation} h(t) = 2 \mathrm{sinc}(2 \pi z(t)), \quad \mathfrak A(y) = \int_0^y e(f(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t \qquad (0\leqslant t,y \leqslant 1). \end{equation} By partial integration in \eqref{fJ_first_presentation}, we have \[ \mathfrak J = \int_0^1 e(f(t)) h(t) {\,{\rm d}} t = \mathfrak A(1) h(1) - \int_0^1 \mathfrak A(y) h'(y) {\,{\rm d}} y. \] Since for the function $ z(t)$ defined in \eqref{def_z} we have $z'(t) \ll |k_2| Q^{2\varepsilon - 1}$, and $\mathrm{sinc}$ has bounded derivative, we have \[ h'(t) \ll |k_2| Q^{2\varepsilon - 1} \] and consequently \begin{equation} \mathfrak J \ll (1 + |k_2| Q^{2\varepsilon - 1}) \max \{ |\mathfrak A(y)|: 0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1 \}. \end{equation} We bound the off-diagonal contribution to $m_2$ by partitioning $\mathcal E^{2K}\setminus \mathcal D$ into appropriately chosen subsets, each of them corresponding to one of the cases that follow. \bigskip \textbf{Case~I.} Recalling the parameter $\phi>0$ from~\eqref{def_delta_phi}, we consider the quadruples $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)$ for which \begin{equation} |q_J - q_J^*| + |q_{J-1} - q_{J-1}^*| \leqslant 3Q^{1-\phi}. \end{equation} Under this assumption, we compute that \[ \begin{aligned} \left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right| &= \frac{|q_{J-1} q_J^*-q_{J} q_{J-1}^*|}{q_{J} q_J^*} \\ &= \frac{\left|q_{J-1} \left(q_J^*-q_J\right)-q_{J}\left(q_{J-1}^*-q_{J-1}\right)\right|}{q_{J}q_J^*}\\ &\ll \frac{|q_J^* - q_J| + |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}|}{q_J^*} \ll Q^{2\varepsilon-\phi}, \end{aligned} \] where at the last step we used Lemma~\ref{lem_FD}~(a) and~\eqref{third_scenario_description}. Thus, by Proposition~\ref{prop_close_ratios}, we have \begin{align*} &(\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) : \text{ \eqref{third_scenario_description} holds}\}) \\ & \qquad \ll Q^{(2\varepsilon - \phi) (2 {\kappa} - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon) + (1 + 2\varepsilon) 2c / (R+c)} , \end{align*} where the constant $c$ is as in Lemma~\ref{vq}. We conclude that the contribution to $m_2$ is \begin{equation} O( Q^{(2\varepsilon - \phi) (2 {\kappa} - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon) + (1 + 2\varepsilon) 2c / (R+c)} ). \end{equation} It remains to deal with the contribution to $m_2$ of $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)$ for which \eqref{third_scenario_description} fails, and we do so by considering two subcases according to the size of $|k_2|.$ \bigskip \textbf{Case~II(i).} Here we examine the contribution to $m_2$ of $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)$ such that \begin{equation} |q_J^* - q_J| + |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| > 3Q^{1- \phi} \end{equation} when \begin{equation} |k_2| \gg Q^{1 + 3\phi}. \end{equation} By the definitions of $\mathfrak J$ and $h(t)$ in \eqref{fJ_first_presentation}, \eqref{sha_def}, we have \[ \mathfrak J \ll \int_0^1 |h(t)|{\,{\rm d}} t \ll \int_0^1 \min \{ 1, |z(t)|^{-1} \} {\,{\rm d}} t, \] where by \eqref{def_z} \[ z(t) = k_2 \frac{t(q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}) + q_J^* - q_J} {(q_J + tq_{J-1}) (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)}. \] First, suppose \begin{equation} |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| > Q^{1-\phi}. \end{equation} Write $S$ for the set of $t \in [0,1]$ such that \[ \left| t + \frac{q_J^* - q_J} {q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}} \right| \leqslant Q^{- \phi}. \] Then \[ \mathfrak J \ll \mathfrak J_1 + \mathfrak J_2, \] where \[ \mathfrak J_1 = \int_S \min \{ 1, |z(t)|^{-1} \} {\,{\rm d}} t, \qquad \mathfrak J_2 = \int_{[0,1]\setminus S} \min \{ 1, |z(t)|^{-1} \} {\,{\rm d}} t. \] For $\mathfrak J_1,$ we bound the integrand by $1$ and deduce that $\mathfrak J_1 \ll Q^{-\phi}.$ Regarding $\mathfrak J_2,$ the inequalities \eqref{denominator_bounds}, \eqref{K_is_big} and \eqref{FirstSuppose} imply that for any $t\in [0,1] \setminus S$ we have \[ |z(t)| \gg \: Q^{3\phi - 1 - 4\varepsilon} |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| \cdot \left| t + \frac{q_J^* - q_J} {q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}} \right| \gg Q^{\phi - 4\varepsilon}. \] Thus, we compute that $ \mathfrak J_2 \ll Q^{4 \varepsilon - \phi},$ whence $\mathfrak J \ll Q^{4 \varepsilon - \phi}.$ Now suppose instead that \begin{equation} |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| \leqslant Q^{1 - \phi}. \end{equation} Then by \eqref{sum_q_big} \[ |q_J^* - q_J| > 2Q^{1 - \phi}, \] and consequently for any $0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1,$ \[ \begin{split} |z(t)| &\gg Q^{3\phi - 1 - 4 \varepsilon} |(q_{J-1}-q_{J-1}^*)t +(q_J-q_J^*)| > Q^{2 \phi - 4\varepsilon}. \end{split} \] Therefore $\mathfrak J \ll Q^{ 4\varepsilon - 2 \phi}$. We have demonstrated that $\mathfrak J \ll Q^{4\varepsilon - \phi}$ in Case II(i). This means that the corresponding contribution to $m_2$ is \begin{equation} O(Q^{4 \varepsilon - \phi}). \end{equation} \bigskip \textbf{Case II(ii).} It remains to deal with the contribution of points for which we have \eqref{sum_q_big} when \begin{equation} |k_2| \ll Q^{1 + 3 \phi}. \end{equation} By \eqref{kk_size} and \eqref{scenario_2}, we have \begin{equation} |k_1| \asymp Q^{2 + {\delta}}, \end{equation} and by~\eqref{ub_J_second} we have \[ \mathfrak J \ll Q^{3 \phi+2\varepsilon} \max \{ |\mathfrak A(y)|: 0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1 \}. \] For the functions $f_1$ and $f_2$ defined in \eqref{f1f2}, we compute that \[ f_1'(t) = (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2} - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2} \] and, using \eqref{gt}, \begin{align*} f_2'(t) &= (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b^*_{k+1}q_k^*. \end{align*} Thus, for $f=k_1f_1 + k_2f_2$ introduced in \eqref{f_def}, we have \begin{align*} f'(t) &= k_1( (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2} - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2}) \\ & \quad + k_2\left( (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b^*_{k+1}q_k^* \right) \\ &= (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2} \left(k_1+k_2\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k\right) \\ & \qquad - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2} \left(k_1+k_2\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}^*q_k^*\right). \end{align*} Setting \begin{equation} s = k_1 + k_2 \sum_{k=0}^{J-1} b_{k+1} q_k, \qquad s^* = k_1 + k_2 \sum_{k=0}^{J-1} b_{k+1}^* q_k^*, \end{equation} the derivative $f'(t)$ can be written as \begin{equation} f'(t) = \frac{(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 s^*}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2}. \end{equation} We partition the set $\mathcal C := \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal E^{2K}: \eqref{sum_q_big} \text{ holds} \}$ into three sets $\mathcal C_0$, $\mathcal C_1$ and $\mathcal C_2$ that are defined as follows: \begin{align*} \mathcal C_0 &= \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal C : ss^* =0 \}, \\ \mathcal C_1 &= \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal C : ss^* <0 \}, \\ \mathcal C_2 &= \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal C : ss^* >0 \}. \end{align*} For the analysis of the sets $\mathcal C_0, \mathcal C_1, \mathcal C_2$, we need to estimate the ${\lambda}^K$-measure of the set where $|s|$ assumes values up to a certain threshold. In the following lemma, we essentially consider $s$ as a random variable, where $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \in \mathcal E^{K}$ is distributed according to $ {\lambda}^{K}$. \begin{lemma} Assume that $k_2 \ne 0$. Then, for $T \geqslant 0$, we have \[ {\lambda}^K(|s| \leqslant T) \leqslant \left(\frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right) Q^{2 \varepsilon - 1}, \] where $Q=\exp\left(J\sigma_m\right)$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} First, note that \[ {\lambda}^K\left(|s| \leqslant T\right)=\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\right), \] where $\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}$ is a characteristic function of the subset of $\mathcal E^K$ defined by the condition $|s| \leqslant T$. Then, by using the tower property of conditional expectation, we have \[ \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\right)=\mathbb E\left(\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)\right). \] We are going to upper bound the random variable $\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)$, and then use the fact that an upper bound for a random variable is also an upper bound for its expectation. To find a suitable upper bound for $\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)$, we observe first that \[ s = k_1 + k_2 N, \qquad N = \sum_{k=0}^{J-1} b_{k+1} q_k. \] Writing $\mathbf a = (\mathbf a^{(1)}, \ldots,\mathbf a^{(J/m)})$, the conditional probability that $N$ takes a specific value is at most $\prod_{i=1}^{J/m} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})|^{-1}$. As $s \equiv k_1 \mmod |k_2|$, the conditional probability that $|s| \leqslant T$ is at most \[ \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right) \leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right) \prod_{i=1}^{J/m} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})|^{-1}. \] By Lemma~\ref{vq} and the inequalities \eqref{R_is_large}, \eqref{Edef}, we infer that \[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right) &\leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)\frac{27^{J/R}} {\prod_{i=1}^{J/m}q_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})} \\ &\leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)\frac{27^{J/R}}{Q^{1-\varepsilon}} \leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)Q^{2\varepsilon-1}. \end{aligned} \] Taking expectations gives the conclusion of the lemma. \end{proof} We may now examine each of the sets $\mathcal C_0, \mathcal C_1, \mathcal C_2$ separately. By Lemma~\ref{SmallProb}, we have ${\lambda}^{2K}(\mathcal C_0) \leqslant 2Q^{2\varepsilon-1}$, and since $|\mathfrak J| \leqslant 2$, this gives \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal C_0} \mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ll Q^{2\varepsilon - 1}. \end{equation} Observe that if $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal C_1$ then, by \eqref{fprime1}, \[ Q^{2+12\varepsilon} |f'(t)| \gg |s| + |s^*| \geqslant 1. \] As $f'$ is monotonic, Lemma \ref{lem_ub_nozero} yields, for every $y\in[0,1]$, \begin{equation} |\mathfrak A(y)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)| \ll \frac{Q^{2+12\varepsilon}} {|s|+|s^*|}. \end{equation} Under the assumption~\eqref{scenario_2}, we have $|k_1|\asymp Q^{2+\delta}$ and thus \[ |k_1| \gg |k_2| Q^{1 + 2 \varepsilon}. \] Then, by the triangle inequality for \eqref{ss_def}, we have \begin{equation} \min\left(|s|, |s^*|\right) \geqslant |k_1| - |k_2| Q^{1+2\varepsilon} \gg Q^{2+{\delta}}. \end{equation} Thus \eqref{ub_J_second}, \eqref{scenario_2}, \eqref{ub_U_C_one} and~\eqref{lb_s_C_one} imply that \[ \mathfrak J \ll Q^{3\phi+2\varepsilon-\delta+12\varepsilon} =Q^{3\phi-\delta+14\varepsilon} \qquad ((\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal C_1). \] Hence \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal C_1} \mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ll Q^{3\phi-\delta+14\varepsilon}. \end{equation} \bigskip Finally, we turn our attention to $\mathcal C_2$. We assume that $s > s^* > 0$. The other cases within $\mathcal C_2$ can be handled by symmetrical reasoning. By \eqref{fprime1}, we have that $f'(t)$ is equal to \begin{align*} & \frac{((q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v - (q_J + tq_{J-1}) v^*) ((q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v + (q_J + tq_{J-1}) v^*)}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2}, \end{align*} where \[ v = \sqrt s, \qquad v^* = \sqrt{s^*}. \] Hence \[ f'(t) = (At + B) G(t), \] where \[ A = q_{J-1}^*v - q_{J-1}v^*, \qquad B = q_J^* v - q_J v^* \] and \[ G(t) = \frac{(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v + (q_J + tq_{J-1}) v^*}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2}. \] Plainly $$|G(t)| \gg Q^{- 3-10\varepsilon} (v+v^*).$$ We compute that \begin{multline*} (q_J + tq_{J-1})^3 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^3 G'(t) = (q_J + tq_{J-1}) (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*) (q_{J-1}^*v + q_{J-1} v^*) \\ \hfill -2(q_{J-1}(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*) + q_{J-1}^* (q_J + tq_{J-1})) \cdot \\ \cdot ((q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v + (q_J + tq_{J-1})v^*), \end{multline*} and so $$|G'(t)| \ll Q^{ - 3 + 18\varepsilon}(v+v^*).$$ Now for the function $\mathfrak A$ defined in \eqref{sha_def}, Lemma \ref{ExpInt} furnishes \begin{equation} \mathfrak A(y)^2 \ll \frac{Q^{3+66\varepsilon}} {|A| (v+v^*)} \ll \frac{Q^{4+68\varepsilon}}{|(q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|} \qquad (0\leqslant y \leqslant 1). \end{equation} In order to make use of the bound \eqref{bound_case_one}, we write the region of integration $\mathcal C_2$ as the union of the three sets \[ \begin{aligned} &\mathcal S_1 = \left\{ |(q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|\geqslant Q^{4+8\phi} \right\},\\ &\mathcal S_2 = \left\{ \min_{t\in [0,1]}\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^*\right|\geqslant Q^{4+8\phi} \right\}, \\ &\mathcal S_3 = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} |(q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|<Q^{4+8\phi} \quad \text{ and } \\ \displaystyle \min_{t\in [0,1]}\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^*\right|< Q^{4+8\phi} \end{array}\right\}. \end{aligned} \] $\bullet$ For $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal S_1,$ the bound~\eqref{bound_case_one} gives $\mathfrak A(y)\ll Q^{34\varepsilon - 4\phi}$ for every $y\in[0,1]$, and thus, by \eqref{ub_J_second} and \eqref{scenario_2}, \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal S_1}\mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ \ll Q^{36\varepsilon - \phi}. \end{equation} $\bullet$ When $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal S_2$, it follows from~\eqref{fprime1} and the definition of $\mathcal S_2$ that $|f'(t)|\geqslant Q^{8\phi - 8\varepsilon}$. We also compute, by differentiating~\eqref{fprime1}, that \[ f''(t) = - \: \frac{2q_{J-1}s}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^3} + \frac{2q_{J-1}^*s^*}{(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^3}. \] This shows that $f''(t)=0$ if and only if \[ q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*=\left(q_J + tq_{J-1}\right)\left(\frac{q_{J-1}^*s^*}{q_{J-1}s}\right)^{1/3}. \] This equation is at most linear in $t$, and we claim that it has at most one solution. Indeed, assume for a contradiction that it has more than one solution. Then $f'' = 0$, so $f'$ is constant. By \eqref{fprime1}, this entails that $f' = 0$, contradicting the definition of $\mathcal S_2$. Therefore $f'$ is monotonic in at most two stretches. We may therefore apply Lemma~\ref{lem_ub_nozero} with $k=1$ and $\lambda=Q^{8\phi - 8\varepsilon}$, to find \[ \mathfrak A(y)\ll Q^{-8\phi + 8\varepsilon}. \] Combining this with \eqref{ub_J_second} and~\eqref{scenario_2} furnishes \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal S_2}\mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ \ll Q^{10\varepsilon-5\phi}. \end{equation} $\bullet$ For $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal S_3$, we use the trivial upper bound $|\mathfrak J| \leqslant 2$, and establish an upper bound for $\lambda^{2K}(\mathcal S_3).$ Recall that we have \eqref{k1large} in the present setting. Now, applying the triangle inequality to the definitions of $s, s^*$ in \eqref{ss_def}, we have \begin{equation} |s|, |s^*| \geqslant |k_1| - |k_2| Q^{1+2\varepsilon} \gg Q^{2+{\delta}}. \end{equation} By definition, for every quadruple in $\mathcal S_3$, we have the following system of linear inequalities: \begin{equation} \begin{cases} &|({q_{J-1}^*})^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|<Q^{4+8\phi},\\ &\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^*\right| < Q^{4+8\phi}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Since $v=\sqrt{s}$ and $v^*=\sqrt{s^*}$ by definition, we see from \eqref{lb_s} that \begin{equation} v, v^* \gg Q^{1+\delta/2}. \end{equation} Furthermore, we have \[ \begin{aligned} (q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*&=\left(q_{J-1}^* v - q_{J-1} v^*\right)\left(q_{J-1}^* v + q_{J-1} v^*\right)\\ (q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^* &=\left((q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*) v - (q_J + t q_{J-1}) v^*\right) \\ & \quad \cdot \left((q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*) v + (q_J + t q_{J-1}) v^*\right). \end{aligned} \] Now \eqref{system_one} and \eqref{lb_v} give \begin{equation} \begin{cases} &|\, q_{J-1}^* v - q_{J-1} v^*|\ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon}, \\ &\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*) v - (q_J + t q_{J-1}) v^*\right| \ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Multiplying the first inequality by $t$ and subtracting the second one yields \[ \begin{cases} &|q_{J-1}^* v - q_{J-1} v^*|\ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon},\\ &\left|q_J^* v - q_J v^*\right| \ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon}. \end{cases} \] Consequently, there exist $X, Y \in \mathbb R$ with \[ |X|,|Y| \ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon} \] such that \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} q_{J-1}^* & - q_{J-1}\\ q_J^* & - q_J \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} v\\v^* \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} X\\Y \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation} In light of \eqref{lb_v} and~\eqref{s_equals_M}, Cramer's rule gives \begin{align*} q_Jq_J^*\left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right| &= \left|\mathrm{det}\begin{pmatrix} q_{J-1}^* & - q_{J-1} \\ q_J^* & - q_J\end{pmatrix}\right| \nonumber \\ &\ll Q^{1+2+8\phi-\delta/2+4\varepsilon-(1+\delta/2)}=Q^{2+8\phi-\delta+4\varepsilon}. \end{align*} By \eqref{denominator_bounds}, we thus have \[ \left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right|\ll Q^{8\phi-\delta+8\varepsilon}. \] It now follows from Proposition~\ref{prop_close_ratios} that \begin{align*} (\lambda^K\times \lambda^K) (\mathcal S_3) \ll Q^{(8\phi-\delta+8\varepsilon)(2\kappa-3-4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon)+(1+2\varepsilon)c/(R+c)}, \end{align*} where the constant $c>0$ is as in Lemma~\ref{vq}. Coupling this with the trivial bound $|\mathfrak J| \leqslant 2,$ we find that \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal S_3} \mathfrak J \mathrm d \lambda^{2K} \ll Q^{(8\phi-\delta+8\varepsilon)(2\kappa-3-4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon)+(1+2\varepsilon)c/(R+c)}. \end{equation} \subsubsection{The size of $m_2$} Combining the various contributions \eqref{Contribution1}, \eqref{Contribution21}, \eqref{Contribution220}, \eqref{Contribution221}, \eqref{Contribution2221}, \eqref{Contribution2222}, \eqref{Contribution2223} to $m_2$, we find that \[ m_2 \ll Q^{(2\varepsilon - \phi) (2 {\kappa} - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon) + (1 + 2\varepsilon) 2c / (R+c)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound $m_2$ by diagonal and off-diagonal contributions.

nodes.name: Set up m_2
nodes.statement: With $B = [0,1] \times [-1, 1]$, the second moment of the function $F(t,u)$ defined in \eqref{F_definition} is \begin{align*} m_2 &= \int_B |F(t,u)|^2 \mathrm{d}t \mathrm{d}u \\ &= \int_{\mathcal E^{2K}} \int_0^1 \int_{-1}^1 e\Big(k_1\Big( \frac{p_J+tp_{J-1}}{q_J+tq_{J-1}} \: - \: \frac{p_J^* +tp_{J-1}^*}{q_J^* +tq_{J-1}^*}\Big)\Big) \\ & \quad e\big(k_2(g(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,t) - g(\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*,t))\big) \\ & \quad e\Big(k_2u\Big( \frac{1}{q_J+tq_{J-1}} \: - \: \frac{1}{q_J^*+tq_{J-1}^*}\Big)\Big) {\,{\rm d}} u {\,{\rm d}} t {\,{\rm d}}\lambda^K(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) {\,{\rm d}}\lambda^K(\mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*). \end{align*} Here and in what follows, for $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b), (\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal E^K$, we write for convenience $q_J=q_J(\mathbf a)$ and $q_J^*=q_J(\mathbf a^*),$ and similarly for $q_{J-1}, q_{J-1}^*.$ Continuing with the estimation of $m_2,$ let us set \begin{equation} f_1(t) = \frac{p_J + t p_{J-1}}{q_J + tq_{J-1}} \: - \: \frac{p_J^* + tp_{J-1}^*}{q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*}, \qquad f_2(t) = g(\mathbf a,\mathbf b, t) - g(\mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*, t) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} z(t) = z(t;k_2) = k_2 \left( \frac1{q_J + tq_{J-1}} \: - \: \frac1{q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*} \right), \end{equation} and write \begin{equation} f(t) = f(t; k_1, k_2) = k_1 f_1(t) + k_2 f_2(t). \end{equation} Now \begin{align} m_2 &= \int_{\mathcal E^{2K}} \mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K}, \end{align} where \[ \mathfrak J = \mathfrak J(\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*) = \int_0^1 e(f(t)) \int_{-1}^1 e(u z(t)) {\,{\rm d}} u {\,{\rm d}} t. \] Observe that if $z \in \mathbb R$ then \[ \int_{-1}^1 e(zu) {\,{\rm d}} u = 2 \mathrm{sinc}(2 \pi z). \] This is immediate if $z = 0$, and otherwise \[ \int_{-1}^1 e(zu) {\,{\rm d}} u = \frac{e(z) - e(-z)}{2 \pi i z} = \frac{\sin (2 \pi z)}{\pi z} = 2 \mathrm{sinc}(2\pi z). \] Therefore \begin{equation} \mathfrak J = \mathfrak J(\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*) = 2 \int_0^1 e(f(t)) \mathrm{sinc}(2 \pi z(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t. \end{equation} We now estimate $m_2$ by partitioning $\mathcal E^K\times \mathcal E^K$ into suitably chosen subsets and bounding the corresponding contribution of $\mathfrak J$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $m_2$ as an average of oscillatory integrals $\mathfrak J$.

nodes.name: Equation (5.10)
nodes.statement: f_1(t) = \frac{p_J + t p_{J-1}}{q_J + tq_{J-1}} \: - \: \frac{p_J^* + tp_{J-1}^*}{q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*}, \qquad f_2(t) = g(\mathbf a,\mathbf b, t) - g(\mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*, t)
nodes.label: f1f2

nodes.name: Equation (5.11)
nodes.statement: z(t) = z(t;k_2) = k_2 \left( \frac1{q_J + tq_{J-1}} \: - \: \frac1{q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*} \right),
nodes.label: def_z

nodes.name: Equation (5.13)
nodes.statement: m_2 &= \int_{\mathcal E^{2K}} \mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K},
nodes.label: m2

nodes.name: Equation (5.14)
nodes.statement: \mathfrak J = \mathfrak J(\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*) = 2 \int_0^1 e(f(t)) \mathrm{sinc}(2 \pi z(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t.
nodes.label: fJ_first_presentation

nodes.name: Diagonal contribution
nodes.statement: Write \[ \mathcal D = \{ (\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf a^*, \mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal E^{2K}: \mathbf a = \mathbf a^* \} \] for the set of quadruples $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal E^{2K}$ such that $\mathbf a = \mathbf a^*$. Since $|\mathfrak J| \leqslant 2,$ the contribution of $\mathcal D$ to the integral in \eqref{m2} is \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal D}\mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ll (\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\mathcal D). \end{equation} The right-hand side of \eqref{diagonal} is equal to \begin{align*} (\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\mathcal D) & = \sum_{\mathbf a \in \mathcal E_1^{K}}\mathop{\sum\sum}_{\mathbf b, \mathbf b^* \in \mathcal V_{KJ_0}(\mathbf a)}(\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a,\mathbf b^*)\\ & = \sum_{\mathbf a \in \mathcal E_1^{K}} \Bigg(\sum_{\mathbf b\in \mathcal V_{KJ_0}(\mathbf a)}\!\!\lambda^K(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\Bigg)^2 . \end{align*} By Lemmas \ref{lem_size_of_cylinder_set} and \ref{vq}, the innermost sum satisfies \begin{align*} \sum_{\mathbf b\in \mathcal V_{KJ_0}(\mathbf a)}\!\!\lambda^K(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) &\leqslant | \mathcal V_{KJ_0}(\mathbf a)| \frac{2^K}{T_m(\kappa)^{j_0K}}Q_0^{(1+2\varepsilon)(1-2\kappa)K}\\ &\leqslant \frac{2^{K}Q_0^{(1-2{\kappa})(1+2\varepsilon)K+(1+2\varepsilon)K}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0K}}. \end{align*} This gives \begin{align*} (\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\mathcal D) &\leqslant \frac{2^{K}Q_0^{(1-2{\kappa})(1+2\varepsilon)K+(1+2\varepsilon)K}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0K}} \sum_{\mathbf a \in \mathcal E_1^{K}} \sum_{\mathbf b\in \mathcal V_{KJ_0}(\mathbf a)}\!\!\lambda^K(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \\ & = \frac{2^{K}Q_0^{(1-2{\kappa})(1+2\varepsilon)K+(1+2\varepsilon)K}}{T_m({\kappa})^{j_0K}}, \end{align*} where in the last step we have used the fact that $\lambda^K$ is a probability measure. The assumption \eqref{T_m_is_large} now yields \[ (\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\mathcal D) \leqslant Q_0^{(1-2{\kappa})(1+2\varepsilon)K+(1+2\varepsilon)K} \] and, recalling that $Q = Q_0^K$, we finally have \[ \int_{\mathcal D}\mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ll Q^{2-2\kappa + 4(1-\kappa)\varepsilon}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal pairs contribute $\ll Q^{2-2\kappa+4(1-\kappa)\varepsilon}$.

nodes.name: Equation (5.15)
nodes.statement: \int_{\mathcal D}\mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ll (\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\mathcal D).
nodes.label: diagonal

nodes.name: Off-diagonal contribution
nodes.statement: We now turn to the contribution of the complement of $\mathcal D$ to the integral in \eqref{m2}. Bounding the ${\lambda}^{2K}$ measure of the domain of integration alone will not be enough, so we aim to establish alternative upper bounds for the integrand $\mathfrak J.$ \par Write \begin{equation} h(t) = 2 \mathrm{sinc}(2 \pi z(t)), \quad \mathfrak A(y) = \int_0^y e(f(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t \qquad (0\leqslant t,y \leqslant 1). \end{equation} By partial integration in \eqref{fJ_first_presentation}, we have \[ \mathfrak J = \int_0^1 e(f(t)) h(t) {\,{\rm d}} t = \mathfrak A(1) h(1) - \int_0^1 \mathfrak A(y) h'(y) {\,{\rm d}} y. \] Since for the function $ z(t)$ defined in \eqref{def_z} we have $z'(t) \ll |k_2| Q^{2\varepsilon - 1}$, and $\mathrm{sinc}$ has bounded derivative, we have \[ h'(t) \ll |k_2| Q^{2\varepsilon - 1} \] and consequently \begin{equation} \mathfrak J \ll (1 + |k_2| Q^{2\varepsilon - 1}) \max \{ |\mathfrak A(y)|: 0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1 \}. \end{equation} We bound the off-diagonal contribution to $m_2$ by partitioning $\mathcal E^{2K}\setminus \mathcal D$ into appropriately chosen subsets, each of them corresponding to one of the cases that follow. \bigskip \textbf{Case~I.} Recalling the parameter $\phi>0$ from~\eqref{def_delta_phi}, we consider the quadruples $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)$ for which \begin{equation} |q_J - q_J^*| + |q_{J-1} - q_{J-1}^*| \leqslant 3Q^{1-\phi}. \end{equation} Under this assumption, we compute that \[ \begin{aligned} \left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right| &= \frac{|q_{J-1} q_J^*-q_{J} q_{J-1}^*|}{q_{J} q_J^*} \\ &= \frac{\left|q_{J-1} \left(q_J^*-q_J\right)-q_{J}\left(q_{J-1}^*-q_{J-1}\right)\right|}{q_{J}q_J^*}\\ &\ll \frac{|q_J^* - q_J| + |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}|}{q_J^*} \ll Q^{2\varepsilon-\phi}, \end{aligned} \] where at the last step we used Lemma~\ref{lem_FD}~(a) and~\eqref{third_scenario_description}. Thus, by Proposition~\ref{prop_close_ratios}, we have \begin{align*} &(\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) : \text{ \eqref{third_scenario_description} holds}\}) \\ & \qquad \ll Q^{(2\varepsilon - \phi) (2 {\kappa} - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon) + (1 + 2\varepsilon) 2c / (R+c)} , \end{align*} where the constant $c$ is as in Lemma~\ref{vq}. We conclude that the contribution to $m_2$ is \begin{equation} O( Q^{(2\varepsilon - \phi) (2 {\kappa} - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon) + (1 + 2\varepsilon) 2c / (R+c)} ). \end{equation} It remains to deal with the contribution to $m_2$ of $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)$ for which \eqref{third_scenario_description} fails, and we do so by considering two subcases according to the size of $|k_2|.$ \bigskip \textbf{Case~II(i).} Here we examine the contribution to $m_2$ of $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)$ such that \begin{equation} |q_J^* - q_J| + |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| > 3Q^{1- \phi} \end{equation} when \begin{equation} |k_2| \gg Q^{1 + 3\phi}. \end{equation} By the definitions of $\mathfrak J$ and $h(t)$ in \eqref{fJ_first_presentation}, \eqref{sha_def}, we have \[ \mathfrak J \ll \int_0^1 |h(t)|{\,{\rm d}} t \ll \int_0^1 \min \{ 1, |z(t)|^{-1} \} {\,{\rm d}} t, \] where by \eqref{def_z} \[ z(t) = k_2 \frac{t(q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}) + q_J^* - q_J} {(q_J + tq_{J-1}) (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)}. \] First, suppose \begin{equation} |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| > Q^{1-\phi}. \end{equation} Write $S$ for the set of $t \in [0,1]$ such that \[ \left| t + \frac{q_J^* - q_J} {q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}} \right| \leqslant Q^{- \phi}. \] Then \[ \mathfrak J \ll \mathfrak J_1 + \mathfrak J_2, \] where \[ \mathfrak J_1 = \int_S \min \{ 1, |z(t)|^{-1} \} {\,{\rm d}} t, \qquad \mathfrak J_2 = \int_{[0,1]\setminus S} \min \{ 1, |z(t)|^{-1} \} {\,{\rm d}} t. \] For $\mathfrak J_1,$ we bound the integrand by $1$ and deduce that $\mathfrak J_1 \ll Q^{-\phi}.$ Regarding $\mathfrak J_2,$ the inequalities \eqref{denominator_bounds}, \eqref{K_is_big} and \eqref{FirstSuppose} imply that for any $t\in [0,1] \setminus S$ we have \[ |z(t)| \gg \: Q^{3\phi - 1 - 4\varepsilon} |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| \cdot \left| t + \frac{q_J^* - q_J} {q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}} \right| \gg Q^{\phi - 4\varepsilon}. \] Thus, we compute that $ \mathfrak J_2 \ll Q^{4 \varepsilon - \phi},$ whence $\mathfrak J \ll Q^{4 \varepsilon - \phi}.$ Now suppose instead that \begin{equation} |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| \leqslant Q^{1 - \phi}. \end{equation} Then by \eqref{sum_q_big} \[ |q_J^* - q_J| > 2Q^{1 - \phi}, \] and consequently for any $0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1,$ \[ \begin{split} |z(t)| &\gg Q^{3\phi - 1 - 4 \varepsilon} |(q_{J-1}-q_{J-1}^*)t +(q_J-q_J^*)| > Q^{2 \phi - 4\varepsilon}. \end{split} \] Therefore $\mathfrak J \ll Q^{ 4\varepsilon - 2 \phi}$. We have demonstrated that $\mathfrak J \ll Q^{4\varepsilon - \phi}$ in Case II(i). This means that the corresponding contribution to $m_2$ is \begin{equation} O(Q^{4 \varepsilon - \phi}). \end{equation} \bigskip \textbf{Case II(ii).} It remains to deal with the contribution of points for which we have \eqref{sum_q_big} when \begin{equation} |k_2| \ll Q^{1 + 3 \phi}. \end{equation} By \eqref{kk_size} and \eqref{scenario_2}, we have \begin{equation} |k_1| \asymp Q^{2 + {\delta}}, \end{equation} and by~\eqref{ub_J_second} we have \[ \mathfrak J \ll Q^{3 \phi+2\varepsilon} \max \{ |\mathfrak A(y)|: 0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1 \}. \] For the functions $f_1$ and $f_2$ defined in \eqref{f1f2}, we compute that \[ f_1'(t) = (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2} - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2} \] and, using \eqref{gt}, \begin{align*} f_2'(t) &= (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b^*_{k+1}q_k^*. \end{align*} Thus, for $f=k_1f_1 + k_2f_2$ introduced in \eqref{f_def}, we have \begin{align*} f'(t) &= k_1( (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2} - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2}) \\ & \quad + k_2\left( (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b^*_{k+1}q_k^* \right) \\ &= (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2} \left(k_1+k_2\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k\right) \\ & \qquad - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2} \left(k_1+k_2\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}^*q_k^*\right). \end{align*} Setting \begin{equation} s = k_1 + k_2 \sum_{k=0}^{J-1} b_{k+1} q_k, \qquad s^* = k_1 + k_2 \sum_{k=0}^{J-1} b_{k+1}^* q_k^*, \end{equation} the derivative $f'(t)$ can be written as \begin{equation} f'(t) = \frac{(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 s^*}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2}. \end{equation} We partition the set $\mathcal C := \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal E^{2K}: \eqref{sum_q_big} \text{ holds} \}$ into three sets $\mathcal C_0$, $\mathcal C_1$ and $\mathcal C_2$ that are defined as follows: \begin{align*} \mathcal C_0 &= \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal C : ss^* =0 \}, \\ \mathcal C_1 &= \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal C : ss^* <0 \}, \\ \mathcal C_2 &= \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal C : ss^* >0 \}. \end{align*} For the analysis of the sets $\mathcal C_0, \mathcal C_1, \mathcal C_2$, we need to estimate the ${\lambda}^K$-measure of the set where $|s|$ assumes values up to a certain threshold. In the following lemma, we essentially consider $s$ as a random variable, where $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \in \mathcal E^{K}$ is distributed according to $ {\lambda}^{K}$. \begin{lemma} Assume that $k_2 \ne 0$. Then, for $T \geqslant 0$, we have \[ {\lambda}^K(|s| \leqslant T) \leqslant \left(\frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right) Q^{2 \varepsilon - 1}, \] where $Q=\exp\left(J\sigma_m\right)$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} First, note that \[ {\lambda}^K\left(|s| \leqslant T\right)=\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\right), \] where $\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}$ is a characteristic function of the subset of $\mathcal E^K$ defined by the condition $|s| \leqslant T$. Then, by using the tower property of conditional expectation, we have \[ \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\right)=\mathbb E\left(\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)\right). \] We are going to upper bound the random variable $\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)$, and then use the fact that an upper bound for a random variable is also an upper bound for its expectation. To find a suitable upper bound for $\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)$, we observe first that \[ s = k_1 + k_2 N, \qquad N = \sum_{k=0}^{J-1} b_{k+1} q_k. \] Writing $\mathbf a = (\mathbf a^{(1)}, \ldots,\mathbf a^{(J/m)})$, the conditional probability that $N$ takes a specific value is at most $\prod_{i=1}^{J/m} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})|^{-1}$. As $s \equiv k_1 \mmod |k_2|$, the conditional probability that $|s| \leqslant T$ is at most \[ \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right) \leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right) \prod_{i=1}^{J/m} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})|^{-1}. \] By Lemma~\ref{vq} and the inequalities \eqref{R_is_large}, \eqref{Edef}, we infer that \[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right) &\leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)\frac{27^{J/R}} {\prod_{i=1}^{J/m}q_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})} \\ &\leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)\frac{27^{J/R}}{Q^{1-\varepsilon}} \leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)Q^{2\varepsilon-1}. \end{aligned} \] Taking expectations gives the conclusion of the lemma. \end{proof} We may now examine each of the sets $\mathcal C_0, \mathcal C_1, \mathcal C_2$ separately. By Lemma~\ref{SmallProb}, we have ${\lambda}^{2K}(\mathcal C_0) \leqslant 2Q^{2\varepsilon-1}$, and since $|\mathfrak J| \leqslant 2$, this gives \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal C_0} \mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ll Q^{2\varepsilon - 1}. \end{equation} Observe that if $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal C_1$ then, by \eqref{fprime1}, \[ Q^{2+12\varepsilon} |f'(t)| \gg |s| + |s^*| \geqslant 1. \] As $f'$ is monotonic, Lemma \ref{lem_ub_nozero} yields, for every $y\in[0,1]$, \begin{equation} |\mathfrak A(y)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)| \ll \frac{Q^{2+12\varepsilon}} {|s|+|s^*|}. \end{equation} Under the assumption~\eqref{scenario_2}, we have $|k_1|\asymp Q^{2+\delta}$ and thus \[ |k_1| \gg |k_2| Q^{1 + 2 \varepsilon}. \] Then, by the triangle inequality for \eqref{ss_def}, we have \begin{equation} \min\left(|s|, |s^*|\right) \geqslant |k_1| - |k_2| Q^{1+2\varepsilon} \gg Q^{2+{\delta}}. \end{equation} Thus \eqref{ub_J_second}, \eqref{scenario_2}, \eqref{ub_U_C_one} and~\eqref{lb_s_C_one} imply that \[ \mathfrak J \ll Q^{3\phi+2\varepsilon-\delta+12\varepsilon} =Q^{3\phi-\delta+14\varepsilon} \qquad ((\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal C_1). \] Hence \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal C_1} \mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ll Q^{3\phi-\delta+14\varepsilon}. \end{equation} \bigskip Finally, we turn our attention to $\mathcal C_2$. We assume that $s > s^* > 0$. The other cases within $\mathcal C_2$ can be handled by symmetrical reasoning. By \eqref{fprime1}, we have that $f'(t)$ is equal to \begin{align*} & \frac{((q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v - (q_J + tq_{J-1}) v^*) ((q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v + (q_J + tq_{J-1}) v^*)}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2}, \end{align*} where \[ v = \sqrt s, \qquad v^* = \sqrt{s^*}. \] Hence \[ f'(t) = (At + B) G(t), \] where \[ A = q_{J-1}^*v - q_{J-1}v^*, \qquad B = q_J^* v - q_J v^* \] and \[ G(t) = \frac{(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v + (q_J + tq_{J-1}) v^*}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2}. \] Plainly $$|G(t)| \gg Q^{- 3-10\varepsilon} (v+v^*).$$ We compute that \begin{multline*} (q_J + tq_{J-1})^3 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^3 G'(t) = (q_J + tq_{J-1}) (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*) (q_{J-1}^*v + q_{J-1} v^*) \\ \hfill -2(q_{J-1}(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*) + q_{J-1}^* (q_J + tq_{J-1})) \cdot \\ \cdot ((q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v + (q_J + tq_{J-1})v^*), \end{multline*} and so $$|G'(t)| \ll Q^{ - 3 + 18\varepsilon}(v+v^*).$$ Now for the function $\mathfrak A$ defined in \eqref{sha_def}, Lemma \ref{ExpInt} furnishes \begin{equation} \mathfrak A(y)^2 \ll \frac{Q^{3+66\varepsilon}} {|A| (v+v^*)} \ll \frac{Q^{4+68\varepsilon}}{|(q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|} \qquad (0\leqslant y \leqslant 1). \end{equation} In order to make use of the bound \eqref{bound_case_one}, we write the region of integration $\mathcal C_2$ as the union of the three sets \[ \begin{aligned} &\mathcal S_1 = \left\{ |(q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|\geqslant Q^{4+8\phi} \right\},\\ &\mathcal S_2 = \left\{ \min_{t\in [0,1]}\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^*\right|\geqslant Q^{4+8\phi} \right\}, \\ &\mathcal S_3 = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} |(q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|<Q^{4+8\phi} \quad \text{ and } \\ \displaystyle \min_{t\in [0,1]}\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^*\right|< Q^{4+8\phi} \end{array}\right\}. \end{aligned} \] $\bullet$ For $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal S_1,$ the bound~\eqref{bound_case_one} gives $\mathfrak A(y)\ll Q^{34\varepsilon - 4\phi}$ for every $y\in[0,1]$, and thus, by \eqref{ub_J_second} and \eqref{scenario_2}, \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal S_1}\mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ \ll Q^{36\varepsilon - \phi}. \end{equation} $\bullet$ When $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal S_2$, it follows from~\eqref{fprime1} and the definition of $\mathcal S_2$ that $|f'(t)|\geqslant Q^{8\phi - 8\varepsilon}$. We also compute, by differentiating~\eqref{fprime1}, that \[ f''(t) = - \: \frac{2q_{J-1}s}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^3} + \frac{2q_{J-1}^*s^*}{(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^3}. \] This shows that $f''(t)=0$ if and only if \[ q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*=\left(q_J + tq_{J-1}\right)\left(\frac{q_{J-1}^*s^*}{q_{J-1}s}\right)^{1/3}. \] This equation is at most linear in $t$, and we claim that it has at most one solution. Indeed, assume for a contradiction that it has more than one solution. Then $f'' = 0$, so $f'$ is constant. By \eqref{fprime1}, this entails that $f' = 0$, contradicting the definition of $\mathcal S_2$. Therefore $f'$ is monotonic in at most two stretches. We may therefore apply Lemma~\ref{lem_ub_nozero} with $k=1$ and $\lambda=Q^{8\phi - 8\varepsilon}$, to find \[ \mathfrak A(y)\ll Q^{-8\phi + 8\varepsilon}. \] Combining this with \eqref{ub_J_second} and~\eqref{scenario_2} furnishes \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal S_2}\mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ \ll Q^{10\varepsilon-5\phi}. \end{equation} $\bullet$ For $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal S_3$, we use the trivial upper bound $|\mathfrak J| \leqslant 2$, and establish an upper bound for $\lambda^{2K}(\mathcal S_3).$ Recall that we have \eqref{k1large} in the present setting. Now, applying the triangle inequality to the definitions of $s, s^*$ in \eqref{ss_def}, we have \begin{equation} |s|, |s^*| \geqslant |k_1| - |k_2| Q^{1+2\varepsilon} \gg Q^{2+{\delta}}. \end{equation} By definition, for every quadruple in $\mathcal S_3$, we have the following system of linear inequalities: \begin{equation} \begin{cases} &|({q_{J-1}^*})^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|<Q^{4+8\phi},\\ &\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^*\right| < Q^{4+8\phi}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Since $v=\sqrt{s}$ and $v^*=\sqrt{s^*}$ by definition, we see from \eqref{lb_s} that \begin{equation} v, v^* \gg Q^{1+\delta/2}. \end{equation} Furthermore, we have \[ \begin{aligned} (q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*&=\left(q_{J-1}^* v - q_{J-1} v^*\right)\left(q_{J-1}^* v + q_{J-1} v^*\right)\\ (q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^* &=\left((q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*) v - (q_J + t q_{J-1}) v^*\right) \\ & \quad \cdot \left((q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*) v + (q_J + t q_{J-1}) v^*\right). \end{aligned} \] Now \eqref{system_one} and \eqref{lb_v} give \begin{equation} \begin{cases} &|\, q_{J-1}^* v - q_{J-1} v^*|\ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon}, \\ &\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*) v - (q_J + t q_{J-1}) v^*\right| \ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Multiplying the first inequality by $t$ and subtracting the second one yields \[ \begin{cases} &|q_{J-1}^* v - q_{J-1} v^*|\ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon},\\ &\left|q_J^* v - q_J v^*\right| \ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon}. \end{cases} \] Consequently, there exist $X, Y \in \mathbb R$ with \[ |X|,|Y| \ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon} \] such that \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} q_{J-1}^* & - q_{J-1}\\ q_J^* & - q_J \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} v\\v^* \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} X\\Y \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation} In light of \eqref{lb_v} and~\eqref{s_equals_M}, Cramer's rule gives \begin{align*} q_Jq_J^*\left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right| &= \left|\mathrm{det}\begin{pmatrix} q_{J-1}^* & - q_{J-1} \\ q_J^* & - q_J\end{pmatrix}\right| \nonumber \\ &\ll Q^{1+2+8\phi-\delta/2+4\varepsilon-(1+\delta/2)}=Q^{2+8\phi-\delta+4\varepsilon}. \end{align*} By \eqref{denominator_bounds}, we thus have \[ \left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right|\ll Q^{8\phi-\delta+8\varepsilon}. \] It now follows from Proposition~\ref{prop_close_ratios} that \begin{align*} (\lambda^K\times \lambda^K) (\mathcal S_3) \ll Q^{(8\phi-\delta+8\varepsilon)(2\kappa-3-4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon)+(1+2\varepsilon)c/(R+c)}, \end{align*} where the constant $c>0$ is as in Lemma~\ref{vq}. Coupling this with the trivial bound $|\mathfrak J| \leqslant 2,$ we find that \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal S_3} \mathfrak J \mathrm d \lambda^{2K} \ll Q^{(8\phi-\delta+8\varepsilon)(2\kappa-3-4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon)+(1+2\varepsilon)c/(R+c)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mathfrak J$ off the diagonal in three cases.

nodes.name: Partial integration
nodes.statement: We now turn to the contribution of the complement of $\mathcal D$ to the integral in \eqref{m2}. Bounding the ${\lambda}^{2K}$ measure of the domain of integration alone will not be enough, so we aim to establish alternative upper bounds for the integrand $\mathfrak J.$ \par Write \begin{equation} h(t) = 2 \mathrm{sinc}(2 \pi z(t)), \quad \mathfrak A(y) = \int_0^y e(f(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t \qquad (0\leqslant t,y \leqslant 1). \end{equation} By partial integration in \eqref{fJ_first_presentation}, we have \[ \mathfrak J = \int_0^1 e(f(t)) h(t) {\,{\rm d}} t = \mathfrak A(1) h(1) - \int_0^1 \mathfrak A(y) h'(y) {\,{\rm d}} y. \] Since for the function $ z(t)$ defined in \eqref{def_z} we have $z'(t) \ll |k_2| Q^{2\varepsilon - 1}$, and $\mathrm{sinc}$ has bounded derivative, we have \[ h'(t) \ll |k_2| Q^{2\varepsilon - 1} \] and consequently \begin{equation} \mathfrak J \ll (1 + |k_2| Q^{2\varepsilon - 1}) \max \{ |\mathfrak A(y)|: 0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1 \}. \end{equation} We bound the off-diagonal contribution to $m_2$ by partitioning $\mathcal E^{2K}\setminus \mathcal D$ into appropriately chosen subsets, each of them corresponding to one of the cases that follow.
nodes.statement_short: Partial integration reduces $\mathfrak J$ to $\max|\mathfrak A(y)|$.

nodes.name: Equation (5.16)
nodes.statement: h(t) = 2 \mathrm{sinc}(2 \pi z(t)), \quad \mathfrak A(y) = \int_0^y e(f(t)) {\,{\rm d}} t \qquad (0\leqslant t,y \leqslant 1).
nodes.label: sha_def

nodes.name: Equation (5.17)
nodes.statement: \mathfrak J \ll (1 + |k_2| Q^{2\varepsilon - 1}) \max \{ |\mathfrak A(y)|: 0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1 \}.
nodes.label: ub_J_second

nodes.name: Case I
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case~I.} Recalling the parameter $\phi>0$ from~\eqref{def_delta_phi}, we consider the quadruples $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)$ for which \begin{equation} |q_J - q_J^*| + |q_{J-1} - q_{J-1}^*| \leqslant 3Q^{1-\phi}. \end{equation} Under this assumption, we compute that \[ \begin{aligned} \left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right| &= \frac{|q_{J-1} q_J^*-q_{J} q_{J-1}^*|}{q_{J} q_J^*} \\ &= \frac{\left|q_{J-1} \left(q_J^*-q_J\right)-q_{J}\left(q_{J-1}^*-q_{J-1}\right)\right|}{q_{J}q_J^*}\\ &\ll \frac{|q_J^* - q_J| + |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}|}{q_J^*} \ll Q^{2\varepsilon-\phi}, \end{aligned} \] where at the last step we used Lemma~\ref{lem_FD}~(a) and~\eqref{third_scenario_description}. Thus, by Proposition~\ref{prop_close_ratios}, we have \begin{align*} &(\lambda^K \times \lambda^K)(\{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) : \text{ \eqref{third_scenario_description} holds}\}) \\ & \qquad \ll Q^{(2\varepsilon - \phi) (2 {\kappa} - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon) + (1 + 2\varepsilon) 2c / (R+c)} , \end{align*} where the constant $c$ is as in Lemma~\ref{vq}. We conclude that the contribution to $m_2$ is \begin{equation} O( Q^{(2\varepsilon - \phi) (2 {\kappa} - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon) + (1 + 2\varepsilon) 2c / (R+c)} ). \end{equation} It remains to deal with the contribution to $m_2$ of $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)$ for which \eqref{third_scenario_description} fails, and we do so by considering two subcases according to the size of $|k_2|.$
nodes.statement_short: Close denominators: Proposition 4.4 bounds the measure.

nodes.name: Equation (5.19)
nodes.statement: O( Q^{(2\varepsilon - \phi) (2 {\kappa} - 3 - 4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon) + (1 + 2\varepsilon) 2c / (R+c)} ).
nodes.label: Contribution1

nodes.name: Case II(i)
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case~II(i).} Here we examine the contribution to $m_2$ of $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)$ such that \begin{equation} |q_J^* - q_J| + |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| > 3Q^{1- \phi} \end{equation} when \begin{equation} |k_2| \gg Q^{1 + 3\phi}. \end{equation} By the definitions of $\mathfrak J$ and $h(t)$ in \eqref{fJ_first_presentation}, \eqref{sha_def}, we have \[ \mathfrak J \ll \int_0^1 |h(t)|{\,{\rm d}} t \ll \int_0^1 \min \{ 1, |z(t)|^{-1} \} {\,{\rm d}} t, \] where by \eqref{def_z} \[ z(t) = k_2 \frac{t(q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}) + q_J^* - q_J} {(q_J + tq_{J-1}) (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)}. \] First, suppose \begin{equation} |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| > Q^{1-\phi}. \end{equation} Write $S$ for the set of $t \in [0,1]$ such that \[ \left| t + \frac{q_J^* - q_J} {q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}} \right| \leqslant Q^{- \phi}. \] Then \[ \mathfrak J \ll \mathfrak J_1 + \mathfrak J_2, \] where \[ \mathfrak J_1 = \int_S \min \{ 1, |z(t)|^{-1} \} {\,{\rm d}} t, \qquad \mathfrak J_2 = \int_{[0,1]\setminus S} \min \{ 1, |z(t)|^{-1} \} {\,{\rm d}} t. \] For $\mathfrak J_1,$ we bound the integrand by $1$ and deduce that $\mathfrak J_1 \ll Q^{-\phi}.$ Regarding $\mathfrak J_2,$ the inequalities \eqref{denominator_bounds}, \eqref{K_is_big} and \eqref{FirstSuppose} imply that for any $t\in [0,1] \setminus S$ we have \[ |z(t)| \gg \: Q^{3\phi - 1 - 4\varepsilon} |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| \cdot \left| t + \frac{q_J^* - q_J} {q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}} \right| \gg Q^{\phi - 4\varepsilon}. \] Thus, we compute that $ \mathfrak J_2 \ll Q^{4 \varepsilon - \phi},$ whence $\mathfrak J \ll Q^{4 \varepsilon - \phi}.$ Now suppose instead that \begin{equation} |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| \leqslant Q^{1 - \phi}. \end{equation} Then by \eqref{sum_q_big} \[ |q_J^* - q_J| > 2Q^{1 - \phi}, \] and consequently for any $0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1,$ \[ \begin{split} |z(t)| &\gg Q^{3\phi - 1 - 4 \varepsilon} |(q_{J-1}-q_{J-1}^*)t +(q_J-q_J^*)| > Q^{2 \phi - 4\varepsilon}. \end{split} \] Therefore $\mathfrak J \ll Q^{ 4\varepsilon - 2 \phi}$. We have demonstrated that $\mathfrak J \ll Q^{4\varepsilon - \phi}$ in Case II(i). This means that the corresponding contribution to $m_2$ is \begin{equation} O(Q^{4 \varepsilon - \phi}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Large $|k_2|$: $z(t)$ is large off a short interval.

nodes.name: Equation (5.23)
nodes.statement: |q_{J-1}^* - q_{J-1}| \leqslant Q^{1 - \phi}.
nodes.label: Case_2i_subcase_one

nodes.name: Equation (5.24)
nodes.statement: O(Q^{4 \varepsilon - \phi}).
nodes.label: Contribution21

nodes.name: Case II(ii)
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case II(ii).} It remains to deal with the contribution of points for which we have \eqref{sum_q_big} when \begin{equation} |k_2| \ll Q^{1 + 3 \phi}. \end{equation} By \eqref{kk_size} and \eqref{scenario_2}, we have \begin{equation} |k_1| \asymp Q^{2 + {\delta}}, \end{equation} and by~\eqref{ub_J_second} we have \[ \mathfrak J \ll Q^{3 \phi+2\varepsilon} \max \{ |\mathfrak A(y)|: 0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1 \}. \] For the functions $f_1$ and $f_2$ defined in \eqref{f1f2}, we compute that \[ f_1'(t) = (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2} - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2} \] and, using \eqref{gt}, \begin{align*} f_2'(t) &= (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b^*_{k+1}q_k^*. \end{align*} Thus, for $f=k_1f_1 + k_2f_2$ introduced in \eqref{f_def}, we have \begin{align*} f'(t) &= k_1( (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2} - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2}) \\ & \quad + k_2\left( (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b^*_{k+1}q_k^* \right) \\ &= (q_J+tq_{J-1})^{-2} \left(k_1+k_2\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}q_k\right) \\ & \qquad - (q_J^*+tq^*_{J-1})^{-2} \left(k_1+k_2\sum_{k=0}^{J-1}b_{k+1}^*q_k^*\right). \end{align*} Setting \begin{equation} s = k_1 + k_2 \sum_{k=0}^{J-1} b_{k+1} q_k, \qquad s^* = k_1 + k_2 \sum_{k=0}^{J-1} b_{k+1}^* q_k^*, \end{equation} the derivative $f'(t)$ can be written as \begin{equation} f'(t) = \frac{(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 s^*}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2}. \end{equation} We partition the set $\mathcal C := \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal E^{2K}: \eqref{sum_q_big} \text{ holds} \}$ into three sets $\mathcal C_0$, $\mathcal C_1$ and $\mathcal C_2$ that are defined as follows: \begin{align*} \mathcal C_0 &= \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal C : ss^* =0 \}, \\ \mathcal C_1 &= \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal C : ss^* <0 \}, \\ \mathcal C_2 &= \{ (\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in \mathcal C : ss^* >0 \}. \end{align*} For the analysis of the sets $\mathcal C_0, \mathcal C_1, \mathcal C_2$, we need to estimate the ${\lambda}^K$-measure of the set where $|s|$ assumes values up to a certain threshold. In the following lemma, we essentially consider $s$ as a random variable, where $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \in \mathcal E^{K}$ is distributed according to $ {\lambda}^{K}$. \begin{lemma} Assume that $k_2 \ne 0$. Then, for $T \geqslant 0$, we have \[ {\lambda}^K(|s| \leqslant T) \leqslant \left(\frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right) Q^{2 \varepsilon - 1}, \] where $Q=\exp\left(J\sigma_m\right)$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} First, note that \[ {\lambda}^K\left(|s| \leqslant T\right)=\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\right), \] where $\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}$ is a characteristic function of the subset of $\mathcal E^K$ defined by the condition $|s| \leqslant T$. Then, by using the tower property of conditional expectation, we have \[ \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\right)=\mathbb E\left(\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)\right). \] We are going to upper bound the random variable $\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)$, and then use the fact that an upper bound for a random variable is also an upper bound for its expectation. To find a suitable upper bound for $\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)$, we observe first that \[ s = k_1 + k_2 N, \qquad N = \sum_{k=0}^{J-1} b_{k+1} q_k. \] Writing $\mathbf a = (\mathbf a^{(1)}, \ldots,\mathbf a^{(J/m)})$, the conditional probability that $N$ takes a specific value is at most $\prod_{i=1}^{J/m} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})|^{-1}$. As $s \equiv k_1 \mmod |k_2|$, the conditional probability that $|s| \leqslant T$ is at most \[ \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right) \leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right) \prod_{i=1}^{J/m} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})|^{-1}. \] By Lemma~\ref{vq} and the inequalities \eqref{R_is_large}, \eqref{Edef}, we infer that \[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right) &\leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)\frac{27^{J/R}} {\prod_{i=1}^{J/m}q_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})} \\ &\leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)\frac{27^{J/R}}{Q^{1-\varepsilon}} \leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)Q^{2\varepsilon-1}. \end{aligned} \] Taking expectations gives the conclusion of the lemma. \end{proof} We may now examine each of the sets $\mathcal C_0, \mathcal C_1, \mathcal C_2$ separately. By Lemma~\ref{SmallProb}, we have ${\lambda}^{2K}(\mathcal C_0) \leqslant 2Q^{2\varepsilon-1}$, and since $|\mathfrak J| \leqslant 2$, this gives \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal C_0} \mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ll Q^{2\varepsilon - 1}. \end{equation} Observe that if $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal C_1$ then, by \eqref{fprime1}, \[ Q^{2+12\varepsilon} |f'(t)| \gg |s| + |s^*| \geqslant 1. \] As $f'$ is monotonic, Lemma \ref{lem_ub_nozero} yields, for every $y\in[0,1]$, \begin{equation} |\mathfrak A(y)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)| \ll \frac{Q^{2+12\varepsilon}} {|s|+|s^*|}. \end{equation} Under the assumption~\eqref{scenario_2}, we have $|k_1|\asymp Q^{2+\delta}$ and thus \[ |k_1| \gg |k_2| Q^{1 + 2 \varepsilon}. \] Then, by the triangle inequality for \eqref{ss_def}, we have \begin{equation} \min\left(|s|, |s^*|\right) \geqslant |k_1| - |k_2| Q^{1+2\varepsilon} \gg Q^{2+{\delta}}. \end{equation} Thus \eqref{ub_J_second}, \eqref{scenario_2}, \eqref{ub_U_C_one} and~\eqref{lb_s_C_one} imply that \[ \mathfrak J \ll Q^{3\phi+2\varepsilon-\delta+12\varepsilon} =Q^{3\phi-\delta+14\varepsilon} \qquad ((\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*) \in \mathcal C_1). \] Hence \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal C_1} \mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ll Q^{3\phi-\delta+14\varepsilon}. \end{equation} \bigskip Finally, we turn our attention to $\mathcal C_2$. We assume that $s > s^* > 0$. The other cases within $\mathcal C_2$ can be handled by symmetrical reasoning. By \eqref{fprime1}, we have that $f'(t)$ is equal to \begin{align*} & \frac{((q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v - (q_J + tq_{J-1}) v^*) ((q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v + (q_J + tq_{J-1}) v^*)}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2}, \end{align*} where \[ v = \sqrt s, \qquad v^* = \sqrt{s^*}. \] Hence \[ f'(t) = (At + B) G(t), \] where \[ A = q_{J-1}^*v - q_{J-1}v^*, \qquad B = q_J^* v - q_J v^* \] and \[ G(t) = \frac{(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v + (q_J + tq_{J-1}) v^*}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^2 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^2}. \] Plainly $$|G(t)| \gg Q^{- 3-10\varepsilon} (v+v^*).$$ We compute that \begin{multline*} (q_J + tq_{J-1})^3 (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^3 G'(t) = (q_J + tq_{J-1}) (q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*) (q_{J-1}^*v + q_{J-1} v^*) \\ \hfill -2(q_{J-1}(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*) + q_{J-1}^* (q_J + tq_{J-1})) \cdot \\ \cdot ((q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)v + (q_J + tq_{J-1})v^*), \end{multline*} and so $$|G'(t)| \ll Q^{ - 3 + 18\varepsilon}(v+v^*).$$ Now for the function $\mathfrak A$ defined in \eqref{sha_def}, Lemma \ref{ExpInt} furnishes \begin{equation} \mathfrak A(y)^2 \ll \frac{Q^{3+66\varepsilon}} {|A| (v+v^*)} \ll \frac{Q^{4+68\varepsilon}}{|(q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|} \qquad (0\leqslant y \leqslant 1). \end{equation} In order to make use of the bound \eqref{bound_case_one}, we write the region of integration $\mathcal C_2$ as the union of the three sets \[ \begin{aligned} &\mathcal S_1 = \left\{ |(q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|\geqslant Q^{4+8\phi} \right\},\\ &\mathcal S_2 = \left\{ \min_{t\in [0,1]}\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^*\right|\geqslant Q^{4+8\phi} \right\}, \\ &\mathcal S_3 = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} |(q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|<Q^{4+8\phi} \quad \text{ and } \\ \displaystyle \min_{t\in [0,1]}\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^*\right|< Q^{4+8\phi} \end{array}\right\}. \end{aligned} \] $\bullet$ For $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal S_1,$ the bound~\eqref{bound_case_one} gives $\mathfrak A(y)\ll Q^{34\varepsilon - 4\phi}$ for every $y\in[0,1]$, and thus, by \eqref{ub_J_second} and \eqref{scenario_2}, \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal S_1}\mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ \ll Q^{36\varepsilon - \phi}. \end{equation} $\bullet$ When $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal S_2$, it follows from~\eqref{fprime1} and the definition of $\mathcal S_2$ that $|f'(t)|\geqslant Q^{8\phi - 8\varepsilon}$. We also compute, by differentiating~\eqref{fprime1}, that \[ f''(t) = - \: \frac{2q_{J-1}s}{(q_J + tq_{J-1})^3} + \frac{2q_{J-1}^*s^*}{(q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*)^3}. \] This shows that $f''(t)=0$ if and only if \[ q_J^* + tq_{J-1}^*=\left(q_J + tq_{J-1}\right)\left(\frac{q_{J-1}^*s^*}{q_{J-1}s}\right)^{1/3}. \] This equation is at most linear in $t$, and we claim that it has at most one solution. Indeed, assume for a contradiction that it has more than one solution. Then $f'' = 0$, so $f'$ is constant. By \eqref{fprime1}, this entails that $f' = 0$, contradicting the definition of $\mathcal S_2$. Therefore $f'$ is monotonic in at most two stretches. We may therefore apply Lemma~\ref{lem_ub_nozero} with $k=1$ and $\lambda=Q^{8\phi - 8\varepsilon}$, to find \[ \mathfrak A(y)\ll Q^{-8\phi + 8\varepsilon}. \] Combining this with \eqref{ub_J_second} and~\eqref{scenario_2} furnishes \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal S_2}\mathfrak J {\,{\rm d}} {\lambda}^{2K} \ \ll Q^{10\varepsilon-5\phi}. \end{equation} $\bullet$ For $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf a^*,\mathbf b^*)\in\mathcal S_3$, we use the trivial upper bound $|\mathfrak J| \leqslant 2$, and establish an upper bound for $\lambda^{2K}(\mathcal S_3).$ Recall that we have \eqref{k1large} in the present setting. Now, applying the triangle inequality to the definitions of $s, s^*$ in \eqref{ss_def}, we have \begin{equation} |s|, |s^*| \geqslant |k_1| - |k_2| Q^{1+2\varepsilon} \gg Q^{2+{\delta}}. \end{equation} By definition, for every quadruple in $\mathcal S_3$, we have the following system of linear inequalities: \begin{equation} \begin{cases} &|({q_{J-1}^*})^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*|<Q^{4+8\phi},\\ &\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^*\right| < Q^{4+8\phi}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Since $v=\sqrt{s}$ and $v^*=\sqrt{s^*}$ by definition, we see from \eqref{lb_s} that \begin{equation} v, v^* \gg Q^{1+\delta/2}. \end{equation} Furthermore, we have \[ \begin{aligned} (q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - q_{J-1}^2 s^*&=\left(q_{J-1}^* v - q_{J-1} v^*\right)\left(q_{J-1}^* v + q_{J-1} v^*\right)\\ (q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*)^2 s - (q_J + t q_{J-1})^2 s^* &=\left((q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*) v - (q_J + t q_{J-1}) v^*\right) \\ & \quad \cdot \left((q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*) v + (q_J + t q_{J-1}) v^*\right). \end{aligned} \] Now \eqref{system_one} and \eqref{lb_v} give \begin{equation} \begin{cases} &|\, q_{J-1}^* v - q_{J-1} v^*|\ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon}, \\ &\left|(q_J^* + t q_{J-1}^*) v - (q_J + t q_{J-1}) v^*\right| \ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Multiplying the first inequality by $t$ and subtracting the second one yields \[ \begin{cases} &|q_{J-1}^* v - q_{J-1} v^*|\ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon},\\ &\left|q_J^* v - q_J v^*\right| \ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon}. \end{cases} \] Consequently, there exist $X, Y \in \mathbb R$ with \[ |X|,|Y| \ll Q^{2+8\phi-\delta/2+2\varepsilon} \] such that \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} q_{J-1}^* & - q_{J-1}\\ q_J^* & - q_J \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} v\\v^* \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} X\\Y \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation} In light of \eqref{lb_v} and~\eqref{s_equals_M}, Cramer's rule gives \begin{align*} q_Jq_J^*\left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right| &= \left|\mathrm{det}\begin{pmatrix} q_{J-1}^* & - q_{J-1} \\ q_J^* & - q_J\end{pmatrix}\right| \nonumber \\ &\ll Q^{1+2+8\phi-\delta/2+4\varepsilon-(1+\delta/2)}=Q^{2+8\phi-\delta+4\varepsilon}. \end{align*} By \eqref{denominator_bounds}, we thus have \[ \left|\frac{q_{J-1}}{q_J}-\frac{q_{J-1}^*}{q_J^*}\right|\ll Q^{8\phi-\delta+8\varepsilon}. \] It now follows from Proposition~\ref{prop_close_ratios} that \begin{align*} (\lambda^K\times \lambda^K) (\mathcal S_3) \ll Q^{(8\phi-\delta+8\varepsilon)(2\kappa-3-4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon)+(1+2\varepsilon)c/(R+c)}, \end{align*} where the constant $c>0$ is as in Lemma~\ref{vq}. Coupling this with the trivial bound $|\mathfrak J| \leqslant 2,$ we find that \begin{equation} \int_{\mathcal S_3} \mathfrak J \mathrm d \lambda^{2K} \ll Q^{(8\phi-\delta+8\varepsilon)(2\kappa-3-4(2-{\kappa})\varepsilon)+(1+2\varepsilon)c/(R+c)}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.6
nodes.statement: First, note that \[ {\lambda}^K\left(|s| \leqslant T\right)=\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\right), \] where $\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}$ is a characteristic function of the subset of $\mathcal E^K$ defined by the condition $|s| \leqslant T$. Then, by using the tower property of conditional expectation, we have \[ \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\right)=\mathbb E\left(\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)\right). \] We are going to upper bound the random variable $\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)$, and then use the fact that an upper bound for a random variable is also an upper bound for its expectation. To find a suitable upper bound for $\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)$, we observe first that \[ s = k_1 + k_2 N, \qquad N = \sum_{k=0}^{J-1} b_{k+1} q_k. \] Writing $\mathbf a = (\mathbf a^{(1)}, \ldots,\mathbf a^{(J/m)})$, the conditional probability that $N$ takes a specific value is at most $\prod_{i=1}^{J/m} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})|^{-1}$. As $s \equiv k_1 \mmod |k_2|$, the conditional probability that $|s| \leqslant T$ is at most \[ \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right) \leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right) \prod_{i=1}^{J/m} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})|^{-1}. \] By Lemma~\ref{vq} and the inequalities \eqref{R_is_large}, \eqref{Edef}, we infer that \[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right) &\leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)\frac{27^{J/R}} {\prod_{i=1}^{J/m}q_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})} \\ &\leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)\frac{27^{J/R}}{Q^{1-\varepsilon}} \leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)Q^{2\varepsilon-1}. \end{aligned} \] Taking expectations gives the conclusion of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Condition on $\mathbf a$; the residue of $s$ mod $|k_2|$ and the digit counts of Lemma 3.4 bound the conditional probability.

Then, by using the tower property of conditional expectation, we have \[ \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\right)=\mathbb E\left(\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)\right). \] We are going to upper bound the random variable $\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)$, and then use the fact that an upper bound for a random variable is also an upper bound for its expectation.
nodes.statement_short: Write the probability as an expectation of a conditional expectation.

nodes.name: Conditional probability
nodes.statement: To find a suitable upper bound for $\mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right)$, we observe first that \[ s = k_1 + k_2 N, \qquad N = \sum_{k=0}^{J-1} b_{k+1} q_k. \] Writing $\mathbf a = (\mathbf a^{(1)}, \ldots,\mathbf a^{(J/m)})$, the conditional probability that $N$ takes a specific value is at most $\prod_{i=1}^{J/m} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})|^{-1}$. As $s \equiv k_1 \mmod |k_2|$, the conditional probability that $|s| \leqslant T$ is at most \[ \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right) \leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right) \prod_{i=1}^{J/m} |\mathcal V_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})|^{-1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Given $\mathbf a$, $s\equiv k_1$ mod $|k_2|$ and each value of $N$ has small probability.

nodes.name: Digit counts
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{vq} and the inequalities \eqref{R_is_large}, \eqref{Edef}, we infer that \[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E\left(\chi_{|s| \leqslant T}\mid \mathbf a\right) &\leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)\frac{27^{J/R}} {\prod_{i=1}^{J/m}q_m(\mathbf a^{(i)})} \\ &\leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)\frac{27^{J/R}}{Q^{1-\varepsilon}} \leqslant \left( \frac{2T}{|k_2|} + 1 \right)Q^{2\varepsilon-1}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.4 bounds the conditional probability by $Q^{2\varepsilon-1}$.

nodes.name: Supremum norm
nodes.statement: We write \[ \|\mathbf k\|_{\infty} = \max\{ |k_1|, |k_2| \} \] for the supremum norm of the integer vector $\mathbf k = (k_1, k_2).$ With \eqref{kk_size} in mind, we now distinguish two cases according to the relative sizes of $|k_1|$ and $|k_2|.$
nodes.statement_short: Split by the relative size of $|k_1|$ and $|k_2|$.

nodes.name: Case I
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case I.} The integers $k_1, k_2$ are such that $|k_1| \leqslant |k_2|.$ Then, by \eqref{kk_size}, we have \begin{equation*} \max\{ |k_1|, |k_2|Q\} = |k_2| Q \asymp Q^{2+\delta} \end{equation*} and therefore $\|\mathbf k\|_\infty = |k_2| \asymp Q^{1+\delta}.$ Now \eqref{obtain} gives \[ \widehat{\nu}(k_1, k_2) \ll \|\mathbf k \|_\infty^{\frac{-\delta (22\kappa -43-4\varepsilon)}{10(1+\delta)(7-2\kappa+4\varepsilon)}+2\varepsilon}. \]

nodes.name: Case II
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case II.} The integers $k_1, k_2$ satisfy $|k_1| > |k_2|.$ Then \[ \|\mathbf k \|_\infty = |k_1| \leqslant \max\{ |k_1|, |k_2|Q \} \asymp Q^{2+\delta}, \] and combining with \eqref{obtain} we get \begin{align*} \widehat{\nu}(k_1, k_2) &\ll \| \mathbf k \|_\infty^{\frac{-\delta (22\kappa -43)} {10(2+\delta)(7-2\kappa)} + 4\varepsilon}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Combining the two cases and using the fact that all norms on $\mathbb R^2$ are equivalent, we deduce that \begin{equation} \widehat{\nu}(k_1, k_2) \ll \|\mathbf k \|_\infty^{\frac{-\delta (22\kappa -43-4\varepsilon)}{10(2+\delta)(7-2\kappa+4\varepsilon)}+2\varepsilon}, \end{equation} as required.

nodes.name: Quantitative divergence Borel-Cantelli lemma
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\ca{B},\mu)$ be a probability space, let $(f_n(x))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of non-negative $\mu$-measurable functions defined on $X$, and let $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N} },\ (\phi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be sequences of real numbers such that \[ 0\leqslant f_n \leqslant \phi_n \qquad (n \in \mathbb N). \] Write $$ \Phi(N)= \sum \limits_{n=1}^{N}\phi_n, $$ and suppose that $\Phi(N) \to \infty$ as $N \to \infty$. Suppose that, for arbitrary $a,b \in \mathbb{N}$ with $a < b$, we have \begin{equation} \int_{X} \left(\sum_{n=a}^{b} \big( f_n(x) - f_n \big) \right)^2\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\, \leqslant\, C\!\sum_{n=a}^{b}\phi_n \end{equation} \noindent for an absolute constant $C>0$. Then, for any $\varepsilon>0$, we have \begin{equation} \sum_{n=1}^N f_n(x)\, =\, \sum_{n=1}^{N}f_n\, +\, O\left(\Phi(N)^{\frac12}(\log(2+\Phi(N)))^{\frac{3}{2}+\varepsilon}+\max_{1\leqslant k\leqslant N}f_k\right) \end{equation} for $\mu$-almost all $x\in X$.
nodes.statement_short: A variance bound on sums of $f_n$ yields an almost sure asymptotic count with error $\Phi^{1/2}(\log\Phi)^{3/2+\varepsilon}$.
assumptions: $(X,\ca{B},\mu)$ be a probability space, let $(f_n(x))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of non-negative $\mu$-measurable functions defined on $X$

for arbitrary $a,b \in \mathbb{N}$ with $a < b$, we have \begin{equation} \label{ebc_condition1} \int_{X} \left(\sum_{n=a}^{b} \big( f_n(x) - f_n \big) \right)^2\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\, \leqslant\, C\!\sum_{n=a}^{b}\phi_n \end{equation}
conclusions: for any $\varepsilon>0$, we have \begin{equation} \label{ebc_conclusion} \sum_{n=1}^N f_n(x)\, =\, \sum_{n=1}^{N}f_n\, +\, O\left(\Phi(N)^{\frac12}(\log(2+\Phi(N)))^{\frac{3}{2}+\varepsilon}+\max_{1\leqslant k\leqslant N}f_k\right) \end{equation} for $\mu$-almost all $x\in X$.
